### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Secondary Harmonizations

Modern concordist writers advance four primary arguments to maintain the thesis of scientific prescience in [Quran 39:21](quran://39/21). Each argument diverges from historical, lexical, and textual evidence:

* **Harmonization 1: The Premise of Pre-Modern Hydrological Ignorance:**
  * Modern writers echo Maurice Bucaille's assertion that prior to Bernard Palissy in AD 1580, pre-modern thinkers universally believed that subterranean springs were forced up from Tartarus by ocean pressure.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* This premise is inconsistent with the historical record. While Plato described Tartarus as an allegory in the *Phaedo* (111c–112e), Plato's view was rejected by Aristotle (*Meteorologica* I.13), Theophrastus (*De Ventis*), Epicurus, Lucretius (*De Rerum Natura* VI), Seneca (*Naturales Quaestiones* III), and Vitruvius (*De Architectura* VIII.1–2). Vitruvius explicitly detailed the precipitation-infiltration model of springs in the 1st century BC—sixteen centuries before Palissy. The Quranic observation that rain enters the ground to form springs reflected standard knowledge in antiquity rather than an unprecedented empirical discovery.
* **Harmonization 2: Attempting to Supply Evaporation via Quran 15:22 (`Lawāqiḥ`):**
  * To compensate for the absence of oceanic evaporation in [Quran 39:21](quran://39/21), concordist commentators frequently cite [Quran 15:22](quran://15/22) (*"And We have sent the fertilizing winds [al-riyāḥa lawāqiḥa], and have sent down water from the sky..."*), proposing that *lawāqiḥ* describes cloud condensation nuclei, electrostatic coalescence, or vapor transport.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* Classical Arabic lexicons (*Lisān al-ʿArab*, *Tāj al-ʿArūs*) and classical commentaries ([Tafsir al-Tabari 15:22](tabari://15/22), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 15:22](ibnkathir://15/22)) do not support this interpretation. In Arabic, *lawāqiḥ* is the feminine plural of *lāqiḥ* (pregnant) or *mulqiḥ* (fecundating). Classical exegetes record two literal 7th-century meanings:
    1. *Pregnant Rain-Bearing Winds:* Winds laden with heavy rain clouds, compared by Bedouin nomads to pregnant female camels carrying their fetuses (*li-annahā talqaḥu bi-l-māʾ*). Both [Tafsir al-Tabari 15:22](tabari://15/22) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 15:22](ibnkathir://15/22) transmit the explicit explanation of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd: *"God sends the wind, which carries water from the sky, and then impregnates the clouds until they pour forth rain just as the pregnant camel gives milk"* (`kamā tudirru al-laqḥah`). In this exegetical tradition as well, the water is described as being carried *from the sky* (`mina al-samāʾ`), rather than evaporated from the oceans.
    2. *Pollinating Plant Winds:* Winds that cross-pollinate flowering trees and date palms (*talqīḥ al-ashjār*).
    Neither meaning addresses microscopic cloud condensation nuclei or the evaporation of water vapor from the oceans. Citing [Quran 15:22](quran://15/22) does not supply the missing mechanism of oceanic evaporation.
* **Harmonization 3: Appealing to Quran 86:11 (`Wa-l-Samāʾi Dhāti al-Rajʿ`) as Evidence of Evaporation and Return:**
  * Some modern concordists argue that the missing upward evaporation phase of the hydrological cycle is supplied by [Quran 86:11](quran://86/11) (*"By the sky of return"*, `وَالسَّمَاءِ ذَاتِ الرَّجْعِ`), proposing that *al-rajʿ* means the sky "returns" water that previously evaporated upward from the earth's oceans.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* Both classical Arabic lexicography (*Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, *Lisān al-ʿArab*) and early Islamic exegesis ([Tafsir al-Tabari 86:11](tabari://86/11), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 86:11](ibnkathir://86/11)) diverge from this modern reinterpretation. In pre-Islamic and classical Arabic, *al-rajʿ* is a standard noun for **rain itself**, so named because seasonal rain clouds return repeatedly time after time and year after year (`tarjiʿu bi-l-maṭari fī kulli ʿām`). In [Tafsir al-Tabari 86:11](tabari://86/11) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 86:11](ibnkathir://86/11), Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, Mujāhid, and al-Ṭabarī unanimously explain *dhāti al-rajʿ* as: *"The sky brings rain, then returns with rain again year after year"* (or returns with the yearly livelihood of servants, `tarjiʿu bi-rizqi al-ʿibādi kulla ʿām`). Early exegetical authorities did not interpret *al-rajʿ* as oceanic evaporation ascending from the sea.
* **Harmonization 4: The Agricultural Parable of Worldly Transience:**
  * Concordist writers isolate the hydrological phrase in [Quran 39:21](quran://39/21) while setting aside the remainder of the verse, which continues: *"...then by means of it He brings forth crops of various colors, then they wither, and you see them turning yellow, then He makes them broken debris. Surely in that is a reminder indeed to those with understanding."*
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* The literary context establishes that the verse is not a technical treatise on hydrogeology, but a homily on human mortality and divine resurrection. The cycle of rain producing green plants that soon turn yellow and crumble into brittle chaff is an ancient Near Eastern homiletic motif that parallels biblical and intertestamental wisdom literature:
    * **[Isaiah 40:6](bible://is/40/6)–[Isaiah 40:8](bible://is/40/8):** *"All flesh is grass, and all its loveliness is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, when the breath of the Lord blows upon it... but the word of our God stands forever."*
    * **[Psalm 90:5](bible://ps/90/5)–[Psalm 90:6](bible://ps/90/6):** *"In the morning they are like grass which sprouts anew. In the morning it flourishes and sprouts anew; toward evening it fades and withers away."*
    * **[James 1:11](bible://jm/1/11):** *"For the sun rises with scorching heat and withers the grass; and its flower falls off and the beauty of its appearance is destroyed; so too the rich man in the midst of his pursuits will fade away."*

In summary, [Quran 39:21](quran://39/21) articulates an empirical, naked-eye observation common to desert and agrarian societies throughout the Near East: seasonal rain falls from the sky, replenishes subterranean springs, and temporarily greens the landscape before the crops dry into yellow chaff. Rather than formulating a modern thermodynamic water cycle, the verse omits the unobservable upward phase—oceanic evaporation—while the downward infiltration of rain into mountain springs had already been documented in detail by Greek and Roman naturalists centuries before the Islamic era.

23:14.claim: Proponents of scientific concordism propose that Quran 23:12–14 accurately anticipates modern embryological stages of human development: a drop of semen (nuṭfah), a clinging clot or leech (ʿalaqah), a chewed lump of flesh (muḍghah), followed by the formation of bones and subsequent clothing of those bones with flesh.
23:14.classification_explanation: Modern concordist writers isolate the embryological sequence in [Quran 23:12](quran://23/12)–[23:14](quran://23/14) and interpret it as an anticipation of modern developmental biology, abstracting the text from the prevailing Greek and Syriac medical paradigm of Late Antiquity. Historically, the specific four-stage progression—from seminal fluid to a blood coagulum, a flesh-like mass, and finally bones that are subsequently wrapped in flesh—was articulated centuries earlier by Galen of Pergamon (*De Semine* I.8–10; *De Usu Partium* XI.18) and taught across Near Eastern medical centers such as the Academy of Gundeshapur. Furthermore, canonical Islamic exegesis ([Tafsir al-Tabari 23:13](tabari://23/13); [Tafsir al-Tabari 23:14](tabari://23/14); [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 23:14](ibnkathir://23/14)) and canonical traditions ([Sahih al-Bukhari 3208](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3208); [Sahih Muslim 2643a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2643a)) demonstrate that early commentators understood these stages as literal 40-day increments of seminal fluid, a piece or clot of blood (*al-qiṭʿatu min al-dam* / *dam jāmid*), and chewed meat, a model that diverges from empirical embryological development.
23:14.summary: In classical Arabic lexicons, early tafsirs, and hadith, Quran 23:12–14 describes a drop of semen (*nuṭfah*) becoming a congealed blood clot (*ʿalaqah*) for 40 days, then a lump of flesh (*muḍghah*) for 40 days, before forming into bones (*ʿiẓām*) that are later clothed with flesh (*laḥm*). In modern embryology, however, an embryo is never a blood clot, and organ development finishes within 56 days rather than 120. Moreover, bones do not form before muscle: muscle tissue and soft cartilage templates develop simultaneously, and muscles form around cartilage before it hardens into bone. Rather than anticipating modern biology, this four-stage sequence mirrors the pre-Islamic medical model taught by the 2nd-century AD physician Galen across the Near East, as detailed in the primary sources below.
23:14.refutation:
Empirical developmental biology, classical Arabic philology, and Late Antique medical history demonstrate that the embryological description in [Quran 23:12](quran://23/12)–[23:14](quran://23/14) does not anticipate modern embryology. Instead, the Quranic sequence reflects the standard Mediterranean and Near Eastern embryological paradigm formulated by Claudius Galen in the 2nd century AD, which circulated throughout pre-Islamic Arabia. Empirically, human development does not proceed through an isolated congealed blood-clot stage, nor does the skeleton develop as a standalone rigid frame that is subsequently "clothed" with flesh; rather, muscles and cartilage templates differentiate concurrently from paraxial and lateral plate mesoderm, and functional muscle tissue differentiates before primary endochondral ossification into true bone begins.

---

### 1. Context of the Claim, Keith L. Moore, & Classical Arabic Philology

The modern thesis that the Quran contains advanced embryological descriptions traces back to Maurice Bucaille (*La Bible, le Coran et la Science*, AD 1976) and gained institutional prominence during the early 1980s through Sheikh Abdul Majeed al-Zindani, founder of the Commission on Scientific Signs in the Quran and Sunnah in Saudi Arabia. Between AD 1982 and AD 1986, al-Zindani invited several Western anatomists to conferences in Jeddah, Cairo, and Riyadh. Among them were Keith L. Moore (Professor of Anatomy and Associate Dean at the University of Toronto), E. Marshall Johnson (Professor of Anatomy at Thomas Jefferson University, Philadelphia), Joe Leigh Simpson (Professor of Obstetrics and Gynecology at Northwestern University), Gerald C. Goeringer (Associate Professor of Medical Embryology at Georgetown University), and T. V. N. Persaud (Professor of Anatomy at the University of Manitoba).

Moore agreed to publish a customized edition of his textbook, *The Developing Human: Clinically Oriented Embryology with Islamic Additions* (Dar al-Qiblah, AD 1983; co-authored with al-Zindani), which interspersed Quranic verses and hadith reports alongside standard embryological chapters. However, the involvement of these Western academics was accompanied by qualifications that are relevant to evaluating the historical record:
1. **Omission from Mainstream Medical Literature:** Moore did not incorporate these Islamic additions into standard international editions of *The Developing Human*, which remain secular medical textbooks (now in their 11th edition, published by Elsevier).
2. **Context of the Testimonials:** In an AD 2002 report by journalist Daniel Golden in *The Wall Street Journal* ("Strange Bedfellows: Western Scholars Play Key Role in Touting 'Science' of the Quran"), these academics clarified the context of their statements. Johnson, Simpson, and Goeringer explained that their remarks at symposia were selectively excerpted and presented out of context. Johnson noted that his statements were responses to hypothetical scenarios posed by the commission, while Gerald C. Goeringer stated that the commission did not engage with the documented pre-Islamic Greek, Hippocratic, and Aristotelian medical origins of these embryological descriptions. Moore declined to reaffirm his earlier statements, noting that nearly twenty years had elapsed and that his commentary had been formulated within a specific institutional setting.

#### Classical Arabic Lexicography of Quran 23:12–14

A philological examination of the key technical terms in [Quran 23:12](quran://23/12)–[23:14](quran://23/14) using authoritative classical Arabic lexicons—including al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad's *Kitāb al-ʿAyn* (8th century AD), Ibn Fāris's *Muʿjam Maqāyīs al-Lughah* (10th century AD), Ibn Manẓūr's *Lisān al-ʿArab* (13th century AD), al-Zabīdī's *Tāj al-ʿArūs* (18th century AD), and Edward William Lane's *Arabic-English Lexicon* (AD 1863)—establishes the macroscopic physical meanings understood by 7th-century Arabic speakers:

* ***Nuṭfah* (نطفة):** Derived from the root *n-ṭ-f*, meaning a dribble, trickle, or drop of fluid. In reproductive contexts across pre-Islamic poetry and the Quran itself (e.g., [Quran 75:37](quran://75/37): *nuṭfatan min maniyyin yumnā*, "a drop of ejaculated semen"), *nuṭfah* refers specifically to the male seminal emission deposited in the female womb ([Quran 23:13](quran://23/13)).
* ***ʿAlaqah* (علقة):** The singular noun of *ʿalaq*. In classical Arabic dictionaries and early medical glossaries, the primary biological definition is a **thick, clotted, or congealed piece of blood** (*dam jāmid* or *dam ʿabīṭ*). Classical lexicographers record: *al-ʿalaqah: al-damu al-jāmidu qabla an yaybas* ("congealed blood before it dries"). While the verbal root *ʿ-l-q* conveys adhesion or suspension (from which the aquatic blood-sucking leech also derives its name because it clings to flesh to draw blood), when applied to gestation in pre-Islamic and early Islamic literature, *ʿalaqah* designated a coagulated blood clot.
* ***Muḍghah* (مضغة):** Derived from the verb *maḍagha* ("to chew"). Lexically, it signifies a small morsel or piece of meat proportionate to what can be chewed in a single mouthful (*qiṭʿat laḥm qadr mā yumḍagh*). In classical usage—such as the prophetic tradition in [Sahih al-Bukhari 52](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:52) regarding the heart: *"Verily, in the body there is a piece of flesh (muḍghah)..."*—it describes a bite-sized, unarticulated lump of flesh, rather than an object defined by tooth indentations.
* ***Fa-khalaqnā al-muḍghata ʿiẓāman fa-kasawnā al-ʿiẓāma laḥmā* (فَخَلَقْنَا الْمُضْغَةَ عِظَامًا فَكَسَوْنَا الْعِظَامَ لَحْمًا):** In classical Arabic grammar (*naḥw*), the conjunction particle ***fa-*** denotes *al-tartīb wa-l-taʿqīb maʿa al-ittiṣāl* (immediate sequential order and direct consequence). It indicates that each developmental state succeeds the previous one in chronological order: the lump is formed into bones (*ʿiẓām*), and *subsequently* the bones are clothed with flesh (*laḥm*).

### 2. Empirical Embryological Analysis & Comparison Table

Modern developmental biology, codified in the internationally standardized **Carnegie Stages of Human Embryonic Development**, diverges from the physical sequence described in [Quran 23:14](quran://23/14) and elaborated in canonical ḥadīth:

| Developmental Stage / Feature | Modern Human Embryology (Carnegie Stages) | Quranic & Classical Islamic Model ([Quran 23:14](quran://23/14)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Fertilization & the Ovum** | Fertilization of a female oocyte by a single spermatozoon in the fallopian tube (Carnegie Stage 1) produces a unicellular diploid zygote. | Conception is initiated by a drop of semen (*nuṭfah*) placed into the uterus as a "secure dwelling place" ([Quran 23:13](quran://23/13)), without mention of the mammalian ovum. |
| **The "Blood Clot" Stage (*ʿAlaqah*)** | The pre-embryo implants as a blastocyst (Carnegie Stage 5, days 7–12) and forms bilaminar and trilaminar embryonic discs; at no stage is the conceptus composed of congealed blood. | The embryo develops into a congealed red blood clot (*dam jāmid*) that persists inside the uterus for a 40-day interval ([Sahih al-Bukhari 3208](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3208)). |
| **Gestation Timeline of Organogenesis** | Complete organogenesis occurs within the first **8 weeks (56 days)** (Carnegie Stages 1–23); by day 56, all major internal organs, digits, eyes, and neural structures are present. | The canonical ḥadīth timeline ([Sahih al-Bukhari 3208](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3208); [Sahih Muslim 2643a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2643a)) assigns 40 days as a drop, 40 days as a clot, and 40 days as a lump (**120 days / 17 weeks**) before bone formation and ensoulment. |
| **Tissue Differentiation vs. Transformation** | Concurrent tri-dermic differentiation during gastrulation (Carnegie Stages 7–8, week 3): ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm develop simultaneously into organ systems. | Sequential transformation: the drop becomes a clot, the clot becomes a lump of flesh, the lump transforms into bones, and the bones are subsequently wrapped in flesh. |
| **Myogenesis vs. Osteogenesis (Muscle vs. Bone)** | Mesenchymal chondroblasts (cartilage models) and somitic myoblasts (skeletal muscle) condense **simultaneously** around week 5–6; muscle fibers differentiate **before** primary endochondral ossification begins at weeks 7–8. | Bones (*ʿiẓām*) are created first as an internal structural framework, and subsequently clothed (*kasawnā*) with flesh (*laḥm*). |

#### Detailed Anatomical Breakdown of Muscle and Bone Development

Standard embryological reference works—such as Gary C. Schoenwolf et al., *Larsen's Human Embryology* (5th ed., Churchill Livingstone, Chs. 8 & 16), Bruce M. Carlson, *Human Embryology and Developmental Biology* (6th ed., Elsevier, Ch. 9), and Scott F. Gilbert, *Developmental Biology* (11th ed., Sinauer Associates)—establish the following empirical sequence for human musculoskeletal development:

1. **Simultaneous Mesodermal Condensation:** During the 5th week of human embryonic development (Carnegie Stages 13–15), paraxial mesoderm segments into somites. Each somite differentiates into a ventromedial **sclerotome** and a dorsolateral **dermomyotome**. Cells from the sclerotome migrate to surround the neural tube and notochord, condensing to form the future axial skeleton, while cells from the dermomyotome delaminate to form migratory **myoblasts** (skeletal muscle precursors). In the developing limb buds, lateral plate somatic mesoderm condenses to form skeletal templates, while somitic hypaxial myoblasts migrate simultaneously into the limb bud to form anterior and posterior muscle masses. Both tissue lineages develop concurrently within the same mesenchymal field.
2. **Hyaline Cartilage Templates Precede True Bone:** The skeletal structures of the limbs and trunk do not appear initially as mineralized bones (*ʿiẓām*). Instead, condensed mesenchymal cells differentiate into chondrocytes that secrete an extracellular matrix to form temporary **hyaline cartilage models**. These unossified cartilage templates are soft, flexible, and radiolucent.
3. **Myogenesis Differentiates Before Endochondral Ossification:** During the 6th and 7th weeks (Carnegie Stages 16–18), premuscle myoblasts aggregate, elongate, and fuse into multinucleated **myotubes**, initiating the synthesis of myofibrillar contractile proteins (actin and myosin) and becoming innervated by motor axon growth cones from the spinal cord. This functional differentiation of skeletal muscle occurs around the unossified cartilage models.
4. **Late Primary Ossification:** True bone (*ʿiẓām*) begins to form at the end of the embryonic period and the beginning of the fetal period—around the 8th week (Carnegie Stage 23)—through the process of **primary endochondral ossification**. Blood vessels penetrate the perichondrium (which becomes periosteum), and osteoblasts replace calcified chondrocytes with bone matrix within the primary ossification centers of the diaphysis (shaft) of long bones (such as the femur and humerus). The majority of the human skeleton remains unossified cartilage throughout embryonic life, with secondary epiphyseal ossification centers forming postnatally and continuing through adolescence.
5. **Histological Summary:** Muscle tissue does not wrap or "clothe" a pre-existing bony skeleton. Rather, muscle tissue differentiates concurrently with and surrounds **unossified cartilage**, prior to the synthesis of the hard osseous tissue termed *ʿiẓām* in Arabic. Describing an embryo as a framework of bones that is subsequently clothed with flesh reverses the histological sequence.

### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (*Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī* & *Ibn Kathīr*) and Canonical Ḥadīth

Classical Islamic scholarship indicates that early commentators understood [Quran 23:14](quran://23/14) not as an allusion to microscopic cellular stages, but as sequential transformations of macroscopic substances governed by a 120-day timeline:

#### Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī (d. 310 AH / AD 923)

In his commentary on [Quran 23:14](quran://23/14) ([Tafsir al-Tabari 23:13](tabari://23/13); [Tafsir al-Tabari 23:14](tabari://23/14); cf. [Tafsir al-Tabari 22:5](tabari://22/5)), Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī compiles early exegetical reports from the Companions and Successors (*al-Salaf*):
* **Ibn Masʿūd's Recitation:** Al-Ṭabarī records that ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd recited the clause as: *thumma khalaqnā al-muḍghata ʿaẓman wa-ʿaṣaban fa-kasawnāhu laḥmā* ("then We made the chewed lump a bone and nerves, so We clothed it with flesh"), indicating that classical authorities understood the phrase as describing an internal skeletal-nervous core that was subsequently covered with flesh.
* **Definition of ʿAlaqah:** In [Tafsir al-Tabari 23:13](tabari://23/13) (and [Tafsir al-Tabari 96:2](tabari://96/2)), al-Ṭabarī defines *ʿalaqah* as *al-qiṭʿatu min al-dam* ("a piece of blood") and *muḍghah* as *al-qiṭʿatu min al-laḥm* ("a piece of flesh").
* **Ensoulment as "Another Creation":** Al-Ṭabarī examines *thumma anshaʾnāhu khalqan ākhar* ("then We produced him as another creature"), citing multiple chains from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, al-Shaʿbī, Mujāhid, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk to show that this refers to the breathing of the soul (*nafkh al-rūḥ*) into the physical body after the bones and flesh have been formed.

#### Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr (d. 774 AH / AD 1373)

In his commentary on [Quran 23:14](quran://23/14) ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 23:14](ibnkathir://23/14); cf. [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 22:5](ibnkathir://22/5)), Ismāʿīl ibn Kathīr presents the standard classical synthesis:
* **The Origin of Semen and the Clot:** Ibn Kathīr prefaces the passage by defining the *nuṭfah*: *"which is the water gushing forth that comes from the loins of man, i.e., his back, and the ribs of woman, i.e., the bones of her chest, between the clavicle and the breast"* (referencing [Quran 86:6](quran://86/6)–[86:7](quran://86/7)). He glosses the clot: *"Then it becomes a red clot, like an elongated clot. ʿIkrimah said: 'This is blood.' Then We made the clot into a little lump of flesh, which is like a piece of flesh with no shape or features."*
* **The Spine and Coccyx (ʿAjb al-Dhanab):** Under *fa-khalaqnā al-muḍghata ʿiẓāman*, Ibn Kathīr cites Ibn ʿAbbās: *"This refers to the bone of the spine."* He then cites the canonical hadith of Abū Hurayrah in [Sahih al-Bukhari 4935](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4935) and [Sahih Muslim 2955b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2955b): *«Every part of the son of Adam will decay except the coccyx (ʿajb al-dhanab); from it he was created and from it he will be reconstructed.»* Embryologically, this report reflects pre-modern anatomical traditions: the coccyx is not the primordium of the embryo (that role belongs to the **primitive streak**, which regresses by the 4th week), and rather than serving as the initial center from which the spine develops, the coccygeal vertebrae are the final vertebral segments to ossify in human development (ossifying postnatally and through puberty).
* **Bones Preceding Flesh:** For *fa-khalaqnā al-muḍghata ʿiẓāman*, Ibn Kathīr writes: *"Meaning: We gave it shape, with a head, two arms, and two legs, with its bones, nerves, and veins."* And for *fa-kasawnā al-ʿiẓāma laḥman*, he writes: *"Meaning: We gave it something to cover it, bind it, and strengthen it."*

#### The Canonical 120-Day Hadith Timeline and Classical Exegetical Assessment of 40-Day Compression

Both al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr corroborate this physical sequence with the tradition of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, recorded in [Sahih al-Bukhari 3208](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3208) and [Sahih Muslim 2643a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2643a):

> *"The creation of each one of you is gathered in the womb of his mother for forty days as a drop (nuṭfah), then he becomes a clot of blood (ʿalaqah) for a similar period [40 days], then a morsel of flesh (muḍghah) for a similar period [40 days]. Then Allah sends an angel who is commanded with four words: to write down his provision, his lifespan, his deeds, and whether he will be wretched or blessed. Then the soul is breathed into him..."*

While modern concordist writers propose compressing these three 40-day intervals into a single 40-day period, the primary historical sources preserved in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 23:14](ibnkathir://23/14) preclude this alternative reading through two explicit Companion reports:
1. **ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd's Explicit Clarification (*Tafsīr al-Rāwī*):** In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 23:14](ibnkathir://23/14), Ibn Abī Ḥātim records from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd—the primary narrator of the hadith:
   > *"When the nuṭfah settles in the womb, it spreads to every hair and nail, remaining for forty days, then it descends in the womb and becomes a clot (ʿalaqah)."* (`fa-tamkuthu arbaʿīna yawman thumma tataḥaddaru fī al-raḥimi fa-takūnu ʿalaqah`)
   Because the Companion who narrated the hadith stated that the *nuṭfah* stage alone lasts 40 days before becoming a clot, an interpretation that compresses all three stages into a single 40-day interval is linguistically and exegetically precluded.
2. **ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib's Explicit Four-Month Report:** In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 23:14](ibnkathir://23/14), Ibn Abī Ḥātim records from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib:
   > *"When the nuṭfah completes four months [120 days], an angel is sent to it and breathes the soul into it within the three darknesses. That is the meaning of His saying: {then We brought it forth as another creation}."*
3. **Universal Classical Juridical Consensus:** Across all four Sunni schools of law (*madhāhib*), classical scholars—including al-Nawawī, Ibn al-Qayyim (*al-Tibyān fī Aqsām al-Qurʾān*; *Tuḥfat al-Mawdūd bi-Aḥkām al-Mawlūd*), Ibn Rajab al-Ḥanbalī (*Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam*), and Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī (*Fatḥ al-Bārī* 11/477–481)—affirmed that the hadith denotes three successive 40-day periods totalling **120 days** (four lunar months) prior to ensoulment.

Furthermore, Ibn Kathīr records in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 23:14](ibnkathir://23/14) an account preserved in the *Musnad* of Imam Aḥmad in which a Jewish scholar questions Muhammad regarding embryology:
> *"A Jew passed by the Messenger of Allah and said: 'O Muhammad, from what is man created?' He replied: 'O Jew, he is created from both: from the nuṭfah of the man and from the nuṭfah of the woman. As for the man's nuṭfah, it is thick and from it come the bones and the nerves; as for the woman's nuṭfah, it is thin and from it come the flesh and the blood.' The Jew said: 'This is what those before you used to say.'"*

This tradition indicates that 7th-century Islamic embryology operated within the shared medical and natural-philosophical environment of the Late Antique Near East, paralleling the classical two-seed doctrine.

### 4. Verbatim Pre-Islamic Greek, Syriac, and Talmudic Precedents

Rather than originating independently in 7th-century Arabia, the sequential four-stage embryological progression and the specific doctrine of bones preceding flesh were taught across the Greco-Roman and Near Eastern worlds centuries prior to Islam:

#### 1. Claudius Galen of Pergamon (AD 129 – c. 216)

In his treatise *De Semine* (*On Semen*, Book I, Chs. 8–10; ed. C. G. Kühn, IV.539–547; trans. Phillip De Lacy, *Corpus Medicorum Graecorum* V 3,1, Berlin, AD 1992, pp. 91–101), Galen presents a **Four-Stage Embryological Model**:

1. **Stage 1 (Seminal Fluid = *Nuṭfah*):** In *De Semine* I.8 (Kühn IV.539), Galen describes the initial state where the seed maintains its fluid form (*gonēs echon schesin*), remaining whitish like semen.
2. **Stage 2 (Blood-Filled Coagulum = *ʿAlaqah*):** In *De Semine* I.9 (Kühn IV.540–542), Galen states that when the seed is filled with maternal blood, it solidifies into an unarticulated, bloody, coagulated mass (*sarkōdes gar ēdē kai ou gonōdes esti*), in which the outlines of the heart, liver, and brain cannot yet be distinguished.
3. **Stage 3 (Flesh-Like Mass with Outlines = *Muḍghah*):** In *De Semine* I.9 (Kühn IV.543), Galen defines the third stage where the principal organs become visible in a mass of flesh, comparing it to a rough carving or silhouette of limbs.
4. **Stage 4 (Bones Formed First, Then Clothed with Flesh = *ʿIẓām* -> *Laḥm*):** In *De Semine* I.10 (Kühn IV.546–547) and *De Usu Partium* (*On the Usefulness of the Parts of the Body*, Book XI, Ch. 18; trans. Margaret May, Cornell University Press, AD 1968, p. 537), Galen articulates the concept that nature hardens the bones first to create an internal scaffold, and subsequently covers the bones with flesh:
   > *"All the parts are clearly visible, with the bones having hardened and reached their proper form... Nature produces the bones first, like the keel of a ship or the foundation and framework of a building, and subsequently surrounds and clothes them with flesh, muscles, and sinews to protect them and provide movement."*

The structural correspondence between Galen's four stages and [Quran 23:14](quran://23/14) (*nuṭfah* -> *ʿalaqah* -> *muḍghah* -> *ʿiẓām* -> clothed with *laḥm*) encompasses both the four-stage progression and the sequence of osteogenesis preceding myogenesis.

#### 2. Hippocrates of Kos (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) & Aristotle (384–322 BC)

* **Hippocrates (*On the Nature of the Child* / *De Natura Pueri*, §§ 12–18; trans. I. M. Lonie, *The Hippocratic Treatises*, AD 1981):** Hippocrates states that semen coagulates with maternal blood inside the womb into a clot surrounded by a membrane. He writes that this coagulum solidifies into flesh and that around day 30 to 42, the bones harden and differentiate before the limbs are covered with muscles.
* **Aristotle (*De Generatione Animalium* I.19–20, 728a–729b; II.3–4, 739b):** Aristotle compared fertilization to the action of rennet curdling milk. The male semen acts as an agent that coagulates the female catamenia (menstrual blood) into a solid mass. From this coagulum, the central skeleton and spine solidify first like the framework of a structure, around which soft flesh is subsequently deposited.

#### 3. Biblical and Talmudic Parallels

The motif of human generation proceeding from fluid to a curdled mass, followed by bone formation and clothing with flesh, was also present in Jewish scripture and rabbinic literature prior to the 7th century:

* **[Job 10:10](bible://jb/10/10)–[10:11](bible://jb/10/11):** The book of Job describes embryonic formation using comparable imagery:
  > *"Did You not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese; clothe me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews?"*
  Here the sequence proceeds from poured fluid to curdled coagulum, bone and sinew framework, and clothing with skin and flesh.
* **[Ezekiel 37:6](bible://ez/37/6)–[37:8](bible://ez/37/8):** In the vision of the valley of dry bones, the assembly of the human body follows the same order: bones assemble first, sinews and flesh are placed over the bones, skin covers them, and finally the breath of life (*rūaḥ*) enters them.
* **Babylonian Talmud (*b. Niddah* 25a–b, 30b, 31a):** In tractate *Niddah* 30b, rabbinic authorities discuss embryological status and state that during the first forty days following conception, the conceptus is regarded as fluid (*maya b'alma*, "mere water"), a close parallel to the 40-day *nuṭfah* interval in [Sahih al-Bukhari 3208](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3208). Furthermore, in *b. Niddah* 31a, the Talmud records the same division between parental seeds cited in Ibn Kathīr's commentary: the father contributes the white seed from which bones, sinews, and nails derive, while the mother contributes the red seed from which flesh, skin, and blood derive.

#### 4. Historical Transmission to 7th-Century Arabia via Gundeshapur

Greek and Syriac medical literature was accessible in the pre-Islamic Near East. By the 6th century AD, Galenic treatises had been translated into Syriac by Christian scholars such as Sergius of Reshaina (d. AD 536). The Sasanian intellectual center of **Gundeshapur** in southwestern Iran functioned as a regional academy and teaching hospital where Greek, Syriac, and Persian medical texts were studied.

The Arab physician of the Prophet's generation, **al-Ḥārith ibn Kalada al-Thaqafī** (from al-Ṭāʾif), travelled to Persia and studied medicine at Gundeshapur before returning to practice in the Hijaz. His son, **al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith**—a Meccan contemporary who engaged in public disputations with Muhammad—was likewise familiar with Persian and Greco-Syriac traditions. Pre-Islamic Arab merchants along regional trade routes maintained regular contact with Byzantine and Persian urban centers where Galenic medicine represented the standard medical paradigm.

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Modern Harmonizations

Modern concordist literature proposes several secondary linguistic and morphological harmonizations to align the Quranic sequence with contemporary developmental biology. Each hypothesis can be evaluated against classical Arabic philology, embryonic chronology, and histological data:

#### 1. The "ʿAlaqah Means Leech or Clinging Blastocyst" Hypothesis
Concordist literature argues that *ʿalaqah* should be rendered not as "blood clot", but as a "clinging thing" (referring to the blastocyst implanting in the endometrium) or an "aquatic leech" (proposing that a 24-day embryo visually resembles the external profile of a leech).
* **Histological & Dimensional Analysis:** Blastocyst implantation occurs around days 6–10 (Carnegie Stage 5). At this stage, the blastocyst is a microscopic, spherical vesicle measuring approximately `0.1–0.2 mm` in diameter. It lacks a caudal appendage, a curved dorsal axis, or morphological similarity to a macroscopic annelid.
* **Chronological & Morphological Inconsistency:** The illustration reproduced by Keith Moore to depict a "leech-like" profile shows a 24-to-26-day human embryo (Carnegie Stage 10–11), which is past implantation and possesses between 8 and 12 somites. However, concordist commentators simultaneously identify somites with the subsequent *muḍghah* ("chewed lump") stage. Consequently, citing a somite-stage embryo (days 24–26) to illustrate the preceding *ʿalaqah* phase introduces a chronological overlap between the two proposed stages.
* **Lexicographical and Exegetical Unanimity:** Classical Arabic lexicons (*Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, *Maqāyīs al-Lughah*, *Lisān al-ʿArab*) and early Quranic exegetes ([Tafsir al-Tabari 23:13](tabari://23/13); [Tafsir al-Tabari 23:14](tabari://23/14); [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 23:14](ibnkathir://23/14)) consistently define *ʿalaqah* in gestational contexts as a piece or clot of congealed blood (*al-qiṭʿatu min al-dam* / *dam jāmid*). The aquatic leech (*al-ʿalaq*) derived its Arabic name from clinging to livestock to draw blood, rather than from a morphological comparison with human embryos.

#### 2. The "Muḍghah Means Chewed Lump with Somite Teeth-Marks" Hypothesis
Concordist commentators propose that *muḍghah* ("chewed lump") describes the embryonic somites, comparing their external contour to dental impressions in chewed material.
* **Anatomical Assessment:** Somites are internal, paired blocks of paraxial mesodermal tissue situated beneath the surface ectoderm along either side of the neural tube. They do not form irregular indentations corresponding to a human dental arch.
* **Classical Linguistic Meaning:** In classical Arabic lexicography and prophetic usage ([Sahih al-Bukhari 52](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:52)), *muḍghah* denotes a piece of meat small enough to be chewed in a mouthful (*qiṭʿat laḥm qadr mā yumḍagh*). Spontaneous abortions at 5 to 6 weeks present to the unaided eye as small, unarticulated lumps of fleshy tissue, an observation accessible without optical magnification.

#### 3. The "Fa- Does Not Signify Strict Sequence" or "Bones Means Cartilage" Hypothesis
To address the developmental sequence of bones preceding muscle, concordist commentators suggest either that the conjunction *fa-* does not denote chronological succession, or that the noun *ʿiẓām* ("bones") refers to hyaline cartilage templates.
* **Grammatical Analysis:** In classical Arabic grammar, the particle *fa-* is defined by grammarians (Sībawayh, al-Farrāʾ, Ibn Hishām) as *ḥarf li-l-tartīb wa-l-taʿqīb* (denoting sequential order without interval). The Quran links the clauses with consecutive *fa-* particles: *fa-khalaqnā al-ʿalaqata muḍghatan fa-khalaqnā al-muḍghata ʿiẓāman fa-kasawnā al-ʿiẓāma laḥmā*. Reading these clauses as describing simultaneous processes diverges from standard classical Arabic syntax.
* **Lexical Distinction:** Classical Arabic possesses a distinct anatomical term for cartilage: ***ghuḍrūf*** (غضروف; plural *ghaḍārīf*), regularly employed in classical Arabic medical texts. The Quran uses *ʿiẓām* (عظام), which designates rigid, mineralized osseous tissue.
* **Histological Sequence:** Even under the alternative reading of *ʿiẓām* as "cartilage," empirical embryology diverges from a sequential model: somitic myoblasts and mesenchymal pre-cartilage condensations aggregate **simultaneously in parallel**, and skeletal muscle fibers differentiate and become innervated *around* unossified cartilage models *before* true endochondral bone (*ʿiẓām*) is deposited. At no point in human embryogenesis does an isolated skeletal framework, whether cartilaginous or osseous, form first and await subsequent covering by muscular tissue.

#### 4. The "Single 40-Day / 42-Night Compression" Harmonization
Concordist commentators (including al-Zindani, Keith Moore's *Islamic Additions*, and Hamza Tzortzis, drawing on a late discussion by Kamāl al-Dīn Ibn al-Zamlakānī, d. 727 AH) propose reconciling the hadith timeline with modern embryology by reading the phrase *mithla dhālika* ("likewise") in [Sahih al-Bukhari 3208](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3208) to mean that all three stages (*nuṭfah*, *ʿalaqah*, *muḍghah*) unfold within a *single* 40-day period, citing the variant narration in [Sahih Muslim 2645a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2645a) (*"When forty-two nights have passed over the nutfah, Allah sends an angel to shape it..."*).
* **Primary Narrator Exegesis (*Tafsīr al-Rāwī*):** This compression is precluded by the explicit statement of the primary narrator himself, ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, preserved in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 23:14](ibnkathir://23/14): *"The nutfah remains in the womb for forty days, then descends and becomes a clot."* Ibn Masʿūd explicitly assigns forty full days to the *nuṭfah* phase alone before the clot is formed, which is incompatible with a single 40-day compression.
* **Companion and Legal Consensus:** ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 23:14](ibnkathir://23/14) affirmed that the angel breathes the soul after four full months (120 days), which formed the basis for classical Islamic legal rulings across the four Sunni schools regarding fetal ensoulment at 120 days.
* **Embryological Assessment of the 42-Night Narration:** Under [Sahih Muslim 2645a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2645a), the report states that the conceptus remains a *nuṭfah* (seminal drop) until day 42, when an angel arrives to form its hearing, sight, skin, flesh, and bones. In empirical human development, cleavage begins within 24 hours of fertilization, the primitive heart begins beating around day 22 (Carnegie Stage 10), optic and otic placodes (eyes and ears) appear at days 24–28, and distinct limb paddles and cerebral vesicles are present by day 42 (Carnegie Stage 17). By 42 days, the embryo has already undergone extensive organogenesis rather than remaining an unformed seminal drop.
* **Persistence of the Osteogenesis–Myogenesis Sequence:** Regardless of whether the timeline is read as 42 days or 120 days, the sequential statement that bones (*ʿiẓām*) are formed first and subsequently covered with flesh (*laḥm*) remains inconsistent with empirical findings, as chondrogenic and myogenic lineages condense simultaneously and functional muscles differentiate prior to endochondral ossification.

#### 5. The "Microscopic Embryo Invisible Without a Microscope" Hypothesis
Concordist writers argue that pre-modern observers could not have described early developmental stages without optical instrumentation because a 4-to-6-week human embryo is assumed to be microscopic.
* **Quantitative Embryonic Dimensions:** In human embryology, by week 4 (28 days; Carnegie Stage 12–13), the embryo measures `4–6 mm` in crown-rump length—approximately the size of a grain of rice or a lentil. By weeks 5–6 (35–42 days; Carnegie Stage 15–17), the embryo measures `8–14 mm` (`0.8–1.4 cm`) and is enclosed within a gestational chorionic sac measuring `20–35 mm` (`2.0–3.5 cm`) in diameter.
* **Macroscopic Visibility in Spontaneous Abortions:** When a miscarriage occurs at 5 to 6 weeks, the expelled gestational sac presents as a macroscopic structure surrounded by dark decidual tissue and clotted maternal blood (*ʿalaqah*), within which a pale, unarticulated fleshy mass (*muḍghah*) of approximately `1 cm` is visible to the unaided human eye without magnification.
* **Documented Ancient Observations:** Classical Greco-Roman and Near Eastern physicians regularly examined spontaneously aborted human conceptuses. In *De Natura Pueri* (§ 13), Hippocrates describes inspecting an aborted 6-day conception, and in §§ 15–18 details the macroscopic inspection of aborted human conceptuses at successive intervals. Aristotle (*Historia Animalium* VII.3, 583b) similarly records macroscopic examinations of aborted conceptuses at 30 and 40 days, noting an entity the size of a large ant or bean surrounded by membranes and blood. Pre-modern pastoralists and herdsmen—who dressed and inspected pregnant livestock across gestation—were likewise familiar with these macroscopic mammalian structures. Describing an early spontaneous abortion as a blood clot or a morsel of flesh aligns with direct macroscopic observation of expelled gestational tissue.

This interpretation abstracts the text from classical Arabic lexicography (*Lisān al-ʿArab*, *Kitāb al-ʿAyn*) and early Islamic exegesis ([Tafsir al-Tabari 22:5](tabari://22/5), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 22:5](ibnkathir://22/5)), which unanimously define *ghayr mukhallaqah* as an unformed miscarried fetus (*al-siqṭ*) rather than cellular tissues, while the developmental sequence directly reflects 2nd-century AD Galenic medicine (*De Semine* I.9) and Late Antique Talmudic legal anatomy (*b.
