### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr)

Early Islamic commentators did not interpret [Quran 51:47](quran://51/47) as describing an ongoing physical increase in the size of the universe. The classical authorities documented in [Tafsir al-Tabari 51:47](tabari://51/47) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 51:47](ibnkathir://51/47) grouped the verse into three distinct, non-expansionist interpretations:

1. **Possession of Boundless Divine Capacity and Power in [Tafsir al-Tabari 51:47](tabari://51/47):**
   In [Tafsir al-Tabari 51:47](tabari://51/47), Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī (d. AD 923) preserves the foundational classical interpretation of this verse. First, for the opening clause `wa-l-samāʾa banaynāhā bi-aydin`, al-Ṭabarī records six authoritative chains (*asānīd*) from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, Manṣūr, Ibn Zayd, and Sufyān al-Thawrī, all of whom unanimously gloss *bi-aydin* as *bi-quwwatin* (*"with strength and power"*). Then, for `wa-innā la-mūsiʿūn`, al-Ṭabarī articulates the primary lexical and grammatical meaning:
   > `وقوله ( وَإِنَّا لَمُوسِعُونَ ) يقول: لذو سعة بخلقها وخلق ما شئنا أن نخلقه وقدرة عليه. ومنه قوله عَلَى الْمُوسِعِ قَدَرُهُ وَعَلَى الْمُقْتِرِ قَدَرُهُ [البقرة: 236] يراد به القويّ`
   > (*"Regarding His statement: {and indeed, We are mūsiʿūn}, He says: Indeed, We are possessors of vast capacity (`la-dhū saʿatin`) in creating it and creating whatever We wish to create, and having capability (`qudrah`) over it. And from this is His statement: {upon the affluent is his measure, and upon the restricted is his measure} [Quran 2:236], by which the strong, capable one (`al-qawiyy`) is intended."*)
   Following this primary lexical deduction, al-Ṭabarī records a single exegetical narration on `la-mūsiʿūn` from Ibn Zayd via Ibn Wahb:
   > `وقال ابن زيد في ذلك ما حدثني يونس، قال: أخبرنا ابن وهب، قال: قال ابن زيد، في قوله ( وَإِنَّا لَمُوسِعُونَ ) قال: أوسعها جلّ جلاله`
   > (*"And Ibn Zayd said concerning that: 'He made it vast (`awsaʿahā`), may His majesty be exalted.'"*)
   Al-Ṭabarī does not record any concept of dynamic, ongoing cosmological stretching; the verse expresses either God's limitless creative capacity (*la-dhū saʿatin*) or His completed past act of establishing the vast spatial expanse of the sky (*awsaʿahā*).
2. **Abundance of Sustenance via Rain Attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī:**
   A separate classical tradition glosses `la-mūsiʿūn` as the abundance of sustenance through rainfall. While absent from al-Ṭabarī's commentary on this verse, this view is explicitly transmitted from the prominent early Basran authority **al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (d. AD 728)** across major classical commentaries, including **al-Baghawī** (*Maʿālim al-Tanzīl*, 51:47), **al-Māwardī** (*al-Nukat wa-l-ʿUyūn*, 51:47), **Ibn al-Jawzī** (*Zād al-Masīr*, 51:47), and **al-Qurṭubī** (*al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān*, 51:47):
   > *"We made sustenance and provision abundant (`awsaʿnā al-rizqa`) for Our creation by sending down rain (`bi-l-maṭar`) from the sky, and We are possessors of abundance in provision."*
   In this classical understanding, the root *w-s-ʿ* describes divine beneficence in agricultural and ecological sustenance for humankind, independent of cosmic spatial metrics.
3. **Spacious Breadth of the High Architectural Ceiling and Spreading of the Earth:**
   In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 51:47](ibnkathir://51/47) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 51:48](ibnkathir://51/48), Ismāʿīl ibn Kathīr (d. AD 1373) explains the cosmological context of the two complementary realms:
   > *"Allah reminds us of the creation of the higher and lower realms: {And the heaven We constructed with strength}, meaning: We made it a high, preserved ceiling (`jaʿalnāhā saqfan maḥfūẓan rafīʿan`) with strength... {and indeed We are mūsiʿūn}, meaning: We have made its regions spacious (`wassaʿnā arjāʾahā`) and raised it without pillars (`rafaʿnāhā bi-ghayri ʿamad`), until it stood independently as it is."*
   Immediately continuing under [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 51:48](ibnkathir://51/48), Ibn Kathīr provides the exact verbatim commentary on the coupled terrestrial clause:
   > `( وَالأرْضَ فَرَشْنَاهَا ) أي : جعلناها فراشا للمخلوقات ، ( فَنِعْمَ الْمَاهِدُونَ ) أي : وجعلناها مهدا لأهلها`
   > (*"(And the earth We spread it out) meaning: We made it a resting place (`firāshan`) for the created beings, (how excellent are the smoothers) meaning: and We made it a cradle/bed (`mahdan`) for its inhabitants."*)
   This matches the verbatim exposition preserved in [Tafsir al-Tabari 51:48](tabari://51/48):
   > `وقوله ( وَالأرْضَ فَرَشْنَاهَا ) يقول تعالى ذكره: والأرض جعلناها فراشا للخلق ( فَنِعْمَ الْمَاهِدُونَ ) يقول: فنعم الماهدون لهم نحن`
   > (*"Regarding His statement: (And the earth We spread it out), He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: And the earth, We made it a resting place (`firāshan`) for the creation... (how excellent are the smoothers), He says: Excellent were the smoothers for them, We [are]."*)
   Both classical exegetes explicitly treat the roofing of the sky and the flattening of the earth as twin completed architectural stages of creation. The spatial breadth (*wusʿ*) in verse 47 refers to the static distance between the sky's raised borders rather than an ongoing dimensional stretching of astrophysical space-time.
4. **Scholastic Consensus Across Major Commentators:**
   This exegetical consensus is affirmed across the major classical schools of *tafsīr*:
   * **Al-Zamakhsharī (d. AD 1144, *al-Kashshāf*):** Explains *la-mūsiʿūn* as *"possessors of power and capacity"* (`qādirūn`), or that God made a vast spatial gulf between the celestial ceiling and the terrestrial earth.
   * **Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī (d. AD 1210, *Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb*):** Notes that *al-mūsiʿ* is the possessor of *saʿah*, emphasizing that constructing so vast an edifice demonstrates that God's power is inexhaustible and unrestricted by material limitations.
   * **Al-Qurṭubī (d. AD 1273, *al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān*):** Enumerates three classical positions: (1) capability through divine strength, citing [Quran 2:236](quran://2/236); (2) making the distance between heaven and earth vast; and (3) expanding provisions through rain.
   * **Al-Jalālayn (15th century AD):** Concisely glosses the phrase as *"possessing capacity and power"* (`qādirūn`).

Across thirteen centuries of pre-modern commentary, classical exegetes consistently interpreted [Quran 51:47](quran://51/47) in terms of divine capacity, abundant provision, or the static architectural expanse of the firmament, rather than a continuous temporal expansion of the physical universe.

### 4. Pre-Islamic Biblical and Near Eastern Precedents

The imagery in [Quran 51:47](quran://51/47) and [Quran 51:48](quran://51/48) parallels the established poetic cosmology of the ancient Near East and the Hebrew Bible. Throughout ancient Semitic literature, the cosmos is depicted as a two-tiered architectural structure in which God pitches the sky like a tent or canopy and spreads out the earth beneath it like a floor:

* **[Isaiah 40:22](bible://is/40/22):**
  > *"It is He who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers; Who stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them out like a tent to dwell in."*
* **[Isaiah 42:5](bible://is/42/5):**
  > *"Thus says God the Lord, Who created the heavens and stretched them out, Who spread out the earth and its offspring..."*
* **[Isaiah 44:24](bible://is/44/24):**
  > *"I, the Lord, am the maker of all things, stretching out the heavens by Myself and spreading out the earth all alone."*
* **[Job 9:8](bible://jb/9/8):**
  > *"Who alone stretches out the heavens and tramples down the waves of the sea."*
* **[Psalm 104:2](bible://ps/104/2):**
  > *"Covering Yourself with light as with a cloak, stretching out heaven like a tent curtain."*
* **[Zechariah 12:1](bible://zc/12/1):**
  > *"Thus declares the Lord who stretches out the heavens, lays the foundation of the earth, and forms the spirit of man within him."*

#### Grammatical and Literary Parallels

1. **The Hebrew Active Participle (*Nōṭēh Shamayim*):** In [Isaiah 42:5](bible://is/42/5), [Job 9:8](bible://jb/9/8), and [Zechariah 12:1](bible://zc/12/1), the biblical text uses the Hebrew *Qal* active participle *nōṭēh* (`נֹטֶה שָׁמַיִם`, *"stretcher-out of the heavens"*), paired in parallel structure with the spreading out of the earth (*rōqaʿ hā-ʾāreṣ*). As in Arabic, the Semitic active participle functions here as a divine epithet denoting architectural creation of the cosmic canopy.
2. **Comparative Methodological Implications for Concordist Hermeneutics:** Applying a concordist reading to the Arabic active participle *mūsiʿūn* in [Quran 51:47](quran://51/47) as an anticipation of Hubble's expanding universe would, by the same grammatical criterion, require interpreting the cognate Hebrew active participle *nōṭēh shamayim* in [Isaiah 42:5](bible://is/42/5) and [Job 9:8](bible://jb/9/8) as describing metric cosmic expansion more than a millennium earlier. From a historical-philological perspective, both Hebrew and Arabic texts employ the shared idioms of ancient Near Eastern tent-canopy cosmology.
3. **The Immediate Context of [Quran 51:48](quran://51/48):** The pairing in the Quran follows the same structural formula. In [Quran 51:47](quran://51/47), God constructs the roof of the sky; in [Quran 51:48](quran://51/48), God spreads out the floor of the earth: *"And the earth We spread it out, and how excellent are the smoothers."* (`wa-l-arḍa farashnāhā fa-niʿma al-māhidūn`). Reading the active participle in verse 47 as continuous ongoing cosmological expansion would, by parallel syntax, imply in verse 48 that the terrestrial surface is undergoing continuous, ongoing flattening and spreading today.

### 5. Philological & Empirical Analysis of Alternative Harmonizations

Modern concordist literature proposes several grammatical and lexical arguments in support of translating *mūsiʿūn* as ongoing cosmic expansion. Below is a philological and textual evaluation of these readings:

1. **Proposed Harmonization 1: 'The active participle (*ism fāʿil*) within a nominal clause (*jumlah ismiyyah*) reinforced by *lām al-tawkīd* denotes continuous, ongoing progressive expansion (*al-istimrār al-tajaddudī*).'**
   * *Primary-Source & Rhetorical Analysis via ʿIlm al-Maʿānī:* In classical Arabic rhetorical theory (*ʿilm al-maʿānī*, codified by foundational scholars such as ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī in *Dalāʾil al-Iʿjāz* and al-Khaṭīb al-Qazwīnī in *al-Īḍāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Balāghah*), a nominal sentence (*jumlah ismiyyah*) primarily conveys **the constancy, permanence, and inherent stability of an attribute or state (*al-thubūt wa-l-dawām*)**, rather than continuous temporal occurrence or progressive renewal. When reinforced with *inna* and the corroborative *lām* (*lām al-ibtidāʾ / lām al-muzahlaqah*), the clause `wa-innā la-mūsiʿūn` grammatically serves to affirm God's **permanent, inherent attribute of boundless power and plenitude (*dhū saʿah*)** or the **established, enduring vastness of the constructed sky**. By contrast, to denote active, continuous, progressive physical expansion occurring across time (*al-tajaddud wa-l-ḥudūth*), classical Arabic syntax and rhetoric employ an **imperfect verbal sentence (*al-fiʿl al-muḍāriʿ*)**, such as `nuwassiʿuhā` (`نُوَّسِّعُهَا`, *"We are continuously expanding it"*), or a temporal verbal circumlocution. Interpreting the nominal sentence structure as progressive Hubble expansion inverts this distinction in classical Arabic rhetoric between timeless ontological capability (*al-thubūt*) and dynamic temporal change (*al-tajaddud*).
   * *Syntactic Parallel with [Quran 51:48](quran://51/48):* Moreover, within the immediate cotext, the coupled verse [Quran 51:48](quran://51/48) reads: `wa-l-arḍa farashnāhā fa-niʿma al-māhidūn` (*"And the earth We spread it out, and how excellent are the spreaders."*). There, `al-māhidūn` is an identical plural active participle (*ism fāʿil* from *mahada*), which classical commentators and modern linguists uniformly understand as referring to the completed cosmological act of laying down the earth (`farashnāhā`), rather than indicating that the surface area of the earth is continuously flattening and expanding today. Interpreting *mūsiʿūn* in verse 47 as dynamic, time-bound progressive expansion (*tajaddud*) while reading *māhidūn* in verse 48 as an established static outcome (*thubūt*) introduces a grammatical inconsistency between two adjacent parallel clauses.
2. **Proposed Harmonization 2: 'The term *al-samāʾ* refers to relativistic outer space rather than a structural ceiling.'**
   * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* Within the Quranic corpus, *al-samāʾ* is consistently described using the terminology of an architectural roof. [Quran 51:47](quran://51/47) itself employs the verb of building and masonry, *banaynāhā* (`بَنَيْنَاهَا`, *"We built it"*), which [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 51:47](ibnkathir://51/47) glosses as *jaʿalnāhā saqfan maḥfūẓan rafīʿan* (*"We made it a high, protected ceiling"*). This structural canopy model appears across multiple Quranic passages:
     * In [Quran 21:32](quran://21/32), the sky is described as *saqfan maḥfūẓan* (*"a protected ceiling/roof"*).
     * In [Quran 22:65](quran://22/65), God prevents this ceiling from falling onto the earth: *"and He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission."*
     * In [Quran 50:6](quran://50/6), observers are invited to inspect the sky above them to see that it contains no structural fractures or fissures: *"Have they not looked at the heaven above them, how We built it and adorned it and how it has no rifts?"*
   A structural canopy described as being held aloft without pillars and prevented from falling or cracking reflects the observational framework of ancient architectural cosmology rather than the relativistic model of unbounded, metric space-time.

### 1. Context of the Claim & Origin of the Speed-of-Light Formula (Mansour Hassab-Elnaby, AD 1990)

The assertion that [Quran 32:5](quran://32/5) calculates the speed of light originated in AD 1990 with Egyptian physicist Dr. Mansour Hassab-Elnaby (*"A New Astronomical Quranic Method for the Determination of the Greatest Speed C"*, 8th Islamic Medical Conference, Cairo), later popularized globally by writers such as Zaghloul El-Naggar and Adnan Oktar (Harun Yahya).

The concordist argument rests on [Quran 32:5](quran://32/5):

> *"He directs the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it will ascend to Him in a Day, the measure of which is a thousand years of those which you count."* (`yudabbiru al-amra mina al-samāʾi ilā al-arḍi thumma yaʿruju ilayhi fī yawmin kāna miqdāruhu alfa sanatin mimmā taʿuddūn`)

Hassab-Elnaby formulated his calculation through several interpretive steps:
* **Equating "Affair" with Light & Transit with Lunar Orbits:** Proponents assume *al-amr* ("the affair/decree") designates physical light traveling at speed $c$, asserting that the distance covered by light in one terrestrial day ($c \cdot t$) equals the distance traversed by the Moon in 1,000 lunar years ($12,000$ lunar orbits, $12,000 \cdot L$).
* **Selecting Modern Sidereal Constants:** Selecting an Earth sidereal day ($t = 86,164.0906\text{ s}$) and Moon sidereal month ($T = 27.321661\text{ days} = 655.719864\text{ h}$), he set $c \cdot t = 12,000 \cdot L$, where $L = v \cdot T$.
* **The Raw Calculation Discrepancy:** With the Moon's mean orbital radius ($R = 384,264\text{ km}$), dividing 12,000 orbits by one sidereal day produces $v_{\text{raw}} = \frac{12,000 \times 2\pi R}{t} \approx 336,247\text{ km/s}$—exceeding $c$ ($299,792.458\text{ km/s}$) by over $36,450\text{ km/s}$ (~12% discrepancy; exceeding 18% with synodic parameters).
* **The Post-Hoc Cosine Adjustment:** To eliminate this discrepancy, Hassab-Elnaby calculated the angle traversed by the Earth around the Sun during one sidereal month ($\alpha = \frac{27.321661}{365.25636} \times 360^\circ = 26.92848^\circ$) and multiplied orbital velocity by $\cos(26.92848^\circ) = 0.89157$:
  $$c = 336,247\text{ km/s} \times 0.89157 = 299,792.5\text{ km/s}$$
This algebraic adjustment yields a numerical value matching modern laboratory definitions, which concordist authors present as a scientific anticipation.

1. **The Unphysical $\cos\alpha$ Projection Factor:** Orbital path length is a scalar line integral ($S = \int |\vec{v}| dt$). Multiplying scalar orbital speed by the cosine of Earth's monthly heliocentric arc represents an arbitrary vector projection onto a static line that disregards Earth's continuous orbital curvature. Hassab-Elnaby introduced $\cos(26.92848^\circ) = 0.89157$ because the raw calculation ($336,247\text{ km/s}$) exceeded $c$ ($299,792.5\text{ km/s}$) by $10.84\%$, and $\frac{299,792.5}{336,247} \approx 0.89158 = \cos(26.93^\circ)$—a retrospective numerical adjustment.

Recalculating with historical synodic reckoning removes the numerical correspondence with $c$.

If celestial transit in [Quran 32:5](quran://32/5) defines velocity $v = d/t = c$, applying the same formula to [Quran 70:4](quran://70/4) yields $v = 50 \times c \approx 14,989,623\text{ km/s}$—exceeding the relativistic invariant speed limit $c$.

### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr)

Early Muslim commentators did not interpret [Quran 32:5](quran://32/5) as an astronomical calculation or the speed of light. Both [Tafsir al-Tabari 32:5](tabari://32/5) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 32:5](ibnkathir://32/5) record the authoritative exegesis of the early Muslim community, citing Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and ʿIkrimah:

* **The 500-Year Distance Between Earth and Heaven (Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Kathīr):** In early Islamic cosmology, the distance between the flat earth and the lowest celestial sphere (*al-samāʾ al-dunyā*) was conceived as a journey of 500 years for a human traveler on foot or camel (*masīrat khamsimiʾat ʿām*). The angel carrying God's decree descends in 500 years of travel time and ascends in 500 years of travel time, completing a round trip equal to **1,000 years of human caravan travel in a single earthly day ($500 + 500 = 1,000\text{ years}$)**.
  * In [Tafsir al-Tabari 32:5](tabari://32/5), Imam Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī endorses this as the primary interpretation: *"Its meaning is: He directs the affair from the sky to the earth, then it will go up to Him in a day the measure of which day—in the ascent of that affair to Him, and its descent to the earth—was a thousand years of what you count of your days: five hundred for the descent, and five hundred for the ascent; because that is the most apparent of its meanings."*
  * In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 32:5](ibnkathir://32/5), Ibn Kathīr confirms: *"The distance between it and the earth is a journey of five hundred years, and the thickness of the heaven is five hundred years. Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ad-Dahhak said: 'The descent of the angel is a journey of five hundred years, and his ascent is a journey of five hundred years, but he traverses it in the blink of an eye; for this reason, Allah the Exalted said: in a day, the measure of which is a thousand years of what you count.'"*
  * This 500-year cosmic yardstick is corroborated in canonical Sunni hadith literature (*Sunan Abī Dāwūd* 4723; *Sunan al-Tirmidhī* 3298; *Musnad Aḥmad* 1770), where Muhammad states: *"Between heaven and earth is a journey of five hundred years, and from each heaven to the next is a journey of five hundred years..."*
* **Mathematical Velocity Implication:** If an ancient traveler covered $\sim 40\text{ km/day}$, a 1,000-year journey equals $\approx 1.46 \times 10^7\text{ km}$. Traversing this distance in one day (86,400 s) yields an average velocity of:
  $$v = \frac{1.46 \times 10^7\text{ km}}{86,400\text{ s}} \approx 169\text{ km/s}$$
  This speed is approximately **1,770 times slower than the speed of light** ($c \approx 300,000\text{ km/s}$).
* **The Theological Day of Judgment View:** The alternate classical view preserved by al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr (from Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrimah) explains that "a day measuring a thousand years" refers to the Day of Judgment or the six days of creation ([Quran 32:4](quran://32/4); [Tafsir al-Tabari 22:47](tabari://22/47); [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 70:4](ibnkathir://70/4)). Under neither classical view is there any notion of physical electromagnetic radiation or lunar orbits.

---

### 4. Verbatim Pre-Islamic Biblical, Apocryphal, and Rabbinic Precedents

The formula *"a day with the Lord is a thousand years"* and the *"500-year cosmic distance between earth and heaven"* were directly inherited from pre-Islamic Judeo-Christian scriptures and Late Antique rabbinic traditions:

1. **The Hebrew Bible: [Psalm 90:4](bible://ps/90/4) (c. 6th–5th Century BC):**
   > *"For a thousand years in Your sight are like yesterday when it passes by, or as a watch in the night."*
   > (Hebrew: כִּ֤י אֶ֪לֶף שָׁנִ֡ים בְּֽעֵינֶ֗יךָ כְּי֣וֹם אֶ֭תְמוֹל כִּ֣י יַעֲבֹ֑ר, *Kī ʾelep̄ šānīm bə-ʿêneyḵā kə-yōm ʾeṯmōl kī yaʿăḇōr*)
   This psalm provided the foundational Near Eastern theological comparison between human mortality and divine eternity.
2. **The New Testament: [2 Peter 3:8](bible://2pt/3/8) (c. 1st Century AD):**
   > *"But do not let this one fact escape your notice, beloved, that with the Lord one day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day."*
   > (Greek: ἓν δὲ τοῦτο μὴ λανθανέτω ὑμᾶς, ἀγαπητοί, ὅτι μία ἡμέρα παρὰ Κυρίῳ ὡς χίλια ἔτη, καὶ χίλια ἔτη ὡς ἡμέρα μία)
   The Arabic text of [Quran 22:47](quran://22/47) (*yawman ʿinda rabbika ka-alfi sanatin*) and [Quran 32:5](quran://32/5) is an exact linguistic calque of this 1st-century Christian formula.
3. **Second Temple Jewish Literature: Book of Jubilees 4:30 (c. 2nd Century BC) & Rabbinic Parallels:**
   In *Jubilees* 4:30, the principle that one day in heaven equals 1,000 earthly years explained why Adam died at age 930 (Genesis 5:5) without violating Genesis 2:17 (*"in the day that you eat of it you shall die"*): *"for one thousand years are as one day in the testimony of the heavens."* This identical exegetical tradition appears in *Genesis Rabbah* 19:8, Justin Martyr (*Dialogue with Trypho* 81, c. AD 155), and the Babylonian Talmud (*b. Sanhedrin* 97a).
4. **The 500-Year Distance in the Babylonian Talmud (*b. Ḥagigah* 13a & *b. Pesachim* 94b, c. AD 500):**
   The cosmological distance cited by Mujāhid, Qatādah, and Ibn Kathīr to explain [Quran 32:5](quran://32/5)—that heaven and earth are separated by a **500-year journey**—is a verbatim parallel to rabbinic cosmology codified in the Babylonian Talmud over a century before Islam:
   > *"Rabbi Yoḥanan said: The distance from the earth to the firmament (raqīaʿ) is a five hundred-year journey, and the thickness of the firmament is a five hundred-year journey, and between each firmament and the next is a five hundred-year journey..."* (cf. *Midrash Tehillim* 92:2; *Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer* 4)
   This confirms that the "500-year descent and 500-year ascent" totaling 1,000 years in [Quran 32:5](quran://32/5) reflects pre-existing Near Eastern rabbinic cosmography.

---

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Modern Harmonizations

Concordist writers addressing these mathematical and textual parameters often propose secondary harmonizations:

* **Concordist Harmonization 1: Relativistic Time Dilation ($\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$):** Proponents suggest that [Quran 32:5](quran://32/5) ($1\text{ day} = 1,000\text{ years}$) and [Quran 70:4](quran://70/4) ($1\text{ day} = 50,000\text{ years}$) anticipate Einstein's special theory of relativity, arguing that celestial beings moving near $c$ experience Lorentz time dilation: $\Delta t' = \Delta t_0 / \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* This reading misconstrues special relativity. Relativistic time dilation is a continuous mathematical gradient dependent on velocity $v$; any ratio from $1$ to infinity can be generated. The numbers 1,000 and 50,000 are not physical constants; they are discrete integers drawn from ancient Semitic literary traditions ([Psalm 90:4](bible://ps/90/4) and Jewish Jubilee cycles of $50 \times 1,000$). Furthermore, for an entity traveling *at* the speed of light ($v = c$), proper time ceases entirely (time dilation factor $\gamma \to \infty$). A photon experiences zero elapsed time, not a finite ratio of 1 day to 1,000 years. Proposing that angels travel at an arbitrary sublight speed producing exactly 1,000:1 or 50,000:1 time dilation is speculative curve-fitting without textual support.
* **Concordist Harmonization 2: Gravitational Time Dilation and Wormholes:** Other commentators propose that the temporal disparity reflects general relativistic gravitational time dilation near black holes or traversable wormholes.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* Gravitational time dilation ($\Delta t_f = \Delta t_0 \sqrt{1 - 2GM/rc^2}$) is likewise a continuous function determined by mass $M$ and radius $r$. Constructing specific gravitational potentials to match round ancient figures represents anachronistic post-hoc correlation. The Quran describes a seven-layered domed cosmology where solid heavens are mounted above a flat earth ([Quran 65:12](quran://65/12); [Quran 32:4](quran://32/4)), with angels ascending through physical celestial gates rather than spacetime singularities.

* **Conclusion:** [Quran 32:5](quran://32/5) contains no reference to the speed of light, electromagnetic waves, or lunar orbital mechanics. The concordist derivation formulated by Mansour Hassab-Elnaby in AD 1990 relies on an unphysical cosine projection factor, selected 20th-century astronomical constants, and a departure from classical Arabic grammar and early Islamic exegesis. When read in its historical and literary context, the verse expresses the cosmic expanse between heaven and earth through the widely attested Late Antique Near Eastern cosmological motif of a 500-year travel distance ([Tafsir al-Tabari 32:5](tabari://32/5); *b. Ḥagigah* 13a) and the biblical formula comparing divine eternity to human temporal mortality ([Psalm 90:4](bible://ps/90/4); [2 Peter 3:8](bible://2pt/3/8)).

79:30.claim: Modern concordist writers propose that the word 'dahaha' describing the Earth in Quran 79:30 derives from an Arabic term for an ostrich egg ('duhiyyah'), thereby anticipating the oblate spheroid geometry of Planet Earth.
79:30.classification_explanation: Concordist commentators interpret the verb 'dahaha' in [Quran 79:30](quran://79/30) as deriving from a term for an ostrich egg, attributing modern oblate spheroid geometry to the 7th-century text. In Classical Arabic lexicography (*Kitab al-Ayn*, *Maqayis al-Lughah*, *Lisan al-Arab*) and early exegesis ([Tafsir al-Tabari 79:30](tabari://79/30), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 79:30](ibnkathir://79/30)), the root *d-h-w* unanimously signifies spreading out, leveling, and expanding a flat surface (*basataha*), while the ostrich nest (*udhiyy*) is named because the bird flattens the sand with its feet.
79:30.summary: In Classical Arabic lexicons (*Kitab al-Ayn*, *Lisan al-Arab*) and early commentaries (al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir), the verb *dahaha* in Quran 79:30 simply means 'He spread it out flat' to prepare the ground for water, pastures, and mountains (79:31–32). Its lexical link to an ostrich comes from the bird using its feet to scrape and flatten a sand hollow (*udhiyy*) for its nest, rather than from the shape of an egg. Geometrically, an ostrich egg is elongated at the poles (a prolate spheroid), the inverse of the Earth's shape flattened at the poles (an oblate spheroid). Moreover, Greek scholars like Aristotle and Eratosthenes had already measured a spherical Earth by c. 240 BC, whereas the Quran's phrasing reflects the traditional Near Eastern imagery of the Earth as a spread-out expanse.
79:30.refutation:
Textual and philological evidence does not support the thesis that [Quran 79:30](quran://79/30) describes the Earth as an egg or anticipates its oblate spheroid geometry. Modern interpretations that *daḥāhā* denotes shaping the Earth like an ostrich egg represent a twentieth-century lexical reinterpretation that diverges from classical Arabic dictionaries, the immediate context of [Quran 79:31](quran://79/31)–[79:32](quran://79/32), foundational Islamic commentaries ([Tafsir al-Tabari 79:30](tabari://79/30), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 79:30](ibnkathir://79/30)), and the physical geometry of an ostrich egg itself.

---

### 1. Context of the Claim & Classical Arabic Lexicography (Daḥāhā / Root d-ḥ-w)

In modern popular commentary, writers such as Rashad Khalifa (AD 1981), Zakir Naik, and Zaghloul El-Naggar propose that [Quran 79:30](quran://79/30) contains scientific foreknowledge of geodesy:

> *"And the earth, after that, He spread it out."* (`wa-l-arḍa baʿda dhālika daḥāhā`)

These commentators propose that *daḥāhā* derives from an Arabic noun for an ostrich egg (*duḥiyyah* or *udḥiyyah*), interpreting the verse as a description of the Earth as an oblate spheroid.

However, pre-modern Arabic lexicography demonstrates that the root *d-ḥ-w* (and *d-ḥ-y*) possesses a single foundational meaning: leveling, flattening, and spreading out. Classical lexicons unanimously define the term in terms of horizontal extension rather than sphericity:

1. **Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad al-Farāhīdī (d. AD 791), *Kitāb al-ʿAyn* (s.v. `d-ḥ-w`):**
   Defines: *"daḥw: to spread out (*al-basṭ*). You say: daḥā Allāhu al-arḍa yadḥūhā daḥwan, meaning He spread it out (*basaṭahā*)."*
2. **Ibn Fāris (d. AD 1004), *Maqāyīs al-Lughah* (Vol. 2, p. 334, s.v. `d-ḥ-w`):**
   Notes that the root has a single semantic core: *"The letters dāl, ḥāʾ, and the semi-vowel indicate the spreading out and expanding of a thing (*basṭu al-shayʾ*). One says: daḥawtu al-shayʾa adḥūhu daḥwan, when you have spread it out."*
3. **Al-Jawharī (d. AD 1003), *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*, and Ibn Manẓūr (d. AD 1311), *Lisān al-ʿArab* (Vol. 14, p. 251, s.v. `d-ḥ-w`):**
   * Define `daḥā al-arḍa yadḥūhā daḥwan` as: *"He spread it out / flattened it (*basaṭahā*)... and Abū ʿUbaydah stated in Majāz al-Qurʾān: daḥāhā means basaṭahā."*
   * Explain the connection to the ostrich: an ostrich does not build a raised nest; it uses its feet to **scrape, clear, and flatten a wide depression in the sand** to lay its eggs. That **flattened sand hollow** is called *al-udḥiyy*, *al-udḥiyyah*, or *al-madḥā* (*mawḍiʿu bayḍi al-naʿāmati fī al-ramli, li-annahā tadḥūhu bi-rijlayhā, ay tabsuṭuhu thumma tabīḍu fīhi, wa-laysa lil-naʿāmati ʿushshun*—*Lisān al-ʿArab*; Edward William Lane, *Arabic-English Lexicon*, Book I, p. 857).
   * Philologists cite two distinct pre-Islamic poetic attestations confirming this meaning:
     * In [Tafsir al-Tabari 79:30](tabari://79/30), al-Ṭabarī quotes **Umayyah ibn Abī al-Ṣalt**:
       > *"An abode which He spread out (daḥāhā), then settled us therein / and He established the other which is more glorious."* (`dārun daḥāhā thumma aʿmaranā bihā / wa-aqāma bi-l-ukhrā allatī hiya amjadū`)
     * In Ibn Hishām's *al-Sīrah al-Nabawiyyah*, al-Zamakhsharī's *al-Kashshāf*, and al-Qurṭubī's *al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān*, **Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl** (d. c. AD 605) proclaims:
       > *"He spread it out (daḥāhā), and when He saw it had become flat and level upon the water, He anchored upon it the mountains."* (`daḥāhā fa-lammā raʾāhā istawat ʿalā al-māʾi arsā ʿalayhā al-jibālā`)
4. **Modern Vernacular Dialect Shift:**
   In certain modern North African vernaculars (e.g., Libyan, Tunisian), *daḥyah* colloquially designates a poultry egg via metonymic shift from the nest (*udḥiyyah*). In 7th-century Classical Arabic, the word for egg was *bayḍah* ([Quran 37:49](quran://37/49)), while the verb *daḥā* did not denote "to shape like an egg." Classical Arabic possessed specific terms for spheres (*kura*, *mustadīr*), none of which appear in this passage.

---

### 2. Geodetic, Geometric & Textual Analysis

The modern concordist reading diverges from solid geometry, textual context, and geodesy:

| Dimension of Analysis | Modern Concordist Reading ("Ostrich Egg / Oblate Spheroid") | Geodesy, Solid Geometry & Quranic Context ([Quran 79:27](quran://79/27)–[79:32](quran://79/32)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Classical Lexical Meaning of *Daḥāhā*** | Proposed to mean "shaped like an ostrich egg" or "molded into an oblate spheroid." | Unanimously defined in classical lexicons as "He spread it out, leveled it, and expanded it" (*basaṭahā* / *wassaʿahā*), with *udḥiyy* denoting the flat depression scraped in sand by an ostrich. |
| **Solid Geometry: Prolate vs. Oblate Spheroid** | Proposes that an ostrich egg mirrors the oblate spheroidal shape of Earth. | An ostrich egg is a **prolate spheroid** (elongated at poles, $c > a$, polar radius ~7.5 cm vs. equatorial ~6.2 cm), whereas Earth is an **oblate spheroid** (flattened at poles, $c < a$, polar 6,356.8 km vs. equatorial 6,378.1 km)—the inverse geometric form. |
| **Immediate Grammatical Explanation ([Quran 79:31](quran://79/31)–[79:32](quran://79/32))** | Reads *daḥāhā* as an isolated geometric description of the planetary orb. | Verses 31–32 provide an explicit grammatical apposition (*tafsīr*) explaining *daḥāhā*: drawing forth water and pastures and anchoring mountains, describing ecological preparation of the terrain. |
| **Cosmic Chronology Sequence (`Baʿda Dhālika`)** | Proposes that the creation sequence matches modern astrophysical history. | [Quran 79:27](quran://79/27)–[79:30](quran://79/30) places the creation of the heavens and day/night *before* spreading the Earth, which diverges from astrophysical chronology (terrestrial day/night requires Earth) and differs from [Quran 41:9](quran://41/9)–[41:12](quran://41/12). |
| **Corroborating Expanse Vocabulary Across the Quran** | Proposes that the Quran uniquely describes a spherical planetary Earth. | Systematically accompanied by planar-expanse terminology: [Quran 88:20](quran://88/20) (*suṭiḥat*, flattened), [Quran 71:19](quran://71/19) (*bisāṭan*, a flat carpet), [Quran 51:48](quran://51/48) (*farashnāhā*, spread like a couch), and [Quran 15:19](quran://15/19) (*madadnāhā*, stretched out). |

#### Detailed Geodetic and Contextual Analysis

1. **Prolate Spheroid vs. Oblate Spheroid:**
   In geometry, an ostrich egg is a **prolate spheroid** ($c > a$, polar-to-equatorial ratio ≈ 1.20), elongated along its rotational axis. Planet Earth is an **oblate spheroid** ($c < a$, equatorial radius 6,378.1 km, polar radius 6,356.8 km, flattening $f \approx 1/298.25$), compressed at the poles and bulging at the equator. An ostrich egg is elongated where Earth is flattened, and narrow where Earth bulges.
2. **Grammatical Apposition in [Quran 79:31](quran://79/31)–[79:32](quran://79/32):**
   The Quran explains *daḥāhā* in the subsequent verses: *"He brought forth from it its water and its pasture – and the mountains, He anchored it (to them) –"* (`akhraja minhā māʾahā wa-marʿāhā wa-l-jibāla arsāhā`, [Quran 79:31](quran://79/31)–[79:32](quran://79/32)). Classical commentators note that verses 31–32 function as an explanatory apposition (*tafsīr*): spreading the earth refers to drawing forth springs, vegetation, and stabilizing mountains, rather than molding a globe.
3. **Cosmic Chronology and Internal Sequence:**
   [Quran 79:27](quran://79/27)–[79:30](quran://79/30) states that God built the heaven, raised its ceiling, darkened its night, brought out its morning, and *"after that"* (*baʿda dhālika*) spread out the Earth. In astrophysics, terrestrial day and night cannot precede the Earth's existence. This sequence also differs from [Quran 41:9](quran://41/9)–[41:12](quran://41/12), where Earth and mountains are created before heaven is fashioned.

---

### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr) and Canonical Ḥadīth

Early Muslim exegetes did not interpret [Quran 79:30](quran://79/30) as describing a spherical or egg-shaped Earth. [Tafsir al-Tabari 79:30](tabari://79/30) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 79:30](ibnkathir://79/30) record unanimous early consensus defining *daḥāhā* as horizontal spreading:

* **Al-Ṭabarī's Exegesis ([Tafsir al-Tabari 79:30](tabari://79/30), [Tafsir al-Tabari 79:31](tabari://79/31)):**
  Al-Ṭabarī notes that while Mujāhid and al-Suddī read *baʿda dhālika* as *maʿa dhālika* ("along with that") to harmonize with [Quran 2:29](quran://2/29), al-Ṭabarī rejects *maʿa dhālika*, maintaining the primary chronological meaning of *baʿda dhālika*: *"The well-known meaning of 'after' (baʿd) is that it is the opposite of 'before' (qabl)... and spreading out (al-daḥw) in the speech of the Arabs is simply spreading wide (al-basṭ) and extending (al-madd)."*
  * Authorities Qatādah, al-Suddī, and Sufyān all define *daḥāhā* as *basaṭahā* ("He spread it wide").
  * **Ibn Zayd** glosses it as *ḥarathahā shaqqahā* (`حَرَثَهَا شَقَّهَا`, "He plowed it and cleft it open" for springs and plants, citing [Quran 80:26](quran://80/26)).
  * Al-Ṭabarī cites traditions from Ibn ʿAbbās stating the Kaaba was set upon the water two thousand years before creation and the earth was spread out beneath it (*duḥiyat al-arḍu min taḥtihi*).
* **Ibn Kathīr's Commentary ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 79:30](ibnkathir://79/30)):**
  Ibn Kathīr notes: *"And His saying, {And the earth, after that, He spread it out}, He explains this statement by His saying, {And brought forth therefrom its water and its pasture} [79:31]... This means that He brought out what was in it from potentiality to actuality."*
* Ibn Kathīr cites Ibn Abī Ḥātim's transmission from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās: *"(He spread it out), and its spreading out is that He brought forth from it the water and the pasture, and He cleaved rivers [in it], and He placed in it the mountains, the sands, the paths, and the hills"* (`وَدَحْيُهَا أَنْ أَخْرَجَ مِنْهَا الْمَاءَ وَالْمَرْعَى، وَشَقَّقَ فِيهَا الْأَنْهَارَ، وَجَعَلَ فِيهَا الْجِبَالَ وَالرِّمَالَ وَالسُّبُلَ وَالْآكَامَ`, *wa-daḥyuhā an akhraja minhā al-māʾa wa-l-marʿā, wa-shaqqaqa fīhā al-anhāra, wa-jaʿala fīhā al-jibāla wa-l-rimāla wa-l-subula wa-l-ākāma*).
* **Ibn ʿAbbās's Canonical Explanation in *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 41:9](ibnkathir://41/9)):**
  In *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* (*Kitāb al-Tafsīr*, Chapter on Sūrat Fuṣṣilat, *muʿallaq* report via al-Minhāl ibn ʿAmr from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, recorded in full in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 41:9](ibnkathir://41/9)), when questioned about the apparent chronological tension between [Quran 79:27](quran://79/27)–[79:30](quran://79/30) and [Quran 41:9](quran://41/9)–[41:12](quran://41/12), Ibn ʿAbbās explained:
  > *"Allah created the earth in two days, then He created the heavens, then He rose over (Istawā ilā) the heaven and gave it its shape in two more days. Then He spread the earth, which means that He brought forth therefrom its water and its pasture. And He created the mountains, inanimate things, hills, and everything in between, in two more days. This is His saying: {(He) spread (the earth)} [79:30] And His saying: {(He) created the earth in two Days} [41:9]. So the earth and everything in it was created in four days, and the heavens were created in two days."*
  Ibn ʿAbbās restricts *daḥāhā* to ecological furnishing, with no mention of spherical shape or ostrich eggs.

---

### 4. Pre-Islamic Greek Geodesy & Late Antique Near Eastern Cosmology

The proposition that a 7th-century reference to a spherical Earth would represent unprecedented scientific knowledge is inconsistent with the history of ancient Mediterranean science:

1. **Greek Geodesy Established and Measured the Spherical Earth Over 900 Years Prior:**
   Terrestrial sphericity was demonstrated, calculated, and widely taught across the Mediterranean long before Islam:
   * **Pythagoras (6th century BC)** proposed a spherical Earth on theoretical principles.
   * **Plato (c. 428–348 BC)** in *Phaedo* (108e–109a) described Earth as a round sphere in the center of the heavens.
   * **Aristotle (384–322 BC)** in *De Caelo* (II.14, 297a–298a, c. 350 BC) provided empirical arguments: the circular shadow of Earth during lunar eclipses, the shifting horizons of southern stars, and mathematical estimates of circumference at 400,000 stadia.
   * **Eratosthenes of Cyrene (c. 276–194 BC)** measured Earth's circumference c. 240 BC using solar shadows between Syene and Alexandria, calculating it to within ~1% to 2% of the modern value (40,075 km).
   * **Claudius Ptolemy (c. AD 100–170)** codified spherical astronomy and geography in the *Almagest* and *Geographia*, standard textbooks in the Byzantine and Sasanian worlds.
   Even if a 7th-century text had described a spherical Earth, such a statement would have reflected long-established Mediterranean scientific knowledge rather than novel empirical discovery.
2. **Late Antique Near Eastern Cosmology in the Quran:**
   The Quran reflects the cosmological world picture of 7th-century Arabia and Late Antique Semitic traditions:
   * Late Antique Syriac Christian authors—such as Ephrem the Syrian (d. AD 373), Severian of Gabala (d. c. AD 408), and Cosmas Indicopleustes in *Christian Topography* (c. AD 550)—favored a literal tent cosmology over Greek sphericity.
   * The Quran's vocabulary aligns with this model: the sky is a raised ceiling (*samkahā*, [Quran 79:28](quran://79/28); *saqfan maḥfūẓan*, [Quran 21:32](quran://21/32)) kept from falling ([Quran 22:65](quran://22/65)); the Earth is spread out flat (*daḥāhā*, [Quran 79:30](quran://79/30); *suṭiḥat*, [Quran 88:20](quran://88/20); *bisāṭan*, [Quran 71:19](quran://71/19); *farashnāhā*, [Quran 51:48](quran://51/48); *madadnāhā*, [Quran 15:19](quran://15/19)); and mountains act as stabilizing tent-pegs (*awtād*, [Quran 78:6](quran://78/6)–[78:7](quran://78/7); *arsāhā*, [Quran 79:32](quran://79/32)).
   Jalāl al-Dīn al-Maḥallī (d. AD 1459) in *Tafsīr al-Jalālayn* on [Quran 88:20](quran://88/20) explicitly wrote: *"{wa-ilā al-arḍi kayfa suṭiḥat}... indicates that the earth is a flat plane (*saṭḥ*), which is the view of the scholars of the Law, not a sphere (*kura*) as the astronomers claim."*

---

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Secondary Harmonizations

Modern commentators advance several secondary arguments to maintain the concordist reading:

1. **Medieval Muslim Sphericity Arguments:**
   Commentators often cite medieval scholars such as Ibn Ḥazm (d. AD 1064, *al-Fiṣal*) and Ibn Taymiyyah (d. AD 1328, *Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā*), who affirmed Earth's sphericity (*kura*). However, these scholars adopted spherical models from 9th-century Abbasid translations of Aristotle and Ptolemy, rather than from early Arabic lexical definitions of *daḥāhā*. Notably, none of these scholars proposed that *daḥāhā* in [Quran 79:30](quran://79/30) meant "egg-shaped." Ibn Ḥazm and Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī (d. AD 1210, *Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb*) noted that *daḥā* and *basaṭa* literally denote spreading flat, harmonizing them with Ptolemaic astronomy by observing that a massive sphere appears flat locally.
2. **The Secondary Appeal to *al-Madāḥī* (Sliding Stones):**
   Concordist writers sometimes cite the pre-Islamic game *al-madāḥī* mentioned in lexicons, proposing that *daḥā* implies rolling spherical balls. However, in *Lisān al-ʿArab* (root `d-ḥ-w`) and [Tafsir al-Tabari 79:30](tabari://79/30), *al-madāḥī* are explicitly defined as **flat, disc-shaped stones like a flatbread** (`أَحْجَارٌ أَمْثَالُ الْقُرْصَةِ`, *aḥjār amthāl al-qurṣah*) that players slid across flat ground toward a shallow hole (*udḥiyyah*). The verb denotes propelling a flat object along the ground rather than rolling a sphere.
3. **The Cross-Verse Appeal to [Quran 39:5](quran://39/5) (*Yukawwiru*):**
   Concordist commentators also appeal to [Quran 39:5](quran://39/5) (*"He wraps the night around the day, and wraps the day around the night"*, `yukawwiru al-layla ʿalā al-nahār`), proposing that *yukawwiru* indicates a spherical Earth. In classical exegesis on this verse ([Tafsir al-Tabari 39:5](tabari://39/5) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 39:5](ibnkathir://39/5)), *yukawwiru* means night and day covering and alternating ceaselessly with one another (`yughshī hādhā ʿalā hādhā` / `yataʿāqabāni lā yaqirrāni`), while the lexical root *takwīr* is explained through the idiom of wrapping a turban (*takwīr al-ʿimāmah*) in [Tafsir al-Tabari 81:1](tabari://81/1), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 81:1](ibnkathir://81/1), and *Lisān al-ʿArab* (s.v. `k-w-r`). It describes the temporal alternation of celestial darkness and light rather than the geodetic shape of Earth, and does not alter the explicit horizontal-spreading verbs applied to the Earth itself ([Quran 79:30](quran://79/30), [Quran 88:20](quran://88/20), [Quran 15:19](quran://15/19), [Quran 2:22](quran://2/22)).
4. **Phenomenological Language Interpretation:**
   Other commentators propose that the Quran speaks phenomenologically from an everyday human visual perspective. While ancient texts frequently describe natural phenomena observationally, this reading is incompatible with the thesis of geodetic foreknowledge: if [Quran 79:30](quran://79/30) describes local horizontal appearance, it does not simultaneously function as a technical disclosure of an oblate spheroid.

In conclusion, philological, contextual, and historical evidence indicates that [Quran 79:30](quran://79/30) describes the terrestrial expanse being spread out and ecologically prepared. Translating *daḥāhā* as an ostrich egg is a modern concordist reinterpretation that is not supported by classical Arabic lexicography or early Islamic exegetical tradition.
