### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr)

Neither the Prophet's companions (*ṣaḥābah*), nor the immediate successors (*tābiʿūn*), nor the classical commentators interpreted [Quran 75:4](quran://75/4) as an allusion to skin ridges or forensic identification. Instead, early Islamic scholarship focused entirely on two interpretations: fusing the fingers into a flat animal hoof, or gathering the bones and making the fingertips equal in length:

* **Consensus of the Early Authorities in [Tafsir al-Tabari 75:4](tabari://75/4):** Al-Ṭabarī records comprehensive chains of transmission (*asānīd*) from the leading early authorities of Quranic commentary, all affirming that *taswiyat al-banān* refers to fusing the fingers like an animal hoof:
  - *Ibn ʿAbbās:* Al-Ṭabarī transmits from Ibn Humayd, from Jarīr, from Mughīrah, from Abu al-Khayr ibn Tamīm, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said: Ibn ʿAbbās said to me: *"Ask."* So I asked about {Does man think that We shall not assemble his bones? Yes indeed, We are (even) able to fashion his fingers (again)}. Ibn ʿAbbās replied: *"If He wished, He would have made it into a padded hoof [like a camel] or a solid hoof [like a donkey]"* (`لو شاء لجعله خفا أو حافرا`). In another narration through Muhammad ibn Saʿd, Ibn ʿAbbās stated: *"I am able to make his palm clustered together like the padded hoof of a camel"* (`أنا قادر على أن أجعل كفه مجمرة مثل خف البعير`).
  - *Mujāhid ibn Jabr:* Transmitted through Ibn Abi Najīḥ, Mujāhid explained regarding {able to fashion his fingers}: *"Meaning his two feet; like the padded hoof of a camel, so he cannot do anything with them"* (`رجليه، قال: كخف البعير فلا يعمل بهما شيئا`).
  - *ʿIkrimah (client of Ibn ʿAbbās):* Transmitted through Wakīʿ from al-Naḍr, ʿIkrimah explained: *"Able to make it like the padded hoof of a camel, or the solid hoof of a donkey"* (`على أن نجعله مثل خف البعير، أو حافر الحمار`).
  - *Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī:* Transmitted through Ibn ʿUlayyah from Abu Rajāʾ, al-Ḥasan stated: *"He made it a hand, and He made it fingers which one can clench and extend; and if He willed, He would have joined them together, so you would have had to protect yourself from the ground with your mouth, but He formed you in a beautiful creation"* (`جعلها يدا، وجعلها أصابع يقبضهن ويبسطهن، ولو شاء لجمعهن، فاتقيت الأرض بفيك، ولكن سواك خلقا حسنا`).
  - *Qatādah ibn Diʿāmah:* Transmitted through Bishr and Ibn Thawr, Qatādah stated: *"Able, by Allah, to make his fingers like the solid hoof of a beast, or like the padded hoof of a camel; and if He willed, He would have made it like that, such that he could only pick up his food with his mouth"* (`قادر والله على أن يجعل بنانه كحافر الدابة، أو كخف البعير، ولو شاء لجعله كذلك، فإنما ينقي طعامه بفيه`).
  - *Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim:* Transmitted through Abu Muʿādh from ʿUbayd, al-Ḍaḥḥāk stated: *"Al-Banān means the fingers. He says: We are able to make his fingers like the padded hoof of a camel"* (`البنان: الأصابع، يقول: نحن قادرون على أن نجعل بنانه مثل خف البعير`).
* **Grammatical Analysis of Qādirīn in [Tafsir al-Tabari 75:4](tabari://75/4):** Al-Ṭabarī examines the grammatical syntax of the accusative participle *qādirīna* (`قَادِرِينَ`). He first cites the Kufan grammatical analysis (noting al-Farrāʾ and quoting the poetic verse of al-Farazdaq: `عَـليَّ قَسَـم لا أشْـتُمُ الدَّهْـرَ مُسْـلِما / وَلا خارِجــا مِـنْ فِـيَّ زُورُ كَـلام`, *"Upon me is an oath that I will not insult a Muslim for all time, nor will any false speech ever come out of my mouth"*), and then records the Basran grammatical position, which he endorses as closer to correctness: *"Some of the grammarians of Basrah used to say: Its accusative case is based on 'We shall assemble' (najmaʿ), meaning: 'Yes indeed, We shall assemble them, being able (qādirīn) to fashion his fingers.' And this second opinion is closer to being correct according to the methodology of the scholars of the Arabic language"* (`وكان بعض نحويِّي البصرة يقول: نصب على نجمع، أي بل نجمعها قادرين على أن نسوّي بنانه، وهذا القول الثاني أشبه بالصحة على مذهب أهل العربية`). Consistent with his explanation in [Tafsir al-Tabari 75:3](tabari://75/3), al-Ṭabarī understands *an nusawwiya banānahu* as making the fingers of the hands and feet into a single undivided entity like a camel's footpad or a donkey's hoof (`فنجعلها شيئا واحدا كخفّ البعير، أو حافر الحمار، فكان لا يأخذ ما يأكل إلا بفيه كسائر البهائم`).
* **Exegetical Synthesis in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 75:4](ibnkathir://75/4):** Ibn Kathīr divides the exegesis of the verse into two distinct paragraphs. First, he records the consensus of the early authorities along with al-Ṭabarī's explanation of it: *"Sa'id bin Jubayr and Al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas: 'That We make it a camel's hoof or a solid hoof.' This was also said by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak, and Ibn Jarir. Ibn Jarir directed this to mean that if Allah, the Exalted, willed, He could have made that in this world"* (`قال سعيد بن جبير والعوفي ، عن ابن عباس : أن نجعله خفا أو حافرا . وكذا قال مجاهد ، وعكرمة ، والحسن ، وقتادة ، والضحاك ، وابن جرير . ووجهه ابن جرير بأنه تعالى لو شاء لجعل ذلك في الدنيا`). Second, in the following paragraph, Ibn Kathīr presents the apparent grammatical and lexical reading (*al-ẓāhir*) cited from Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjāj: *"The apparent meaning of the Ayah is that His statement: (able) is a circumstantial expression (Hal) for His statement: (We assemble), meaning, 'does man think that We will not assemble his bones? Yes, We will assemble them while We are able to put together the tips of his fingers,' meaning, 'Our power is suitable to assemble them, and if We wished We could surely resurrect him with more than what he originally had, so We would make his Banan (which are the tips of his fingers) equal.' This is the meaning of what Ibn Qutaybah and Az-Zajjaj said"* (`والظاهر من الآية أن قوله : ( قادرين ) حال من قوله : ( نجمع ) أي : أيظن الإنسان أنا لا نجمع عظامه ؟ بلى سنجمعها قادرين على أن نسوي بنانه ، أي : قدرتنا صالحة لجمعها ، ولو شئنا لبعثناه أزيد مما كان ، فنجعل بنانه - وهي أطراف أصابعه - مستوية . وهذا معنى قول ابن قتيبة والزجاج`).
* **The Skeptic's Doubt Regarding Decayed Bones in [Tafsir al-Tabari 75:3](tabari://75/3) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 75:3](ibnkathir://75/3):** Under [Tafsir al-Tabari 75:3](tabari://75/3), al-Ṭabarī explains the verse as follows: *"Does the son of Adam think that We shall not be able to gather his bones after their scattering? Yes, We are capable of greater than that: that We make his fingertips uniform. And they are the fingers of his hands and his feet, so We make them a single entity like the footpad of a camel, or the hoof of a donkey, such that he would not take what he eats except with his mouth, like the rest of the beasts. But He separated the fingers of his hands; he takes with them, grasps, clenches when he wishes, and extends, thus He made his creation beautiful"* (`يقول تعالى ذكره: أيظنّ ابن آدم أن لن نقدر على جمع عظامه بعد تفرّقها، بلى قادرين على أعظم من ذلك، أن نسوي بنانه، وهي أصابع يديه ورجليه، فنجعلها شيئا واحدا كخفّ البعير، أو حافر الحمار، فكان لا يأخذ ما يأكل إلا بفيه كسائر البهائم، ولكنه فرق أصابع يديه يأخذ بها، ويتناول ويقبض إذا شاء ويبسط، فحسن خلقه`). Similarly, in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 75:3](ibnkathir://75/3), Ibn Kathīr explains: *"meaning, 'on the Day of Judgement does he think that We are not able to return his bones and gather them from their various places?'"* (`أي يوم القيامة أيظن أنا لا نقدر على إعادة عظامه وجمعها من أماكنها المتفرقة`). Both commentaries establish that [Quran 75:3](quran://75/3)–[Quran 75:4](quran://75/4) was revealed specifically to address skepticism regarding the osteological gathering of scattered bones.

### 4. Verbatim Pre-Islamic Osteological, Biblical & Dactyloscopic Precedents

The linguistic usage of *banān* for fingers and limbs, the teleological contrast between articulated fingers and animal hooves, the theological motif of reassembling scattered skeletal fragments down to the extremities, and the practical application of fingerprint identification were all well-attested throughout the ancient Near East and Mediterranean world centuries prior to Islam:

* **Pre-Islamic Arabian Poetry & Classical Lexicography Attesting Banān as Fingers and Joints:**
  - *Al-Nābighah al-Dhubyānī (6th Century AD):* In one of the most celebrated pre-Islamic descriptive verses, al-Nābighah explicitly uses *banān* to denote the whole henna-dyed fingers of a woman (`بِمُخَضَّبٍ رَخْصٍ كَأَنَّ بَنَانَهُ / عَنَمٌ يَكَادُ مِنَ اللَّطَافَةِ يُعْقَدُ` — *"With a henna-dyed, tender hand, as though its fingers [banānahu] were the red fruit of the ʿanam tree, so delicate they could almost be tied in knots"*), paralleling Imruʾ al-Qays's description of delicate fingers (`وَتَعْطُو بِرَخْصٍ غَيْرِ شَثْنٍ كَأَنَّهُ / أَسَارِيعُ ظَبْيٍ أَوْ مَسَاوِيكُ إِسْحِلِ`, *Muʿallaqah*, line 34).
  - *Classical Lexicography & [Quran 8:12](quran://8/12):* As codified in al-Khalīl's *Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, al-Jawharī's *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*, and Ibn Manẓūr's *Lisān al-ʿArab*, *al-banān* denotes the physical fingers and their phalangeal segments (*al-aṣābiʿ* / *aṭrāf al-aṣābiʿ*), matching the military usage in [Quran 8:12](quran://8/12) (*"So strike above (their) necks, and strike (off) all their fingers [kulla banān]!"*).
* **Greco-Roman Anatomical Precedent — Galen's *De Usu Partium* (Book I, c. AD 165–175):**
  - Five centuries before the Quran, the physician Galen of Pergamon devoted the entire first book of his teleological treatise *De Usu Partium* (*On the Usefulness of the Parts of the Body*, Book I, Chapters 1–24) to the anatomical configuration of the human hand and fingers. Galen explicitly contrasted the divided, multi-jointed human fingers of unequal lengths—which equalize (`taswiyah`) when grasping spherical or cylindrical tools—with the undivided hooves (*ḥāfir*) and pads (*khuff*) of quadrupeds, noting that if humans possessed hooves instead of articulated fingers, they would be forced to feed directly with their mouths like grazing beasts. This Greco-Roman anatomical analysis, translated into Syriac in the 6th century AD, closely parallels the exegetical tradition preserved by Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, and Qatādah under [Quran 75:4](quran://75/4).
* **Biblical and Intertestamental Osteological Precedents:**

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Modern Harmonizations

Modern concordist literature advances four primary arguments to propose that [Quran 75:4](quran://75/4) anticipates forensic dactyloscopy. Each proposal can be evaluated through philological, anatomical, and contextual analysis:

* **Harmonization 1: "Why Would the Quran Single Out the *Banān* in [Quran 75:4](quran://75/4) Immediately After Mentioning Bones (*ʿIẓām*) in [Quran 75:3](quran://75/3) Unless Fingertips Possess a Special Identifying Property?":** Concordist writers suggest that moving from general bones in verse 3 to fingers/fingertips in verse 4 is best explained if the fingertips contain each person's unique biometric identity.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* Both classical *tafsīr* and human osteology directly explain why *banān* follows *ʿiẓām* without recourse to 19th-century dactyloscopy. First, as unanimously recorded by the earliest exegetes in [Tafsir al-Tabari 75:3](tabari://75/3)–[Tafsir al-Tabari 75:4](tabari://75/4) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 75:4](ibnkathir://75/4), singling out the fingers (`الأصابع` / `أطراف أصابعه`) highlights the anatomical distinction between articulated human hands and animal hooves (`أن نجعله خفا أو حافرا`): God can not only gather human bones, but could also deprive a person of separated fingers by fusing them into a single entity like a camel's footpad or donkey's hoof (`فنجعلها شيئا واحدا كخفّ البعير، أو حافر الحمار`), or could resurrect him and make the tips of his fingers equal in length (`مستوية`, per Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjāj). Second, in human osteology (and later classical *tafsīr* discussions), the distal phalanges of the digits (*banān*) are the smallest and most delicate bones of the skeleton (*aṣghar al-ʿiẓām*, `أصغر العظام`), containing multiple intricate joints that disintegrate and scatter first upon decomposition; singling out the *banān* after *ʿiẓām* thus functions as a classical *a fortiori* (*bi-l-awlā*) osteological argument.
* **Harmonization 2: Proposing that *Sawwā* (*Nusawwiya*) Means "To Restore Identically Down to the Fingerprint Ridges":** Concordist proponents argue that the Form II verb *sawwā* means "to fashion in exact proportion" or "to restore identically," proposing that restoring a person's fingertips identically necessarily includes their epidermal friction ridges (*baṣamāt al-aṣābiʿ*, `بصمات الأصابع`).
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* This interpretation conflates gross anatomical proportioning with microscopic epidermal dermatoglyphics and diverges from both classical Arabic lexicography and early exegesis. In classical Arabic morphology, *taswiyah* (from *sawwā*) means "making level, even, equal, or uniform." As Ibn Kathīr explicitly records in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 75:4](ibnkathir://75/4) (`فنجعل بنانه - وهي أطراف أصابعه - مستوية . وهذا معنى قول ابن قتيبة والزجاج`), even the philologists Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjāj—who read *nusawwiya* in connection with gathering the bones—explained *taswiyah* as making the tips of the fingers *mustawiyah* (equal in length) rather than engraving unique epidermal ridges. Furthermore, as [Quran 8:12](quran://8/12) (*"So strike above (their) necks, and strike (off) all their fingers [kulla banān]!"*) demonstrates, *banān* refers to the physical fingers and digits rather than epidermal skin ridges.
* **Harmonization 3: Semantic Shift from Anatomical Digits to Dermal Friction Ridges:** Concordist authors suggest that *banān* refers specifically to the microscopic friction ridges of the fingertip.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* This reading introduces a retrospective semantic shift. As documented in classical Arabic lexicography (*Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, *Lisān al-ʿArab*) and intratextual usage in [Quran 8:12](quran://8/12) (where swords strike *kulla banān* to disarm combatants), *banān* denotes the physical fingers and fingertips (*al-aṣābiʿ* / *aṭrāf al-aṣābiʿ*). Seventh-century Arabic did not employ *banān* as technical vocabulary for dermatoglyphics (*baṣamāt*, `بصمات`), making the projection of 19th-century epidermal histology onto classical gross anatomical terminology anachronistic.
* **Harmonization 4: The Monozygotic Twins Argument:** Some modern commentators note that identical (monozygotic) twins share the same DNA sequence yet possess distinct fingerprint patterns, suggesting that the text highlighted the fingertips because they are more uniquely individual than DNA.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* This reading is anachronistic and diverges from the immediate literary context. The skeptical inquiry in [Quran 75:3](quran://75/3) (*"Does the human think that We shall not gather his bones?"*) concerned the physical gathering of decayed bones (*ʿiẓām*), not genetic differentiation between twins. Identical twins possess two physically separate skeletons; resurrecting an individual person requires reconstructing their entire anatomy. Singling out the *banān* illustrates divine omnipotence to fashion or level the fingers and gather even the smallest distal bones of the skeleton, rather than referencing genetic or dermatoglyphic variation.

### 1. Context of Claim & Classical Arabic Philology

Beginning in the late 20th century, concordist authors popularized the assertion that [Quran 16:15](quran://16/15) and related verses ([Quran 21:31](quran://21/31), [Quran 31:10](quran://31/10), [Quran 78:6](quran://78/6), [Quran 78:7](quran://78/7)) contain miraculous foreknowledge of modern geophysics. Writers such as Maurice Bucaille (*The Bible, The Qur'an and Science*, AD 1976), Keith L. Moore, Zaghloul El-Naggar (*The Geological Concept of Mountains in the Qur'an*, AD 1991), and Harun Yahya argued that the Quran describes mountains as "pegs" (*awtād*) and "stabilizers" that secure the Earth's crust, supposedly corresponding to Airy isostasy and deep crustal roots that prevent earthquakes and stabilize continental plates.

A rigorous examination of classical Arabic lexicography, syntax, and grammar demonstrates that the vocabulary of [Quran 16:15](quran://16/15) describes the physical deposition of stationary ballast weights to halt the mechanical rocking of a floating surface, rather than deep-seated tectonic processes:

* **The Verb *Alqā* (أَلْقَىٰ):** In classical Arabic grammar and lexicography (*Kitāb al-ʿAyn* by al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, d. AD 786; *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* by al-Jawharī, d. AD 1003; *Lisān al-ʿArab* by Ibn Manẓūr, d. AD 1312; *Lane's Lexicon*, Book I, Part 8, pp. 3012–3013), *alqā* is the Form IV transitive verb derived from the root *l-q-y* (ل-ق-ي). Its primary, unambiguous meaning is "to throw, cast, drop, or fling something down from above upon a surface" (*ramā bi-hi wa-ṭaraḥahu min fawq*). Across the Quranic corpus, *alqā* consistently denotes casting an object downward or forward from an external position:
  * Moses casting his staff to the ground ([Quran 7:107](quran://7/107), [Quran 20:19](quran://20/19), [Quran 26:32](quran://26/32)).
  * The casting of divining pens or lots into water ([Quran 3:44](quran://3/44)).
  * Throwing Joseph into the bottom of a pit ([Quran 12:10](quran://12/10)).
  * Casting an ornament or garment upon a person or fire ([Quran 12:96](quran://12/96), [Quran 20:87](quran://20/87)).
  
  Crucially, the external downward direction of this action is explicitly confirmed in [Quran 41:10](quran://41/10), which describes the exact same event: *"And He placed therein firm mountains from above it"* (*wa-jaʿala fīhā rawāsiya min fawqihā*). The text envisions mountains as pre-existing entities cast down from above onto the pre-existing surface of the earth, an image incompatible with endogenous tectonic uplift from within the lithosphere.

* **The Substantive *Rawāsiya* (رَوَاسِيَ):** In classical Arabic, *rawāsiya* is the broken plural of the feminine active participle *rāsiyah* (or an adjective modifying the elided noun *jibāl*, "firmly anchored mountains"), derived from the root *r-s-w* (ر-س-و). In *Lisān al-ʿArab*, *Tāj al-ʿArūs*, and *Lane's Lexicon* (Book I, p. 1083), the root denotes being stationary, firmly fixed, or anchored in fluid. The foundational nominal derivative is *mirsāh* (مِرْسَاة), meaning the anchor or heavy stone ballast of a ship dropped into water to keep it stationary (*rasat al-safīnah* = "the ship anchored and ceased to drift or rock on the water"). The Quran itself uses this exact maritime verbal noun in [Quran 11:41](quran://11/41) regarding Noah's Ark: *bi-smi Allāhi majrāhā wa-mursāhā* (*"In the name of Allah is its course and its anchoring"*). Thus, *rawāsī* in 7th-century Arabic conveys the precise mechanical imagery of heavy, stabilizing ship anchors or ballast weights placed upon a floating body.

* **The Grammatical Construction *An Tamīda Bikum* (أَنْ تَمِيدَ بِكُمْ):** In classical Arabic syntax (*al-naḥw*), as documented by early grammarians such as al-Farrāʾ (d. AD 822) in *Maʿānī al-Qurʾān*, al-Zajjāj (d. AD 923) in *Maʿānī al-Qurʾān wa-Iʿrābuh*, and al-Ṭabarī (d. AD 923) in *Jāmiʿ al-Bayān* under [Quran 16:15](quran://16/15), the particle *an* functions with an elided governing noun expressing aversion or negative purpose (*mafʿūl lahu* / *li-ajlih*): *karāhiyata an tamīda bikum* ("out of aversion that it should sway with you") or *li-allā tamīda bikum* ("lest it sway with you" / "so that it does not tilt with you"). Al-Ṭabarī notes that this construction directly parallels [Quran 4:176](quran://4/176): *yubayyinu Allāhu lakum an taḍillū* (*"Allah makes [this] clear to you lest you go astray"*).

* **The Classical Meaning of *Māda / Yamīdu* (مَادَ / يَمِيدُ):** In foundational Arabic lexicons (*Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*, *Lisān al-ʿArab*, and *Lane's Lexicon*, Book I, pp. 2741–2742), *al-mayd* denotes the tilting, listing, swaying, rolling, and pitching of a vessel upon water, or the reeling of an intoxicated person:
  * *Mādat al-safīnatu tamīdu maydan*: "The ship rocked, listed from side to side, and pitched upon the waves."
  * *Al-mayd*: Seasickness and vertigo brought about by the rolling motion of the sea (*al-dūwār alladhī yaʿtarī rākiba al-baḥr*).
  
  The phrase *an tamīda bikum* specifically conveys preventing the terrestrial disc from tilting, pitching, and rolling underneath its inhabitants like a ship tossed on waves. It does not refer to high-frequency seismic shockwaves propagating through solid rock.

### 2. Seismological & Plate Tectonic Empirical Analysis (With Markdown Comparison Table)

Modern geophysics, structural geology, and observational seismology establish an empirical picture of mountain building (orogeny) and lithospheric dynamics that directly diverges from the cosmological framework of [Quran 16:15](quran://16/15):

| Parameter | Modern Empirical Geophysics & Seismology | Quranic Account ([Quran 16:15](quran://16/15), [Quran 41:10](quran://41/10)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Causal Relationship to Earthquakes** | Mountain belts are created by convergent tectonic collisions; they represent the exact zones where over 95% of continental earthquakes occur. | Asserts that mountains were placed specifically to prevent the earth from shaking or swaying with humans (*an tamīda bikum*). |
| **Physical Mechanism of Formation** | Endogenous tectonic process: horizontal plate convergence, crustal thickening, folding, and thrust faulting over tens of millions of years. | Exogenous physical deposition: cast down (*alqā*) onto the pre-existing earth from above (*min fawqihā*). |
| **Density & Isostatic Buoyancy** | Mountains are composed of low-density felsic continental crust (~2.7 g/cm³) floating buoyantly upon denser mantle rock (~3.3 g/cm³). | Conceived as heavy dead-weights or ballast stones (*rawāsī*) placed on top of the earth to weigh it down. |
| **Global Geographic Distribution of Seismicity** | Mountainous collision zones (Himalayas, Zagros, Andes, Alps) suffer the most violent, frequent earthquakes on the continents. | Implies mountainous terrain is stabilized against shaking, whereas flat plains without mountains should experience instability. |
| **Dynamic Nature of Earth's Crust** | Lithospheric plates are in perpetual horizontal motion (1–10 cm/year) across the ductile asthenosphere, driven by mantle convection. | The earth is depicted as a stationary foundation anchored in place by dead-weights to remain perpetually motionless. |

#### Detailed Geological Analysis

1. **Causal Inversion: Mountain Belts Generate Earthquakes:**
   A primary empirical divergence in this reading lies in its causal inversion. [Quran 16:15](quran://16/15) asserts that mountains were established to prevent shaking (*an tamīda bikum*). In reality, mountains are the direct geological byproduct of the very tectonic collisions that generate catastrophic earthquakes.
   According to plate tectonics, the Earth's lithosphere is divided into rigid tectonic plates that constantly move relative to one another over the underlying asthenosphere. When two continental plates collide at convergent boundaries (such as the Indian Plate colliding with the Eurasian Plate, or the Arabian Plate colliding with the Eurasian Plate), the immense compressive stress causes crustal shortening, ductile folding, and brittle thrust faulting. This process—known as orogeny—pushes rock upward to form mountain ranges while simultaneously building up immense elastic strain energy along fault zones. When these faults slip, that stored energy is released as seismic waves: an earthquake.
   Consequently, continental mountain belts are not zones of seismic stability; they are the most seismically hazardous and volatile regions on the planet:
   * **The Alpine-Himalayan Orogenic Belt:** Stretches from the Atlas Mountains through the Pyrenees, Alps, Carpathians, Zagros, Hindu Kush, and Himalayas. This mountain belt accounts for approximately 15% of the world's total seismic energy release and over 95% of catastrophic continental earthquakes (e.g., the 2005 Kashmir earthquake, Mw 7.6, over 86,000 deaths; the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake in the Longmen Shan mountains, Mw 7.9, over 87,000 deaths; the 2015 Gorkha earthquake in Nepal, Mw 7.8; and the 2023 Turkey-Syria earthquakes along the East Anatolian Fault, Mw 7.8, over 55,000 deaths).
   * **The Circum-Pacific Orogenic Belt (Ring of Fire):** Home to the Andes, Cascades, and the mountainous island arcs of Japan, producing over 80% of global seismic energy.
   
   Conversely, the most geologically stable regions on Earth—known as continental cratons or shields (such as the Canadian Shield, the Western Australian Shield, and the Baltic Shield)—are flat, low-relief plains entirely devoid of young mountain ranges. If mountains had been placed to prevent the ground from shaking with humans, mountain valleys would be the safest seismic zones, and flat cratonic plains would be prone to violent shaking. Empirical geography demonstrates the exact opposite.

2. **Endogenous Formation vs. External Deposition (*Alqā*):**
   [Quran 16:15](quran://16/15) states that God *cast* (*alqā*) mountains into the earth, and [Quran 41:10](quran://41/10) clarifies that they were placed *from above it* (*min fawqihā*). In historical geology, mountains were never cast down onto a pre-existing earth from above. Mountain building is an entirely internal, endogenous, bottom-up process. Marine sedimentary rocks containing fossilized ammonites, trilobites, and shells at the summit of Mount Everest demonstrate that mountains are formed by the uplift of former seafloors through lithospheric compression, crustal thickening, and magmatic intrusion over spans of 30 to 100 million years.

3. **Isostasy and Crustal Roots: Buoyancy vs. Ballast Pegs:**
   Concordist writers frequently propose a secondary harmonization of the verse by appealing to Airy isostasy (formulated by astronomer George Biddell Airy in AD 1855), pointing out that mountains have deep crustal "roots" extending into the mantle, which they equate with stabilizing "pegs" (*awtād*, [Quran 78:6](quran://78/6), [Quran 78:7](quran://78/7)). This argument misrepresents the physics of isostasy:
   * **Archimedean Buoyancy, Not Anchoring:** Under Airy isostasy, the Earth's crust floats in hydrostatic equilibrium upon the denser, semi-fluid mantle rock below, governed by Archimedes' principle. Continental crust is predominantly felsic (granitic) with an average density of approximately 2.7 g/cm³, whereas the underlying mantle peridotite has a density of approximately 3.3 g/cm³. Because the crust is lighter than the mantle, a mountain range with high surface elevation must possess a corresponding downward projection of low-density crust (a root) to displace the denser mantle and achieve gravitational equilibrium—precisely analogous to an iceberg floating in water, where 90% of the ice mass lies submerged beneath the waterline.
   * **Roots Do Not Inhibit Motion:** An iceberg's submerged mass does not "peg" it to the ocean floor or prevent it from drifting with ocean currents; likewise, crustal roots do not "peg" or anchor continental plates to the Earth's interior. The entire lithosphere (crust plus rigid upper mantle) slides horizontally over the ductile asthenosphere. Mountain roots move along with the drifting plates.
   * **Gravitational Instability:** Far from preventing movement, the thickened crustal roots of mountain ranges create immense lateral gravitational potential energy gradients. When tectonic convergence slows, over-thickened mountain roots undergo extensional thinning, gravitational spreading, and crustal relaxation, generating intense faulting and additional earthquakes.

  * *"Then Allah mentions the earth and what He placed in it of towering firm mountains and anchored peaks (`al-rawāsī al-shāmikhāt wa-l-jibāl al-rāsiyāt`), so that the earth would settle and not sway (`li-taqarra al-arḍu wa-lā tamīda`), that is, shake with the creatures upon it so that life would not be pleasant for them; hence He said: {And the mountains He has fixed firmly} ([Quran 79:32](quran://79/32))."*
  * Ibn Kathīr quotes ʿAbd al-Razzāq from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: *"When the earth was created, it was swaying (`kānat tamīdu`). The angels said: 'This cannot support anyone on its back.' By the morning, the mountains had been created, and the angels did not know what the mountains were created from."* ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 16:15](ibnkathir://16/15)).

* **Canonical Ḥadīth in Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 3369 and Musnad Aḥmad 12409:**
  This cosmological tradition is explicitly attributed to the Prophet Muhammad in canonical hadith collections. In **[Jami` at-Tirmidhi 3369](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3369)** (Book 47, Hadith 3369; recorded also by Imam Aḥmad in *Musnad Aḥmad* 12409, and cited by Ibn Kathīr under [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 79:32](ibnkathir://79/32)), Anas ibn Mālik reports that the Prophet said:
  * *"When Allah created the earth, it began to sway and tilt (`lammā khalaqa Allāhu al-arḍa jaʿalat tamīdu`), so He created the mountains and cast them upon it, and it stabilized (`fa-alqāhā ʿalayhā fa-staqarrat`). The angels were amazed at the strength of the mountains and asked: 'O Lord, is there anything among Your creation stronger than the mountains?' God replied: 'Yes, iron.' They asked: 'Is there anything stronger than iron?' He said: 'Yes, fire.' They asked: 'Is there anything stronger than fire?' He said: 'Yes, water.' They asked: 'Is there anything stronger than water?' He said: 'Yes, wind...'"*
  
  This canonical report unambiguously confirms that early Islamic tradition understood *alqā rawāsiya* not as tectonic forces operating over geological epochs, but as God literally dropping mountains as physical weights upon an unstable, swaying earth so that it ceased to rock.

* **Cosmic Ocean Exegesis under Quran 21:31 and Quran 68:1:**
  This narrative is further elaborated across classical exegesis regarding the foundation of the earth upon the primordial waters. In [Tafsir al-Tabari 21:31](tabari://21/31) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 21:31](ibnkathir://21/31), Ibn Kathīr explicitly explains why the earth required heavy mountain ballast weights: God weighted the earth down with mountains lest it sway and toss with its inhabitants (`jibālan arsā al-arḍa bihā wa-qarrarahā wa-thaqqalahā li-allā tamīda bi-l-nāsi, ay taḍṭariba wa-tataḥarraka, fa-lā yaḥṣulu lahum ʿalayhā qarārun`), specifically *"because it is submerged in water except for a quarter of it, which is exposed to the air and the sun"* (`li-annahā ghāmiratun fī al-māʾi illā miqdāra al-rubʿi, fa-innahu bādin li-l-hawāʾi wa-l-shamsi`). Furthermore, under the cosmic letter *Nūn* in [Quran 68:1](quran://68/1) ([Tafsir al-Tabari 68:1](tabari://68/1); [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 68:1](ibnkathir://68/1)), leading early authorities including Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid (along with al-Baghawī in Ibn Kathīr) record that God created the earth upon the back of a cosmic fish or whale (*al-ḥūt* / *al-nūn*) floating in the cosmic ocean, and when the creature moved and caused the earth to rock, God anchored heavy mountains upon the earth's surface so that it settled.

---

### 4. Verbatim Pre-Islamic Arabian, Biblical, Rabbinic & Syriac Precedents

The portrayal of the earth as a flat platform floating on primordial waters that requires anchoring by mountains was not unique to the Quran. It was an established cosmological conception circulating throughout pre-Islamic Arabia, biblical literature, rabbinic midrash, and Syriac Christian poetry:

* **Pre-Islamic Arabian Poetry:**
  The exact imagery, verbal roots, and theological ideas found in [Quran 16:15](quran://16/15) appear in the poetry of pre-Islamic Arabian monotheists (*ḥunafāʾ*) and contemporaries of Muhammad:
  * **Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl (d. c. AD 605):** Zayd was a celebrated pre-Islamic monotheist in Mecca, the cousin of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who rejected pagan idolatry prior to Muhammad's prophetic mission. His poetry is preserved by Ibn Isḥāq in *Sīrat Rasūl Allāh*, by al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār in *Jamharat Nasab Quraysh*, by Ibn Kathīr in *al-Bidāyah wa-l-Nihāyah* (Vol. 2, p. 223), and by al-Ālūsī in *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*:
    > دَحَاهَا فَلَمَّا رَآهَا اسْتَوَتْ عَلَى الْمَاءِ أَرْسَى عَلَيْهَا الْجِبَالَا
    > *"He spread it [the earth] out, and when He saw it resting upon the water, He anchored [arsā] the mountains upon it."*
    
    This pre-Islamic verse from the late 6th century AD contains the identical thematic and lexical components found in [Quran 16:15](quran://16/15) and [Quran 79:30](quran://79/30), [Quran 79:32](quran://79/32): spreading the earth (*daḥāhā*), observing it floating upon water (*istawat ʿalā al-mā'*), and anchoring the mountains upon it using the exact root *r-s-w* (*arsā* / *rawāsī*).
  * **Umayyah ibn Abī al-Ṣalt (d. c. AD 626):** Umayyah was a contemporary Thaqafi poet from al-Ṭā'if who composed theological verse regarding creation and ancient prophets. In his *Dīwān* (ed. F. Schulthess, Leipzig, AD 1911; cited also by al-Jāḥiẓ in *Kitāb al-Ḥayawān*), Umayyah writes:
    > وَبَثَّ عَلَيْهَا رَوَاسِيَ الْجِبَالِ فَقَرَّتْ وَكَانَتْ مَائِدَةً تَمِيدُ
    > *"And He scattered upon it the firm mountains [rawāsiya al-jibāl], so it settled, whereas it had been swaying and rocking [mā'idatan tamīdu]."*
    
    The phrasing in Umayyah's poem matches [Quran 16:15](quran://16/15) word for word: *rawāsiya al-jibāl* (firm mountains) and *kānat mā'idatan tamīdu* (swaying and rocking). This demonstrates that the motif of mountains preventing the earth from swaying was an existing idiom of pre-Islamic Arabian oral cosmology.
  * **Labīd ibn Rabīʿah (d. c. AD 661):** The author of one of the celebrated *Muʿallaqāt* describes the towering mountain ranges as timeless anchors (*rawāsin*) fixed to steady the land against the elements.

* **Biblical Imagery of Cosmic Foundations and Pillars:**
  In ancient Hebrew poetry, the terrestrial world is depicted as resting securely upon deep subterranean pillars or foundations set amidst cosmic seas, kept from tottering or shaking:
  * **[Psalm 104:5](bible://ps/104/5):** *"He established the earth upon its foundations, so that it will not totter forever and ever"* (*bal-timmōṭ ʿōlām wā-ʿed*). The Hebrew verb *mōṭ* (מוֹט, to shake, tilt, slip, or totter) is the exact functional semantic equivalent of classical Arabic *māda* (ماد).
  * **[Psalm 75:3](bible://ps/75/3):** *"The earth and all who dwell in it melt; it is I who have firmly set its pillars."*
  * **[Psalm 24:2](bible://ps/24/2):** *"For He has founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the rivers."*
  * **[Job 38:4](bible://jb/38/4), [Job 38:6](bible://jb/38/6):** *"Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? ... On what were its bases sunk, or who laid its cornerstone?"*

* **Rabbinic Midrash and Talmudic Cosmography:**
  In Late Antique Jewish cosmography, the relationship between mountains, the foundation of the earth, and the underlying primordial waters was explicitly debated:
  * **Babylonian Talmud, *b. Ḥagigah* 12b (compiled c. AD 500):** Rabbi Yosi explains the structure of the cosmos: *"The earth stands upon the pillars, and the pillars upon the waters, and the waters upon the mountains, and the mountains upon the wind, and the wind upon the tempest, and the tempest is suspended upon the arm of the Holy One..."*
  * **Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, Chapter 5 (c. 6th–8th century AD):** Records that when God gathered the primordial waters into the seas, the newly formed dry land was unstable and threatened to rock upon the abyssal deep, until the Holy One fastened it with mountains like stakes and anchors to secure its borders.

* **Syriac Christian Hexaemeral Literature (4th–6th Centuries AD):**
  Prominent Syrian church fathers composed poetic verse on the Six Days of Creation (*Hexaemeron*) that circulated throughout Mesopotamia, the Levant, and northern Arabia:
  * **Ephrem the Syrian (d. AD 373), *Commentary on Genesis*:** Depicts God placing the foundations of the dry land upon the waters and consolidating the mountains as massive boundary stones so that the terrestrial platform would not slip into the surrounding ocean.
  * **Jacob of Serugh (d. AD 521), *Homilies on the Six Days of Creation*:** Jacob states that God cast down the massive crags of the mountains onto the earth as heavy weights and balance stones, preventing the floating terrestrial realm from pitching or capsizing amidst the lower cosmic waters.
  * **The Cave of Treasures (*Meʿārath Gazzē*, 6th century AD):** Depicts the Creator gathering the dust of the earth and anchoring it with mountain roots so that it would sit immovably upon the surface of the waters.

---

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Modern Harmonizations

To reconcile [Quran 16:15](quran://16/15) with empirical plate tectonics, modern theological commentators propose three primary harmonizations. Each reading encounters substantive difficulties when evaluated against classical Arabic linguistics and physical science:

* **Harmonization 1: Reinterpreting *Alqā* as Endogenous Magmatic Extrusion:**
  Concordists argue that *alqā* ("cast") does not denote external deposition from above, but rather metaphorical extrusion: God "casting forth" molten lava from within the Earth's interior to form volcanic mountains.
  * *Assessment from Quranic Context:* This reading is directly contradicted by [Quran 41:10](quran://41/10), which describes the exact same placement of mountains: *wa-jaʿala fīhā rawāsiya min fawqihā* (*"And He placed therein firm mountains from above it"*). The prepositional phrase *min fawqihā* ("from above it") explicitly fixes the spatial trajectory of the action as downward from above onto the terrestrial surface.
  * *Assessment from Classical Lexicography:* In classical Arabic, *alqā* means to cast downward or forward away from oneself; it is never used in classical prose or poetry to denote the subterranean upwelling or effusive eruption of magma from deep underground.
  * *Assessment from Tectonic Geology:* Magmatic extrusion accounts for only a minor fraction of the world's mountain belts. The major continental collision belts—including the Himalayas, the Alps, the Zagros, the Urals, and the Appalachians—are non-volcanic fold-and-thrust belts formed by horizontal compression and shortening of continental crust, not by volcanic lava extruded from below.

* **Harmonization 2: Claiming *Tamīda* Refers to Planetary Rotational Wobble (Precession or Nutation):**
  Some modern commentators claim that *tamīda* does not mean local earthquakes, but planetary rotational instability, such as axial precession, Chandler wobble, or polar motion. They argue that mountain roots act as stabilizing counterweights that balance the spinning globe like wheel weights on an automobile.
  * *Assessment from Classical Lexicography:* The verb *māda / yamīdu* specifically designates the mechanical listing, swaying, and rocking of a ship upon water (*takaffu' al-safīnah*) that induces nausea and dizziness (*al-mayd*) in those riding it ([Tafsir al-Tabari 16:15](tabari://16/15)). It does not describe the smooth, gyroscopic rotation of a celestial sphere in vacuum.
  * *Assessment from Geophysics and Planetary Mechanics:* 
    1. *Scale and Topography:* Mountain ranges represent an infinitesimal fraction of Earth's total planetary mass. Mount Everest stands approximately 8.8 kilometers above sea level on a planet with an equatorial radius of approximately 6,378 kilometers (a surface relief of less than 0.14%). Scaled down to the size of a regulation bowling ball or billiard ball, the Earth's surface—including its deepest ocean trenches and highest peaks—is significantly smoother than the allowable tolerance of the ball. Such minuscule surface variations do not stabilize planetary rotation.
    2. *Tectonic Disturbances:* In geophysics, mountains do not stabilize Earth's rotation; on the contrary, large-scale plate motions, orogenic mass redistribution, and megathrust earthquakes actually cause subtle perturbations in Earth's moment of inertia, shifting the figure axis and altering the length of day by microseconds.
    3. *True Planetary Stabilizer:* The primary physical stabilizer of Earth's axial tilt (obliquity) is not terrestrial topography, but the gravitational torque exerted by the Moon. Without the Moon's tidal interaction, Earth's obliquity would experience chaotic variations over millions of years, regardless of how many mountains exist on its crust.

* **Harmonization 3: Conflating Isostasy and Crustal Roots with Earthquake Reduction:**
  Concordist commentators claim that the isostatic roots of mountains penetrate deeply into the lithosphere to "anchor" tectonic plates, thereby dampening seismic shocks and stabilizing the crust for human habitation.
  * *Assessment from Seismology and Rheology:*
    1. *Roots Do Not Inhibit Fault Rupture:* Airy isostasy is a hydrostatic, vertical balance of buoyant crust floating on mantle rock. It provides zero mechanical resistance to the horizontal compressive and shear forces driving plate tectonics. Fault ruptures occur in the brittle upper crust (the seismogenic zone, typically 0–20 km depth), precisely where orogenic stresses are highest.
    2. *Empirical Seismicity:* If mountain roots functioned to dampen seismic activity, regions situated directly atop deep mountain roots would experience fewer and weaker earthquakes than plains. In observational reality, mountain roots are the locus of intense crustal shortening, high strain rates, and recurrent destructive earthquakes. The continental regions with the lowest seismic hazard on Earth are the ancient cratons, which have no mountain roots and no mountain topography.
    3. *Evaluation of the "Tectonic Crumple-Zone / Shock-Absorber" Reading:* A secondary modern harmonization argues that even though mountain belts experience earthquakes, orogenic fold belts act like automotive "crumple zones" or shock absorbers at plate boundaries that absorb kinetic convergence energy so that distant continental interiors do not shake even more violently. This alternative reading is inconsistent with both geophysical mechanics and the textual phrasing. Geophysically, mountain fold-and-thrust belts do not quietly dissipate plate convergence without shaking; rather, brittle-ductile crustal thickening accumulates vast elastic strain energy along major thrust and strike-slip fault networks (often propagating 1,000–2,000 km inland, as across the Tibetan Plateau and Tien Shan) and releases that stored energy catastrophically as high-magnitude earthquakes. Textually, [Quran 16:15](quran://16/15) states that God cast mountains into the earth *"lest it shake with you"* (*an tamīda bikum*)—presenting mountains as stabilizers that prevent the earth from shaking beneath human inhabitants, not as sacrificial seismic zones where millions of mountain inhabitants are subjected to the planet's most lethal earthquakes.

In conclusion, [Quran 16:15](quran://16/15) reflects the observational perspective of ancient Near Eastern antiquity: looking upon massive mountains, ancient peoples intuited them as stationary, heavy anchors cast onto a floating terrestrial surface to keep it from swaying like a ship upon the waters. Transforming this ancient cosmological motif into a prediction of modern seismology requires reversing the physical realities of plate tectonics, in which mountains are the primary product and locus of intense seismic shaking.

21:33.claim: Modern concordist writers claim that Quran 21:33 ('And it is He who created the night and the day and the sun and the moon; all in an orbit are swimming') miraculously reveals that celestial bodies move in curved orbits through space, specifically predicting the Sun's 225–250 million-year galactic orbit around the Milky Way and its axial rotation over a millennium before modern astrophysics.
21:33.classification_explanation: Modern concordist commentators (such as Maurice Bucaille in AD 1976 and Zakir Naik) isolate the classical Arabic phrasing of [Quran 21:33](quran://21/33) (*kullun fī falakin yasbaḥūn*, 'each in an orbit is swimming') and [Quran 36:40](quran://36/40) to assert that the text miraculously anticipates the Sun's 225–250 million-year galactic orbit around the center of the Milky Way or its axial rotation. This claim relies on anachronistic scientific eisegesis that dehistoricizes the verse from classical Arabic lexicography, early Islamic exegetical consensus, and the geocentric cosmology of the 7th-century Near East. In classical Arabic lexicons (*Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*, *Lisān al-ʿArab*), the noun *falak* denotes the circular whorl of a hand-spindle (*falakat al-mighzal*) or the hemispherical vault of heaven, while *yasbaḥūn* denotes gliding across that celestial dome. Early Islamic exegetes ([Tafsir al-Tabari 21:33](tabari://21/33); [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 21:33](ibnkathir://21/33)) unanimously explained the verse as describing the Sun and Moon revolving above a stationary Earth to cause day and night. The Quran repeatedly depicts the Earth as motionless and anchored ([Quran 16:15](quran://16/15); [Quran 27:61](quran://27/61); [Quran 35:41](quran://35/41)), while canonical Prophetic traditions ([Sahih al-Bukhari 3199](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3199)) explicitly define the Sun's daily motion as a physical transit setting beneath the Divine Throne each evening.
21:33.summary: In classical Arabic and early Islamic exegesis (al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir), Quran 21:33's statement that the night, day, sun, and moon are each 'swimming in a falak' describes the Sun and Moon gliding across the dome of the sky (*falak*, a circular spindle-whorl) around a stationary Earth. Rather than predicting the Sun's 230-million-year galactic orbit or axial rotation, the Quran pairs the Sun and Moon as twin luminaries producing day and night while depicting the Earth as fixed and anchored. Canonical hadith (Sahih al-Bukhari 3199) likewise explain the Sun's daily motion as traveling beneath the Divine Throne each night. Historically, this phrasing reflects the pre-Islamic Near Eastern and Greco-Roman geocentric model of celestial spheres revolving around a motionless Earth.
21:33.refutation:
Textual, astronomical, and philological evidence does not support the claim that [Quran 21:33](quran://21/33) anticipates modern orbital mechanics, the Sun's galactic orbit around the Milky Way, or stellar astrophysics. Rather than describing 20th-century astrophysical discoveries, the statement that the night, the day, the sun, and the moon are each *"swimming in an orbit"* (`kullun fī falakin yasbaḥūn`) reflects the standard geocentric cosmology of the 7th-century Near East. In this ancient framework, the Sun and Moon were regarded as twin sister luminaries gliding across the dome of the sky around a stationary, anchored Earth. This meaning is confirmed by classical Arabic lexicography, demonstrated by early Islamic exegesis ([Tafsir al-Tabari 21:33](tabari://21/33); [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 21:33](ibnkathir://21/33)), and corroborated by canonical Prophetic traditions ([Sahih al-Bukhari 3199](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3199)) defining the Sun's daily motion as a physical journey setting beneath the Divine Throne each night.

---

### 1. Context of the Claim & Classical Arabic Philology (Falak and Yasbaḥūn)

Following descriptions of heaven and earth split apart ([Quran 21:30](quran://21/30)), mountains cast down as stabilizing pegs lest the earth shake ([Quran 21:31](quran://21/31)), and the sky constructed as a *"guarded roof"* (`saqfan maḥfūẓan`, [Quran 21:32](quran://21/32)), [Quran 21:33](quran://21/33) declares:

> *"He (it is) who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon, each floating [yasbaḥūn, literally 'swimming'] in (its own) orbit [falak]."* (`wa-huwa al-ladhī khalaqa al-layla wa-l-nahāra wa-l-shamsa wa-l-qamara kullun fī falakin yasbaḥūn`)

This concept is repeated in identical terms in [Quran 36:40](quran://36/40):

> *"It is not fitting for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outrun the day, but each floats [yasbaḥūn, 'swims'] in (its own) orbit [falak]."* (`lā al-shamsu yanbaghī lahā an tudrika al-qamara wa-lā al-laylu sābiqu al-nahāri wa-kullun fī falakin yasbaḥūn`)

Beginning in the late 20th century with Maurice Bucaille (*The Bible, The Qur'an and Science*, AD 1976, pp. 155–164) and popularized by modern concordist writers such as Zakir Naik, commentators claimed that these passages miraculously anticipate the Sun's ~225–250 million-year galactic orbit around the Milky Way center (discovered observationally in AD 1925–1927 by Bertil Lindblad and Jan Oort) and the Sun's axial rotation (discovered observationally via sunspots in AD 1610–1611 by Johannes Fabricius, Christoph Scheiner, and Galileo Galilei).

However, classical Arabic philology indicates that this vocabulary reflects ancient observational cosmology:
* **Etymology of *Falak* (فلك):** The noun *falak* is an ancient Semitic loanword cognate with Akkadian *pilakku* ("spindle whorl") and Aramaic/Syriac *pelakkā* (ܦܠܟܐ, "spindle whorl / sphere"). Classical Arabic lexicons (*Kitāb al-ʿAyn* by al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, d. AD 786; *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* by al-Jawharī, d. AD 1003; *Lisān al-ʿArab* by Ibn Manẓūr, d. AD 1311; *Lane's Lexicon*, vol. 6, pp. 2444–2445) define *falak* primarily through its concrete origin: *falakat al-mighzal* (فلكة المغزل, the rounded whorl on the shaft of a hand-spindle). By extension, early Arabs applied *falak* to any circular structure, specifically designating the revolving dome of the sky (*falak al-samāʾ*) in which celestial bodies revolve daily around the Earth. As recorded in [Tafsir al-Tabari 21:33](tabari://21/33) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 21:33](ibnkathir://21/33), early authorities such as Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī defined *falak* as *"the iron axis of a hand-mill"* (*ka-hayʾati ḥadīdati al-raḥā*) or *"the whorl of a spinning-spindle"* (*ka-falakati al-mighzal*). In classical Arabic, *falak* did not denote an invisible gravitational ellipse in empty space.
* **Semantics of *Yasbaḥūn* (يسبحون):** Derived from the root *s-b-ḥ*, the verb signifies smooth, continuous gliding through a fluid or across an expanse. Classical lexicons record its use for a swift horse whose legs glide smoothly forward without stumbling (*farasun sabūḥ*), a swimmer gliding through water, or a ship cutting through the waves. Applied to celestial bodies, it describes the smooth visual transit of luminaries across the vault of heaven (*fī falakin*). In classical Arabic, *sabaḥa* denotes translatory motion *through* a pathway; it did not mean internal rotation upon an axis (*dāra ḥawla miḥwarihi*). Furthermore, because [Quran 21:33](quran://21/33) uses the same verb for both the Sun and the Moon, interpreting it as axial rotation is inconsistent with observational astronomy: the Moon is tidally locked to Earth, displaying no independent visible rotation to an earthly observer.

---

### 2. Astrophysical & Geocentric Empirical & Textual Analysis & Comparison Table

The cosmological framework established in [Quran 21:33](quran://21/33) and [Quran 36:38](quran://36/38)–[36:40](quran://36/40) exhibits the defining characteristics of ancient geocentrism and diverges from modern heliocentric and galactic astrophysics:

| Astronomical Feature | Modern Heliocentric & Galactic Astrophysics | Quranic & Classical Geocentric Model ([Quran 21:33](quran://21/33); [36:38](quran://36/38)–[36:40](quran://36/40)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Primary Cause of Day and Night** | Caused by Earth's 24-hour axial rotation on its tilted axis while in a 365.25-day heliocentric orbit around the stationary Sun. | Attributed directly to the celestial transit of the Sun and Moon revolving across the sky above a stationary Earth ([Quran 21:33](quran://21/33); [36:40](quran://36/40)). |
| **Dynamical Motion of the Earth** | The Earth undergoes rapid motion: rotating at ~1,670 km/h, orbiting the Sun at ~107,000 km/h, and revolving around the galactic core at ~828,000 km/h. | The Earth is never described as possessing an orbit or rotation; it is explicitly described as fixed and established (*qarār*, [Quran 27:61](quran://27/61); [40:64](quran://40/64)), anchored by mountains lest it shake ([Quran 16:15](quran://16/15); [21:31](quran://21/31)), and held lest it shift ([Quran 35:41](quran://35/41)). |
| **Cosmological Pairing of Sun and Moon** | The Sun is a massive star containing 99.86% of solar system mass; the Moon is a small rocky satellite orbiting the Earth. | The Sun and Moon are treated as twin sister luminaries of comparable significance traveling parallel tracks across the dome of the sky ([Quran 14:33](quran://14/33); [21:33](quran://21/33); [36:40](quran://36/40)). |
| **Grammatical Agreement of Kullun and Yasbaḥūn** | Celestial motions occur on completely separate physical scales: lunar orbit (27.3 days), terrestrial rotation (24 hours), solar galactic orbit (230 million years). | Uses the plural masculine verb *yasbaḥūn* ("they [three or more] swim") rather than the dual, which classical exegetes ([Tafsir al-Tabari 21:33](tabari://21/33)) explain encompasses the night, day, sun, and moon revolving together, or the sun, moon, and stars. |
| **The Sun's Motion at Sunset** | The Sun does not travel anywhere at sunset; the horizon of a rotating spherical Earth turns away from solar illumination. | The Sun physically travels to a resting place (*mustaqarr*, [Quran 36:38](quran://36/38)), which canonical traditions ([Sahih al-Bukhari 3199](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3199)) state is beneath the Divine Throne where it prostrates each night before rising again. |

#### Detailed Breakdown of the Cosmological Evidence

1. **The Alternation of Day and Night as Geocentric Transit:** In [Quran 21:33](quran://21/33), the creation of night and day is paired directly with the sun and moon: *"He (it is) who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon, each floating [yasbaḥūn] in (its own) orbit [falak]."* This pairing is reiterated in [Quran 36:37](quran://36/37)–[36:40](quran://36/40), which states that *"It is not fitting for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outrun the day, but each floats in (its own) orbit."* In modern physics, night and day are optical conditions caused by Earth's axial rotation, not independent entities traveling in orbits. Stating that the sun cannot overtake the moon reflects the geocentric perception of celestial luminaries progressing along the ecliptic path across the sky above a stationary Earth.
2. **The Absence of Terrestrial Orbit:** Across all 114 Surahs, the Quran mentions the sun and moon moving, running (*tajrī*), and swimming (*yasbaḥūn*) dozens of times ([Quran 13:2](quran://13/2); [14:33](quran://14/33); [21:33](quran://21/33); [29:61](quran://29/61); [31:29](quran://31/29); [35:13](quran://35/13); [36:38](quran://36/38); [39:5](quran://39/5)). Conversely, the Quran does not state that the Earth orbits or rotates. Instead, the Earth is uniformly described as a stationary expanse (*firāsh*, *bisāṭ*, *mihād*, [Quran 2:22](quran://2/22); [71:19](quran://71/19); [78:6](quran://78/6)), an established resting place (*qarār*, [Quran 27:61](quran://27/61); [40:64](quran://40/64)), anchored by heavy mountains lest it shake ([Quran 16:15](quran://16/15); [21:31](quran://21/31); [31:10](quran://31/10); [78:7](quran://78/7)), and held alongside the heavens lest they shift from their places ([Quran 35:41](quran://35/41)). Omitting the Earth's orbit—the core parameter of heliocentric astronomy—while emphasizing the Sun's transit over Earth is a standard feature of ancient geocentrism.
3. **The Geocentric Pairing of Sun and Moon:** In heliocentric mechanics, the Moon orbits the Earth, the Earth orbits the Sun, and the entire Solar System orbits the Milky Way core. In ancient geocentric astronomy, the Sun and Moon were paired because both appeared to circle the stationary Earth along the zodiac (the Moon in ~27.3 days, the Sun in ~365.25 days). Pairing the Sun and Moon while excluding the Earth is a characteristic feature of geocentric models. Furthermore, [Quran 21:33](quran://21/33) uses the plural masculine verb *yasbaḥūn* ("they [three or more] swim") rather than the dual (*yasbaḥān*). As classical exegetes ([Tafsir al-Tabari 21:33](tabari://21/33); al-Qurṭubī; al-Rāzī) demonstrate, this plural verb either includes all four entities named in the verse (the night, the day, the sun, and the moon, all four understood as revolving around the Earth) or encompasses the sun, moon, and planets (*al-kawākib*) swimming through the celestial vault.

### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr) and Canonical Ḥadīth

Early Islamic commentators operated without the concept of a heliocentric solar system or a galactic orbit. They interpreted [Quran 21:33](quran://21/33) through the observable geocentric motion of celestial bodies revolving around the Earth:

* **Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī (d. AD 923):** In [Tafsir al-Tabari 21:33](tabari://21/33), Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī compiles the early exegetical consensus:
  * **Ibn ʿAbbās & Mujāhid (d. AD 722):** Reported that *falak* is *"like the shape of the iron axis of a hand-mill"* (*ka-hayʾati ḥadīdati al-raḥā*).
  * **Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (d. AD 728) & Qatādah (d. AD 735):** Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī stated: *"The orbit [falak] is a mill like the shape of the whorl of a spindle"* (*al-falak ṭāḥūnah ka-hayʾati falakati al-mighzal*), while Qatādah stated: *"It runs in the orbit of the heaven as you have seen"* (*yajrī fī falaki al-samāʾi kamā raʾayta*).
  * **The Contained Wave & *Yasbaḥūn*:** Al-Ṭabarī notes that others defined *falak* as *"a contained wave [mawj makfūf] in which the sun, moon, and stars run,"* and records from Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd that *yasbaḥūn* means *"they run"* (*yajrūn*). Commenting on parallel verses in [Tafsir al-Tabari 36:38](tabari://36/38) and [Tafsir al-Tabari 36:40](tabari://36/40), al-Ṭabarī writes: *"And all that We have mentioned of the sun, the moon, the night, and the day, they run in an orbit"* (*wa-kullu mā dhakarnā min al-shamsi wa-l-qamari wa-l-layli wa-l-nahāri fī falakin yajrūn*), confirming that the luminaries traverse designated hemispherical tracks over an Earth-centered realm.
* **Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr (d. AD 1373):** In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 21:33](ibnkathir://21/33), Ibn Kathīr confirms this classical understanding:
  * *"Ibn ʿAbbās said: 'They revolve like a spindle in a whorl' [yadūrūna kamā yadūru al-mighzalu fī al-falakah]. Mujāhid said similarly: 'The spindle does not turn except with the whorl, nor does the whorl turn except with the spindle. Likewise, the stars, the sun, and the moon do not revolve except with it [the celestial sphere], nor does it revolve except with them.'"*
  * In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 36:38](ibnkathir://36/38) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 36:40](ibnkathir://36/40), he reiterates that each luminary has its own appointed circuit and heavenly sphere (*falak*) circling above the earth, stating under [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 36:40](ibnkathir://36/40) that *kullun fī falakin yasbaḥūn* *"means, night and day, the sun and the moon, all of them are floating, i.e., revolving, in their orbits in the heaven. This was the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī."*
* **The Canonical Prophetic Ḥadīth of Abū Dharr:** The nature of the Sun's motion in early Islamic theology is documented by the canonical tradition narrated by Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī in **[Sahih al-Bukhari 3199](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3199)** (parallel in **[Sahih al-Bukhari 4802](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4802)**, **[Sahih al-Bukhari 7424](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7424)**, and **[Sahih Muslim 159a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:159a)**), directly interpreting the Sun's course in [Quran 36:38](quran://36/38):
  > *"The Prophet asked me at sunset, 'Do you know where the sun goes (at the time of sunset)?' I replied, 'Allah and His Apostle know better.' He said, **'It goes (i.e. travels) till it prostrates itself underneath the Throne and takes the permission to rise again, and it is permitted and then (a time will come when) it will be about to prostrate itself but its prostration will not be accepted, and it will ask permission to go on its course but it will not be permitted, but it will be ordered to return whence it has come and so it will rise in the west.'**"*

This canonical tradition demonstrates that the Sun's motion in early Islam was understood as its daily geocentric circuit setting in the west, traveling beneath the Divine Throne during the night, and rising again in the east each morning, rather than a 225-million-year orbit around the Milky Way galaxy.

### 4. Verbatim Pre-Islamic Babylonian, Egyptian, and Greco-Roman Precedents

The concept of the sun and moon traveling in circular courses or celestial spheres across the sky was a standard cosmological model across the ancient Near East and Mediterranean for centuries prior to Islam:

1. **Mesopotamian & Babylonian Astronomy (c. 1100–500 BC):** In the Babylonian astronomical compendium *MUL.APIN* (c. 1000 BC) and the creation epic *Enūma Eliš* (Tablet V, lines 1–24, c. 1100 BC), the celestial sphere is mapped into three concentric paths (*harrānu*) belonging to Anu, Enlil, and Ea. The Sun (Šamaš), Moon (Sîn), and five visible wandering planets were observed to move along established circular courses (*kippatu*, "circle / whorl") across the sky above a fixed Earth. Akkadian texts specifically used *pilakku* ("spindle whorl") to describe the rotational motion of the celestial vault around the cosmic axis.
2. **Greco-Roman Geocentric Astronomy (4th Century BC – 2nd Century AD):**
   * **Eudoxus of Cnidus (c. 390–337 BC):** Formulated concentric homocentric spheres (*sphairai*) carrying celestial bodies in nested circular revolutions around a stationary Earth.
   * **Aristotle (*De Caelo* II.7–8, c. 350 BC):** Established the physical model wherein Earth sits motionless at the universe's center, surrounded by nested crystalline spheres (*sphairai*, translated into Arabic as *aflāk*, singular *falak*) carrying the Moon, Sun, planets, and stars in circular revolutions.
   * **Claudius Ptolemy (c. AD 100–170):** Codified the mathematical geocentric model in his *Syntaxis Mathematica* (*al-Majisṭī* / *The Almagest*) and *Planetary Hypotheses* (translated into Syriac and subsequently Arabic in the 8th and 9th centuries AD), describing the Sun and Moon as each occupying its own spherical shell (*sphaira* / *falak*) revolving around Earth. The phrase *kullun fī falakin* directly reflects this standard Late Antique conception of nested celestial spheres.
3. **Ancient Egyptian Solar Barque & Near Eastern "Cosmic Ocean":** In Ancient Egyptian solar religion (*Book of the Dead* Spell 15; *Amduat*, c. 1500–1000 BC), the Sun god Re navigates across the daytime sky in the *Māndjet* barque and through underworld waters at night in the *Meskett* barque, sailing across the celestial waters of Nun. In broader ancient Near Eastern cosmology, the sky was understood as a firmament holding back celestial waters above (cf. [Genesis 1:6](bible://gn/1/6)–[1:7](bible://gn/1/7); [Psalm 148:4](bible://ps/148/4), *"Praise Him, highest heavens, and you waters that are above the heavens"*). Because the heavens were conceived as containing upper celestial waters, celestial luminaries were naturally described as "gliding" or "swimming" (*yasbaḥūn*) across the heavenly expanse—a concept preserved directly in [Tafsir al-Tabari 21:33](tabari://21/33) under the view that the *falak* is *mawj makfūf* ("a contained wave").

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Modern Harmonizations

Modern concordist commentators seek to reconcile the geocentric language of [Quran 21:33](quran://21/33) with modern astrophysics through three primary proposals:

* **Proposal 1: The Claim That *Yasbaḥūn* Refers to Axial Rotation:**
  * *Concordist Argument:* Commentators propose that *yasbaḥūn* ("they swim") refers to the Sun's rotation on its own axis, identified through sunspot tracking by Galileo and subsequent astronomers.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* This interpretation is not supported on either linguistic or astrophysical grounds. Linguistically, *sabaḥa* denotes translatory motion *through* an external medium or pathway (*fī falakin*, "in a sphere/orbit"), not intrinsic rotation upon an internal stationary axis (*dāra ḥawla miḥwarihi*). Astronomically, [Quran 21:33](quran://21/33) applies *yasbaḥūn* equally to both the Sun and the Moon (*kullun fī falakin yasbaḥūn*). The Moon is tidally locked to Earth; its rotational period matches its orbital period, meaning it perpetually presents the same face to Earth and exhibits no visible independent rotation to an earthly observer. Describing both bodies with the identical verb *yasbaḥūn* in their *falak* reflects their observed daily orbital progression across the sky rather than independent axial rotation.
* **Proposal 2: The Claim That *Falak* Refers to the Sun's Galactic Orbit:**
  * *Concordist Argument:* Concordist writers propose that *falak* refers to the Solar System's ~230-million-year revolution around the center of the Milky Way galaxy.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* This interpretation diverges from physical and textual analysis. In [Quran 21:33](quran://21/33) and [Quran 36:37](quran://36/37)–[36:40](quran://36/40), motion in the *falak* is directly tied to the alternating cycle of human day and night (*al-layla wa-l-nahār*). The Sun's galactic orbit takes ~230 million years and has no physical connection to the 24-hour diurnal cycle of day and night on Earth. Furthermore, in galactic astrophysics, Earth and Moon are gravitationally bound to the Sun and orbit the galactic center alongside the Sun at the same orbital velocity (~220–230 km/s). If [Quran 21:33](quran://21/33) described galactic motion, singling out the Sun and Moon while excluding Earth would be inconsistent with empirical findings.
* **Proposal 3: The Claim of Phenomenological Language:**
  * *Concordist Argument:* When addressing geocentric implications, commentators frequently propose that the Quran employs "phenomenological language"—describing celestial phenomena as they appear from the perspective of an Earth-bound observer.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* While it is historically accurate that [Quran 21:33](quran://21/33) employs phenomenological language reflecting the observational perspective of ancient humans watching the sun and moon travel across the sky, this reading is incompatible with the concordist hypothesis. If the text describes how the cosmos appears to a pre-scientific human observer on the ground, it does not constitute an empirical disclosure of modern astrophysics. The appearance of the sun and moon traveling across the sky above a stationary earth was the shared perception of ancient Near Eastern cultures, accounting for the phrasing of the verse without requiring modern astrophysical foreknowledge.

This interpretation separates [Quran 10:5](quran://10/5) from its historical and linguistic context in classical Arabic lexicography (*Lisān al-ʿArab*, *Maqāyīs al-Lughah*), internal Quranic usage ([Quran 24:35](quran://24/35), [Quran 2:17](quran://2/17), [Quran 33:46](quran://33/46)), early Islamic exegetical traditions ([Tafsir al-Tabari 10:5](tabari://10/5), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 10:5](ibnkathir://10/5), [Tafsir al-Tabari 17:12](tabari://17/12)), and over a millennium of established pre-Islamic Greek and Indian astronomy (Parmenides, Anaxagoras, Aristotle, Ptolemy, Āryabhaṭa), which had already documented that the moon reflects the sun's light.

Classical Arabic lexicons define *nūr* as light broadly rather than reflected light, and the Quran itself calls God *nūr* (24:35) while using both *ḍiyāʾ* and *nūr* for a single burning fire (2:17). Moreover, early authorities like Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAlī explained under Quran 17:12 that the moon originally shone with its own light like the sun before being dimmed. Historically, Greek and Indian astronomers (Anaxagoras, Aristotle, Ptolemy, and Āryabhaṭa) had already demonstrated that the moon reflects sunlight centuries before the 7th century AD.
10:5.refutation:
Textual, philological, exegetical, and historical evidence indicates that [Quran 10:5](quran://10/5) does not describe the optical physics of lunar reflection. The verse employs standard 7th-century Arabic vocabulary describing the observable contrast between intense daytime illumination and gentle nighttime light for calendrical reckoning. Classical Arabic lexicons define *nūr* as intrinsic light broadly rather than reflected light, while Greek, Roman, and Indian astronomers had mathematically demonstrated that the moon reflects sunlight more than a millennium prior to the 7th century AD.

### 1. Philological & Intratextual Analysis of Ḍiyāʾ and Nūr

In [Quran 10:5](quran://10/5), the text describes the creation of the two primary luminaries:

> *"He it is who made the sun a radiance (`ḍiyāʾan`) and the moon a light (`nūran`) and determined for it stations, that you might know the number of years and the reckoning of time..."* (`huwa al-ladhī jaʿala al-shamsa ḍiyāʾan wa-l-qamara nūran wa-qaddarahu manāzila li-taʿlamū ʿadada al-sinīna wa-l-ḥisāb`)

In the late 20th century, concordist authors such as Maurice Bucaille (*The Bible, The Qur'an and Science*, AD 1976) and subsequent commentators proposed that this verse encodes an astrophysical distinction. Under this reading, designating the sun as *ḍiyāʾ* (or *sirāj*, a burning lamp, in [Quran 71:16](quran://71/16) and [Quran 25:61](quran://25/61)) and the moon as *nūr* (or *munīr*) indicates that the sun generates its own light whereas the moon passively reflects it.

#### Classical Arabic Lexicography

This lexical hypothesis is not supported by foundational classical Arabic dictionaries, including *Kitāb al-ʿAyn* by al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad (d. c. AD 786), *Maqāyīs al-Lughah* by Ibn Fāris (d. AD 1004), *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* by al-Jawharī (d. AD 1003), *al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān* by al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. AD 1108), *Lisān al-ʿArab* by Ibn Manẓūr (d. AD 1311), and Lane's *Arabic-English Lexicon*:

* **Nūr Signifies Light Broadly, Not Reflection:** In classical Arabic, *nūr* denotes light or illumination in an unrestricted sense (`al-ḍawʾ ayyan kāna`). Ibn Manẓūr records in *Lisān al-ʿArab* that *al-nūr* is *al-ḍawʾ*. Classical lexicography does not define *nūr* as "reflected light."
* **Classical Terms for Reflection:** When Arabic writers described optical reflection, they used roots such as *ʿ-k-s* (*inʿakasa*, *inʿikās al-ḍawʾ*, "reflection of light") or *r-d-d* (*irtidād al-shuʿāʿ*, "rebounding of rays"), as attested in the optical treatises of al-Kindī (d. c. AD 873) and Ibn al-Haytham (d. AD 1040). Neither *inʿikās* nor any cognate term for reflection appears in the Quran regarding the moon.
* **Perceptual Intensity vs. Physical Mechanism:** Classical philologists distinguished *ḍiyāʾ* from *nūr* on the basis of naked-eye perceptual intensity and heat: *ḍiyāʾ* denotes dazzling, heat-bearing radiance (midday sun, lightning, or fire), whereas *nūr* denotes cooler, softer illumination (moonlight, dawn, or a lamp). The distinction is observational and phenomenological rather than astrophysical.

#### Intratextual Quranic Usage

The interpretation that *nūr* denotes passive reflection diverges from intratextual usage across the Quran:

1. **Allah Designated as Nūr ([Quran 24:35](quran://24/35)):** In the Verse of Light, the Quran states: *"Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth"* (`Allāhu nūru al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍ`), comparing this divine *nūr* to a lamp (`miṣbāḥ`) in a glass vessel, *"kindled from a blessed olive tree... whose oil would almost glow forth even if untouched by fire."* If *nūr* signified "reflected light," the passage would characterize God as a passive reflector of an external source and an actively burning olive-oil lamp as emitting only reflected light—a reading inconsistent with classical Islamic theology.
2. **Fire Producing Both Ḍiyāʾ and Nūr Interchangeably ([Quran 2:17](quran://2/17)):** Describing one who kindles a fire (*nār*), the text states: *"When it illuminated (`aḍāʾat`, root `ḍ-w-ʾ`) what was around him, Allah took away their light (`bi-nūrihim`, root `n-w-r`) and left them in darkness."* The identical flame generates both *ḍiyāʾ* and *nūr* within a single sentence, demonstrating that both roots describe the direct emission of a wood fire.
3. **Lightning, Daylight, and Scripture as Ḍiyāʾ and Nūr:** In [Quran 2:20](quran://2/20), the flash of lightning is described with *aḍāʾa*, while in [Quran 28:71](quran://28/71), daytime illumination dispelling continuous night is called *ḍiyāʾ*. In [Quran 21:48](quran://21/48), the Torah given to Moses is called *ḍiyāʾan*, while in [Quran 5:44](quran://5/44) it is described as containing *hudan wa-nūr* ("guidance and light"). Across these passages, the terms function as stylistic variants for luminous clarity rather than distinct physical categories of emission and reflection.
4. **The Prophet Muhammad as Sirājan Munīran ([Quran 33:46](quran://33/46)):** In [Quran 33:46](quran://33/46), the Prophet is commissioned as *"an illuminating lamp"* (`sirājan munīran`). The noun *sirāj* designates a burning oil lamp, while *munīr* is the Form IV active participle of *anāra* (root *n-w-r*). If *munīr* signified a passive reflector, pairing it with *sirāj* would be semantically incongruous; in classical Arabic grammar, *munīr* denotes an entity actively radiating light.
