### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr) and Early Exegetical Traditions

In classical Islamic exegesis, commentators interpreted [Quran 10:5](quran://10/5) within temporal and calendrical frameworks rather than as an account of lunar optical reflection.

#### Exegesis of Quran 10:5 in al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr

In [Tafsir al-Tabari 10:5](tabari://10/5), Abu Jaʿfar al-Ṭabarī (d. AD 923) explains the verse in observational and temporal terms:

> *"He, exalted be His mention, says: Verily your Lord is Allah who created the heavens and the earth. {He it is who made the sun an illumination}, during the day, {and the moon a light}, during the night. And the meaning of that is: He is the One who illuminated the sun and gave light to the moon."* (`wa-maʿnā dhālika: huwa al-ladhī aḍāʾa al-shamsa wa-anāra al-qamar`)

Al-Ṭabarī notes that God established distinct stations (*manāzil*) for the moon so human observers could compute months and years by tracking the lunar phases, without mentioning optical reflection from the sun.

In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 10:5](ibnkathir://10/5), Ibn Kathīr (d. AD 1373) characterizes the distinction as one between two varieties of emitted rays rather than between emission and reflection:

> *"He made the rays issuing from the body of the sun `ḍiyāʾ` and the rays of the moon `nūr`—this is one kind and that is another kind; He varied between them so that they would not be confused with one another."* (`jaʿala al-shuʿāʿa al-ṣādira ʿan jarmi al-shamsi ḍiyāʾan wa-shuʿāʿa al-qamari nūran, hādhā fannun wa-hādhā fannun ākhar`)

Describing the lunar phases, Ibn Kathīr states that the moon initially appears small, *"then its light and its body increase (`yatazāyadu nūruhu wa-jarmuhu`), until it becomes complete and its fullness is perfected."* Citing [Quran 36:39](quran://36/39)–[36:40](quran://36/40) and [Quran 6:96](quran://6/96), Ibn Kathīr frames the passage around calendrical observation rather than optical reflection.

#### Early Exegetical Traditions on the Effacement of the Moon's Light ([Quran 17:12](quran://17/12))

Classical exegetical compilations also preserve early traditions indicating that the first Muslim generations understood the moon to have been created as an intrinsic, self-luminous body similar to the sun. Under [Quran 17:12](quran://17/12) (*"And We made the night and the day two signs, and We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day sight-giving"*, `fa-maḥawnā āyata al-layli wa-jaʿalnā āyata al-nahāri mubṣiratan`), both [Tafsir al-Tabari 17:12](tabari://17/12) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 17:12](ibnkathir://17/12) record traditions transmitted from the Companions and early Successors, including Caliph ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, ʿAbdallāh ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿAbdallāh ibn Kathīr, and Qatādah:

1. **Ibn ʿAbbās Applying the Root of Ḍiyāʾ to the Moon:** In reports recorded in both [Tafsir al-Tabari 17:12](tabari://17/12) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 17:12](ibnkathir://17/12), ʿAbdallāh ibn ʿAbbās stated:
   > `كَانَ الْقَمَرُ يُضِيءُ كَمَا تُضِيءُ الشَّمْسُ، وَالْقَمَرُ آيَةُ اللَّيْلِ، وَالشَّمْسُ آيَةُ النَّهَارِ، فَمَحَوْنَا آيَةَ اللَّيْلِ: السَّوَادُ الَّذِي فِي الْقَمَرِ`
   > *"The moon used to shine just as the sun shines (`kāna al-qamaru yuḍīʾu kamā tuḍīʾu al-shams`), and the moon is the sign of the night, and the sun is the sign of the day. `{We have blotted out the sign of the night}`: the blackness that is in the moon (`al-sawādu alladhī fī al-qamar`)."*
   In this statement, Ibn ʿAbbās applies the verb *yuḍīʾu* (the verbal form of *ḍiyāʾ*) to the moon's original intrinsic light, indicating that early Islamic authorities did not treat the root *ḍ-w-ʾ* as an exclusive physical property of solar emission.
2. **ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib on the Lunar Blotch (`al-Laṭkhah` / `al-Sawād`):** In a report graded by Ibn Kathīr in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 17:12](ibnkathir://17/12) as transmitted via *"multiple good routes"* (`min ṭuruqin mutaʿaddidatin jayyidah`), ʿAbdallāh ibn al-Kawwāʾ asked Caliph ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib about the dark markings on the lunar surface: *"O Commander of the Faithful, what is this smudge/blotch (`al-laṭkhah` / `al-sawād`) in the moon?"* ʿAlī answered: *"Woe to you, do you not read the Quran: `{We have blotted out the sign of the night}`? So this is its blotting out (`fa-hādhihi maḥwuhu`)."*
3. **Qatādah Using Anwar (Comparative of Nūr) for the Sun:** In [Tafsir al-Tabari 17:12](tabari://17/12) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 17:12](ibnkathir://17/12), the early commentator Qatādah stated: *"We used to be told that the blotting out of the sign of the night is the blackness of the moon that is in it... And He created the sun more luminous and greater than the moon (`wa-khalaqa al-shamsa anwara min al-qamari wa-aʿẓam`)."* Qatādah specifically employed *anwar* (the comparative form of *nūr*) to describe the sun, showing that early commentators viewed the two luminaries as differing in degree of luminous intensity (*anwar*) rather than in emission versus reflection.
4. **The Wing of Gabriel Tradition in Classical Chronicles:** In his historical chronicle *Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk* (vol. 1, pp. 72–73), al-Ṭabarī records an early narrative (also cited in later commentaries by al-Thaʿlabī, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Suyūṭī's *al-Durr al-Manthūr* on 17:12) stating that Allah sent the angel Gabriel (*Jibrīl*), who passed his wing across the face of the moon three times to dim its brightness, leaving the dark lunar maria as the trace of that effacement.

These early traditions indicate that 7th-century exegetes understood *ḍiyāʾ* and *nūr* as graduations of intrinsic luminescence rather than a distinction between active nuclear emission and passive optical reflection.

---

### 4. Pre-Islamic Greek, Roman, Indian, and Near Eastern Astronomical Precedents

From the standpoint of the history of science, the principle that the moon shines by reflected solar light had been geometrically modeled and documented across the Mediterranean, Near East, and India for over a millennium prior to the 7th century AD.

#### 1. Visual Contrast Between Sun and Moon in Ancient Literature

Observing that the sun is dazzling and heat-bearing while the moon is mild and cool is a universal sensory experience. In the Hebrew Bible ([Genesis 1:16](bible://gn/1/16)), composed centuries before the Quran, the text records:

> *"God made the two great lights: the greater light to govern the day, and the lesser light to govern the night; He made the stars also."*

Pairing a greater daytime luminary with a lesser nighttime luminary for calendrical governance was standard literary convention across ancient Near Eastern traditions.

#### 2. Documentation of Lunar Reflection in Antiquity (500 BC – AD 500)

More than a thousand years before the compilation of the Quran, ancient natural philosophers demonstrated that the moon is an opaque sphere reflecting sunlight:

1. **Parmenides of Elea (Early 5th Century BC):** In his philosophical poem (DK 28 B14–15), Parmenides wrote of the moon: *"Shining by night with borrowed light (`allotrion phōs`), wandering around the earth... Always looking toward the rays of the sun."*
2. **Anaxagoras of Clazomenae (c. 500–428 BC):** Anaxagoras formulated the physical principle (DK 59 B18; Plato *Cratylus* 409a–b): *"It is the sun that puts the brightness into the moon (`hēlios entithēsi tēi selēnēi to lampron`)."* He demonstrated that lunar phases depend on geometric position relative to the sun, and deduced that solar eclipses occur when the moon interposes between the sun and earth, while lunar eclipses occur when the earth blocks sunlight.
3. **Empedocles of Acragas (c. 494–434 BC):** Empedocles described the moon as reflecting solar rays (DK 31 B42–45), characterizing it as an opaque body whose illumination rebounds from the sun.
4. **Aristotle (384–322 BC):** Across *Posterior Analytics* (I.13, 78b4–11; II.8, 93a30–b7), *De Caelo* (II.11, 291b18–23), and *De Generatione Animalium* (IV.10, 777b24–27), Aristotle demonstrated the moon's sphericity (`σφαιροειδής`, *sphairoeidēs*) from its crescent and gibbous phases, defined lunar eclipses as the earth's screening (`ἀντίφραξις ὑπὸ γῆς`, *antiphraxis hypo gēs*) of solar rays, and stated that the moon's illumination derives *"from its sharing in the light of the sun"* (`διὰ τὸ τῆς τοῦ ἡλίου κοινωνεῖν φωτός`, *dia to tēs tou hēliou koinōnein phōtos*), consistent with standard Greek doxography using *phōtizesthai hypo tou hēliou* (`φωτίζεσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου`, "to be illuminated by the sun"; Plato *Cratylus* 409a–b; Plutarch *De Facie* 929b; Aëtius *Placita* II.28).
5. **Plutarch (c. AD 46–119) and Ptolemy (c. AD 100–170):** In *De Facie in Orbe Lunae* (chs. 16–21), Plutarch analyzed optical reflection (*anaklasis*) from the lunar surface. In the *Almagest* (Book V), Ptolemy modeled celestial orbits on the premise that the moon is an opaque sphere illuminated by the sun.
6. **Āryabhaṭa (AD 476–550):** In classical Indian astronomy, Āryabhaṭa recorded the physical mechanism in the *Āryabhaṭīya* (Golapāda, verse 5, AD 499): *"The halves of the earth, the planets, and the moon are dark due to their own shadows; the other halves facing the sun are lighted according to their distance from the sun."*

#### Comparative Terminological Analysis

Whereas Greek, Roman, and Indian astronomical treatises centuries before Islam employed explicit technical terminology for borrowed or reflected light (*allotrion phōs*, *anaklasis*), [Quran 10:5](quran://10/5) employs the general noun *nūr* ("light") without specifying an optical reflection mechanism.

---

### 5. Evaluation of Secondary Concordist Harmonizations

Several secondary linguistic and historical arguments have been advanced in concordist literature regarding [Quran 10:5](quran://10/5); each can be evaluated against primary philological and historical sources:

* **Appeal to Quran 25:61, 71:16, and 78:13 (Sirāj vs. Munīr):**
  * *Concordist Argument:* Proponents suggest that pairing *sirāj* ("lamp") with the sun in [Quran 25:61](quran://25/61), [Quran 71:16](quran://71/16), and [Quran 78:13](quran://78/13) (*sirājan wahhājan*, "a blazing lamp") while designating the moon as *munīr* ("illuminating") indicates that the moon is an inert reflector.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* Associating the daytime sun with heat and burning (*wahaj*, *sirāj*) and the nighttime moon with cool illumination (*nūr*) reflects direct sensory experience in the Arabian environment. Grammatically, *munīr* is the Form IV active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) of *anāra* ("to illuminate, give light"), signifying an active agent shedding light. This grammatical function is corroborated in [Quran 33:46](quran://33/46), where the Prophet Muhammad is designated *sirājan munīran* ("an illuminating lamp"), and in [Quran 3:184](quran://3/184) and [Quran 35:25](quran://35/25), where scripture is called *al-kitāb al-munīr* ("the illuminating book"). Applying *munīr* to an actively burning lamp (*sirāj*) confirms that the root *n-w-r* denotes active illumination rather than passive reflection.
* **Post-Abbasid Scholastic Tafsīrs (al-Rāzī & al-Bayḍāwī) and Ibn al-Haytham:**
  * *Concordist Argument:* Later medieval commentaries by Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī (d. AD 1210) and al-Bayḍāwī (d. AD 1286), as well as the optical works of Ibn al-Haytham (d. AD 1040), are sometimes cited as evidence that classical Islam derived lunar reflection from [Quran 10:5](quran://10/5).
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* When al-Rāzī and al-Bayḍāwī discussed whether *ḍiyāʾ* is essential (*bi-l-dhāt*) and *nūr* is acquired (*bi-l-ʿaraḍ*), they wrote five to six centuries after the 7th century—long after Ptolemaic Greek astronomy had been translated into Arabic during the Abbasid translation movement. Both al-Rāzī and al-Bayḍāwī explicitly attributed the lunar-reflection model to astronomers (*ahl al-hayʾah*) rather than deriving it from early Islamic tradition or classical Arabic lexicography. Similarly, when the 11th-century polymath Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen, *Kitāb al-Manāẓir*) analyzed primary and secondary light, he built upon Euclidean and Ptolemaic optics four centuries after the Quran, demonstrating that illuminated bodies radiate secondary light from every point on their surface without attributing his optical physics to [Quran 10:5](quran://10/5).
* **Hypothesis of Seventh-Century Scientific Isolation:**
  * *Concordist Argument:* It is occasionally proposed that 7th-century Arabia had no access to ancient astronomical concepts, rendering any distinction between solar and lunar light extraordinary.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* Historical scholarship documents the circulation of Hellenistic and Syriac astronomical traditions across the Late Antique Near East, while the phrasing of [Quran 10:5](quran://10/5) itself remains grounded in naked-eye observations of daytime and nighttime luminaries for calendrical reckoning.

In summary, [Quran 10:5](quran://10/5) employs standard 7th-century Arabic terminology to contrast the intense daytime sun with the cooler nighttime moon for calendrical utility. Projecting modern astrophysical models of nuclear emission and planetary reflection onto *ḍiyāʾ* and *nūr* diverges from classical Arabic lexicography, intratextual Quranic usage, early Islamic exegesis, and over a millennium of pre-Islamic astronomical literature.

This assertion dehistoricizes the Quranic text by overlooking that ancient Near Eastern agricultural societies had practiced artificial pollination of dioecious date palms for millennia—as documented in the Babylonian Code of Hammurabi (§§ 64–65, c. 1750 BC), Herodotus's *Histories* (I.193, c. 440 BC), Theophrastus's *Historia Plantarum* (II.8.4, c. 300 BC), and Pliny the Elder's *Naturalis Historia* (XIII.7.31–35, AD 77). Furthermore, this reading diverges from classical Islamic exegesis—which defines *zawjayni ithnayn* as 'two kinds and two types' (*nawʿayni wa-ḍarbayn*, [Tafsir al-Tabari 13:3](tabari://13/3)) or 'from each form, two sorts' (*min kulli shaklin ṣinfān*) of fruits varying in colors, shapes, tastes, and scents ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 13:3](ibnkathir://13/3)), illustrated in the adjoining verse ([Quran 13:4](quran://13/4)) by contrasting varieties such as sweet and sour or white and black ([Tafsir al-Tabari 13:4](tabari://13/4); [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 13:4](ibnkathir://13/4))—and does not account for canonical prophetic traditions ([Sahih Muslim 2361](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2361), [Sahih Muslim 2362](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2362), and [Sahih Muslim 2363](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2363)), in which Muhammad explicitly disclaimed possessing specialized botanical revelation regarding date palm pollination.
13:3.summary: In classical Arabic and early exegesis, [Quran 13:3](quran://13/3)'s "two in pairs" (*zawjayni ithnayn*) of all fruits (*thamarāt*) means "two kinds and two types" ([Tafsir al-Tabari 13:3](tabari://13/3)) or "two sorts" varying in color, shape, taste, and scent ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 13:3](ibnkathir://13/3))—such as sweet and sour or white and black ([Tafsir al-Tabari 13:4](tabari://13/4))—not male and female floral organs. Botanically, fruits have no sex, many (like bananas and figs) grow asexually without pollination, and 85–90% of flowering plants are hermaphroditic in one bloom rather than male-female pairs. Hand-pollinating date palms was standard since Hammurabi's Code (c. 1750 BC), and in [Sahih Muslim 2361](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2361) Muhammad called it human farming conjecture rather than revelation.
13:3.refutation:
Botanical, philological, and historical evidence indicates that [Quran 13:3](quran://13/3) does not anticipate modern plant reproductive biology. Rather than describing angiosperm reproduction via male stamens and female pistils, the clause *wa-min kulli al-thamarāti jaʿala fīhā zawjayni ithnayn* (*"And of all fruits He made therein two pairs/kinds"*) reflects a classical Arabic idiom for complementary agricultural varieties—"two kinds and two types" (*nawʿayni wa-ḍarbayn*, [Tafsir al-Tabari 13:3](tabari://13/3)) or "from each form, two sorts" (*min kulli shaklin ṣinfān*) varying in color, shape, taste, and scent ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 13:3](ibnkathir://13/3)), such as sweet and sour or white and black ([Tafsir al-Tabari 13:4](tabari://13/4); [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 13:4](ibnkathir://13/4)). Moreover, empirical botanical data diverge from the concordist reading: fruits are post-fertilization structures lacking biological sex, many fruits develop asexually without fertilization (parthenocarpy and apomixis), and the vast majority of flowering plants are hermaphroditic rather than separate male and female pairs. Finally, artificial pollination of date palms was standard agricultural practice across the ancient Near East for millennia prior to Islam, as documented in Mesopotamian law, Greek treatises, and canonical hadith ([Sahih Muslim 2361](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2361)).

---

### 1. Context of the Claim & Classical Arabic Philology (Thamarāt and Zawjayn Ithnayn)

Concordist writers propose that [Quran 13:3](quran://13/3) anticipated the botanical discoveries of Rudolf Jakob Camerarius (*De Sexu Plantarum Epistola*, AD 1694) and Carl Linnaeus (*Systema Naturae*, AD 1735), who demonstrated that flowering plants reproduce sexually through male stamens and female pistils. Proponents assert that stating God made "two pairs" of all fruits describes this universal botanical reality.

However, classical Arabic lexicography (*Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, *Lisān al-ʿArab*, and *Lane's Lexicon*, Book I, p. 356) and intra-Quranic usage do not support this interpretation:

* **The Meaning of *Al-Thamarāt* (الثمرات):** In classical Arabic, *thamarah* refers strictly to the edible fruit or yield of a plant—the ripened ovary and pericarp produced *after* pollination. It is linguistically distinct from the flower (*zahr* / *nawr*) or the palm pollen cluster (*ṭalʿ*; cf. [Quran 26:148](quran://26/148); [Quran 50:10](quran://50/10)). Fruits themselves possess no biological sex: an apple or olive is neither male nor female. Even in dioecious species where separate male and female trees exist (such as date palms), only the female tree bears fruit (*thamarah*); the male tree produces pollen clusters and never bears fruit. Thus, asserting that God made male and female pairs *of the fruits* is biologically inaccurate.
* **The Classical Idiom of *Zawjayni Ithnayn* (زوجين اثنين):** In Arabic grammar, *zawj* denotes a counterpart, class, sort, or species that complements another. In the Quran, the plural *azwāj* repeatedly designates distinct categories rather than sexual mates:
  * In [Quran 56:7](quran://56/7), humanity on the Day of Resurrection is divided into *azwājan thalāthah* (*"three kinds"*), referring to the companions of the right, the companions of the left, and the foremost.
  * In [Quran 20:53](quran://20/53), the text refers to *azwājan min nabātin shattā* (*"diverse kinds of vegetation"*).
  * In [Quran 38:58](quran://38/58), it describes punishments of *ākharu min shaklihī azwāj* (*"others of its shape, of various kinds"*).
  Consequently, *zawjayni ithnayn* in [Quran 13:3](quran://13/3) signifies "two contrasting kinds" or "varieties" of every fruit crop, not male and female floral organs.

---

### 2. Botanical & Taxonomic Empirical & Textual Analysis

Modern plant biology demonstrates that flowering plants do not conform to the concordist interpretation of [Quran 13:3](quran://13/3):

| Botanical Category | Modern Plant Reproductive Biology | Concordist Claim vs. Classical Meaning of [Quran 13:3](quran://13/3) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Fruit (*Thamarah*) vs. Flower (*Zahr*)** | A fruit is a mature, ripened ovary formed post-fertilization; fruits themselves possess no biological sex. In dioecious species like date palms, only female trees produce fruit, while male trees bear pollen spathes (*ṭalʿ*) and never bear fruit. | The concordist reading conflates the fruit (*thamarah*) with the flower (*zahr*). There is no male apple or female apple; the Quran specifies *thamarāt* (edible produce), not floral reproductive organs. |
| **Asexual / Parthenocarpic & Apomictic Fruits** | Numerous plants produce mature fruit without fertilization (parthenocarpy) or form seeds asexually without meiosis (apomixis), including cultivated bananas, figs, pineapples, navel oranges, persimmons, and dandelions. | Diverges from the universal scope (*min kulli al-thamarāt*, 'of all fruits'). Many edible fruits develop entirely without a male-female pairing or sexual union. |
| **Hermaphroditic vs. Dioecious Angiosperms** | Approximately 85–90% of flowering plants are hermaphroditic (perfect flowers containing both stamens and carpels in a single bloom). Only ~6% of angiosperms are dioecious (separate male and female individuals). | Concordist writers interpret the verse as depicting plants in separate male and female pairs (*zawjayn*). In botanical taxonomy, the overwhelming majority of plant species are bisexual single individuals. |
| **Classical Exegetical Meaning** | Botanical varieties exhibit diverse sensory, climatic, and phenotypic traits (color, flavor, shape, scent) without requiring sexual dimorphism. | Classical exegetes define *zawjayni ithnayn* as "two kinds and two types" ([Tafsir al-Tabari 13:3](tabari://13/3)) or "two sorts" varying in color, shape, taste, and scent ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 13:3](ibnkathir://13/3)), illustrated in [Quran 13:4](quran://13/4) by sweet/sour and white/black ([Tafsir al-Tabari 13:4](tabari://13/4); [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 13:4](ibnkathir://13/4)) and glossed by al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī as sweet/sour, black/white, and small/large. |

#### Detailed Botanical Breakdown

1. **Fruits Possess No Biological Sex:** Sexual organs exist exclusively in flowers: stamens produce pollen, while carpels contain ovules. Upon pollination, floral petals and stamens senesce, and the ovary ripens into a fruit. An individual fruit is therefore an asexual structure. In dioecious species, fruit production is confined strictly to female specimens.
2. **Exceptions to Universal Floral Pairing (*Min Kulli al-Thamarāt*):** The verse states that of *all* fruits, God made two pairs. However, numerous fruits develop without sexual union:
   * **Parthenocarpy:** Development of fruit without fertilization. Cultivated bananas (*Musa acuminata*) produce fruit without pollination. Common cultivars of the edible fig (*Ficus carica*—cf. [Quran 95:1](quran://95/1)), such as Common/Adriatic figs, develop fruit parthenocarpically without caprification. Pineapples (*Ananas comosus*), navel oranges (*Citrus sinensis*), and Asian persimmons (*Diospyros kaki*) similarly produce fruit without fertilization.
   * **Apomixis:** Asexual seed and fruit formation without fertilization or meiosis, occurring in hundreds of genera including blackberries (*Rubus*), dandelions (*Taraxacum*), and hawthorns (*Crataegus*).
3. **Prevalence of Hermaphroditism Over Sexual Pairs:**
   * **Hermaphroditic Flowers:** Roughly **85% to 90%** of angiosperm species produce perfect flowers containing both stamens and carpels within the same bloom (e.g., apples, pears, cherries, citrus, tomatoes).
   * **Monoecious Species:** Approximately **5%** possess separate male and female flowers on the same plant (e.g., maize, oaks, squashes).
   * **Dioecious Species:** Only **~6%** exist as distinct male and female plants (e.g., date palms, willows).
   Describing angiosperms as fundamentally divided into separate sexual "pairs" does not reflect the botanical distribution in which hermaphroditism is the predominant condition.

### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr) and Canonical Ḥadīth

Early Muslim commentators did not interpret [Quran 13:3](quran://13/3) as a description of floral reproductive anatomy:

* **Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī ([Tafsir al-Tabari 13:3](tabari://13/3); [Tafsir al-Tabari 13:4](tabari://13/4)):** In [Tafsir al-Tabari 13:3](tabari://13/3), al-Ṭabarī notes an unnamed view (*fī qawli baʿḍihim*, "from every male two, and from every female two, making four"), explains the Arabic dual usage of *zawjayn*, and concludes in his own words: *wa-innamā ʿanā bi-qawlihī: (zawjayni ithnayn), nawʿayni wa-ḍarbayn* ("Rather, He meant by His statement {two in pairs}: two kinds and two types"). On the immediately following verse ([Quran 13:4](quran://13/4), *wa-nufaḍḍilu baʿḍahā ʿalā baʿḍin fī al-ukul*, "Yet We favor some of it over others in fruit"), [Tafsir al-Tabari 13:4](tabari://13/4) cites transmissions from Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and Abū Hurayrah illustrating these contrasting fruit varieties as sweet and sour (*al-ḥulw wa-l-ḥāmiḍ*) and white and black (*al-abyaḍ wa-l-aswad*). Classical commentators such as al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī likewise gloss [Quran 13:3](quran://13/3) directly as contrasting agricultural varieties—sweet and sour, black and white, and small and large.
* **Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 13:3](ibnkathir://13/3); [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 13:4](ibnkathir://13/4)):** In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 13:3](ibnkathir://13/3), Ibn Kathīr explains: *wa-min kulli al-thamarāti jaʿala fīhā zawjayni ithnayn, ay: min kulli shaklin ṣinfān* ("{And of all the fruits He placed on it two in pairs}, meaning: from each form, two sorts"), noting that God waters crops to bring forth fruits of diverse colors, shapes, tastes, and scents (*min al-thamarāti al-mukhtalifati al-alwāni wa-l-ashkāli wa-l-ṭuʿūmi wa-l-rawāʾiḥ*), and in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 13:4](ibnkathir://13/4) he likewise cites the prophetic tradition via Abū Hurayrah contrasting sweet and sour (*al-ḥulw wa-l-ḥāmiḍ*).

#### The Canonical Hadith on Date Palm Pollination (*Taʾbīr al-Nakhl*)

That 7th-century Arab farmers possessed practical knowledge of plant pollination—and that Muhammad disclaimed specialized divine revelation on botany—is established in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*:

1. In **[Sahih Muslim 2361](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2361)**, Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbayd Allāh (via Mūsā ibn Ṭalḥah) reported that farmers explained: *"They are pollinating it, placing the male within the female so that it is fertilized (*yulaqqiḥūnahu yajʿalūna al-dhakara fī al-unthā fa-yalqaḥ*)."* After Muhammad doubted its utility and the yield declined once the practice was abandoned, he stated: *"If that benefits them, let them do it; for I only conjectured a conjecture (`fa-innī innamā ẓanantu ẓannan`), so do not hold me to conjecture; rather, when I relate something to you from God, accept it."*
2. In **[Sahih Muslim 2362](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2362)**, Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj reported that the Prophet observed Medinans pollinating date palms (*yaʾburūna al-nakhla yaqūlūna yulaqqiḥūna al-nakhl*) and suggested leaving them unpollinated. When the crop shed and failed (*fa-nafaḍat*), he stated: *"I am only a human being. When I command you regarding something of your religion, accept it; and when I command you regarding something from my own opinion, then I am only a human being."*
3. In **[Sahih Muslim 2363](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2363)** (narrated via ʿĀʾishah and Anas ibn Mālik), after the unpollinated trees bore unfertilized dates (*fa-kharaja shīṣan*), the Prophet concluded: *"You know better the affairs of your worldly life"* (`antum aʿlamu bi-amri dunyākum`).

This canonical episode demonstrates that Medinan farmers already possessed practical empirical knowledge of dioecious plant fertilization, and that Muhammad explicitly distinguished his prophetic mission from technical agronomy.

---

### 4. Verbatim Pre-Islamic Mesopotamian, Greek, and Roman Botanical Precedents

Artificial pollination and plant sexual dimorphism were documented across the Near East for over two millennia prior to Islam:

1. **Mesopotamian Artificial Pollination & the Code of Hammurabi (§§ 64–65, c. 1750 BC):** In ancient Babylonia, date palm culture was legally regulated. The **Code of Hammurabi** (laws §§ 64–65, c. 1750 BC) stipulated the duties of the date gardener (*rakkābu*, "pollinator"), requiring hand-pollination to guarantee yields. Neo-Assyrian palace reliefs of Ashurnasirpal II at Nimrud (883–859 BC) depict winged figures holding male inflorescences to fertilize the sacred palm tree.
2. **Herodotus's *Histories* (I.193, c. 440 BC):** Herodotus described Babylonian artificial pollination in *Histories* (I.193):
   > *"The natives tie the fruit of the male palms, as the Greeks call them, to the date-bearing palms, so that the gall-fly may enter the dates and ripen them, and the fruit of the palm tree will not fall off; for the male palm bears gall-flies in its fruit, just like the wild fig tree."*
3. **Theophrastus's *Historia Plantarum* (II.8.4 & *De Causis Plantarum* II.9.15, c. 300 BC):** Theophrastus, the "Father of Botany," described date palm pollination in *Historia Plantarum* (II.8.4, c. 300 BC):
   > *"With dates it is helpful to bring the male to the female; for they say that the male makes the fruit persist and ripen... They take the flower of the male palm when the spathe opens, and shake the dust (*konis*, pollen) and down upon the fruit of the female; and when this is done, the female retains the fruit and does not cast it."*
   In *De Causis Plantarum* (II.9.15), Theophrastus compared this directly to sexual copulation (*symplokē*).
4. **Pliny the Elder's *Naturalis Historia* (XIII.7.31–35, AD 77):** Pliny articulated an explicit theory of plant sexuality:
   > *"Naturalists who are skilled in the properties of trees state that all trees, and indeed all herbs of the earth, possess both sexes (*arboribus... immo vero et herbis omnibus utriusque sexus*)... In the date palm, however, this distinction is particularly evident. The male tree blossoms with flowers, while the female tree puts forth the fruit... The female trees, it is said, will not bear fruit unless they are impregnated by the pollen dust (*pulvis*) of the male trees, either carried by the winds or scattered by human hands."* (Pliny, *Naturalis Historia* XIII.7.31–35).

These texts demonstrate that artificial pollination and botanical sex differentiation were standard agricultural knowledge throughout the Near East centuries before the 7th century AD.

---

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Secondary Harmonizations

Modern concordist literature frequently cites secondary passages to support the hypothesis of botanical prescience:

1. **The Wind Pollination Reading in [Quran 15:22](quran://15/22):** Concordist authors cite [Quran 15:22](quran://15/22)—*wa-arsalnā al-riyāḥa lawāqiḥa* (*"And We sent the winds as fecundating/fertilizing"*)—proposing that it anticipates anemophily (wind pollination of flowers). However, in [Tafsir al-Tabari 15:22](tabari://15/22), early authorities such as Ibn Masʿūd, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, Qatādah, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk explain *lawāqiḥ* strictly as the winds fecundating rain clouds (*tulqiḥu al-saḥāb*, Form IV from *alqaḥa / mulqiḥah*)—matching the verse's immediate continuation (*fa-anzalnā min al-samāʾi māʾan fa-asqaynākumūhu*, *"so We sent down from the sky water and gave it to you to drink"*)—while other reports (such as Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, alongside al-Ṭabarī and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 15:22](ibnkathir://15/22)) include winds pollinating or opening trees (*tulqiḥu al-shajar*) alongside clouds, a traditional observation already documented centuries earlier by Pliny the Elder (*Naturalis Historia* XIII.7.35, AD 77: *vento aut aura tantum fieri conceptionem*).
2. **The Universal Duality Reading in [Quran 51:49](quran://51/49):** Proponents cite [Quran 51:49](quran://51/49)—*wa-min kulli shayʾin khalaqnā zawjayn* (*"And of everything We created two pairs"*)—proposing that it describes universal binary duality across physics and biology. Empirical findings in physics and biology indicate otherwise:
   * In particle physics, neutral bosons (such as photons and neutral Z bosons) are their own antiparticles and lack an opposite counterpart.
   * In microbiology, numerous organisms reproduce strictly through mitosis, binary fission, or budding without sexes (e.g., bacteria, archaea, amoebae).
   * In mycology, many fungi possess thousands of mating types rather than two sexes (*Schizophyllum commune* has over 23,000 distinct mating types).
   * Early commentators understood [Quran 51:49](quran://51/49) not as particle physics, but as observable cosmological contrasts: night/day, heaven/earth, sun/moon, land/sea, life/death ([Tafsir al-Tabari 51:49](tabari://51/49); [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 51:49](ibnkathir://51/49)).

In conclusion, the textual, philological, and botanical evidence indicates that [Quran 13:3](quran://13/3) describes observable agricultural varieties rather than modern plant taxonomy or floral reproductive anatomy. Interpreting *zawjayni ithnayn* as male and female floral organs diverges from classical Arabic lexicography and early Quranic commentaries, does not account for parthenocarpic and hermaphroditic plant reproduction, and overlooks millennia of documented Near Eastern agricultural practice.

Niddah* 25a–26a).
39:6.refutation:
Textual, anatomical, and historical evidence indicates that the phrase *fī ẓulumātin thalāth* ("within three darknesses") in [Quran 39:6](quran://39/6) does not describe modern microscopic embryological or obstetrical discoveries. Rather than enumerating histological tissue layers or surgical planes, the Quran employs an ancient, macroscopic description of mammalian gestation that was widely recognized by ancient livestock herders, midwives, and Greco-Roman physicians centuries prior to the 7th century AD—and interpreted accordingly by the earliest Islamic exegetes ([Tafsir al-Tabari 39:6](tabari://39/6), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 39:6](ibnkathir://39/6)).

---

### 1. Context of the Claim & Classical Arabic Philology

The contemporary assertion that [Quran 39:6](quran://39/6) contains a scientific miracle regarding fetal development was popularized in late 20th-century concordist literature, beginning with Maurice Bucaille (*The Bible, The Qur'an and Science*, AD 1976) and Canadian anatomist Keith L. Moore (*The Developing Human: Clinically Oriented Embryology with Islamic Additions*, AD 1986). Bucaille and Moore contended that the phrase *fī ẓulumātin thalāth* ("in three darknesses") corresponds directly to modern clinical obstetrics, designating:
1. The anterior abdominal wall of the mother,
2. The uterine wall, and
3. The amniochorionic membrane enclosing the amniotic fluid.

Other modern concordist commentators reassign the triad to three fetal membranes: the amnion, chorion, and decidua capsularis. Proponents argue that because microscopic histology and sterile abdominal surgery were unknown in 7th-century pre-Islamic Arabia, the mention of three protective "darknesses" constitutes divine foreknowledge.

#### The Literary and Theological Context of Quran 39:6
When examined within its textual and rhetorical setting, [Quran 39:6](quran://39/6) is not a specialized medical treatise outlining cellular boundaries. It is a Late Antique theological appeal directed to a pastoral Arabian audience, invoking ubiquitous, everyday observations of livestock, marriage, and human birth to demonstrate God's unshared creative power:

> *"He created you from one person, (and) then made from him his wife, and He sent down to you four kinds of livestock [lit. eight mates, thamāniyata azwāj]. He creates you in the bellies of your mothers, creation after creation, in three darknesses. That is God, your Lord. To Him (belongs) the kingdom. (There is) no god but Him. How (is it that) you are turned away?"* ([Quran 39:6](quran://39/6))

Notably, immediately before mentioning the formation of the human infant in maternal bellies, the exact same verse states: *wa-anzala lakum mina al-anʿāmi thamāniyata azwāj* ("And He sent down for you from the grazing livestock eight mates"). In Quranic cosmological parlance, the verb *anzala* ("sent down") is used for the eight domesticated pastoral animals—two (a male and a female, i.e., one pair) each of sheep, goats, camels, and cattle (cf. [Quran 6:143](quran://6/143)–[6:144](quran://6/144)). Just as the verb *anzala* expresses divine provision in phenomenological language rather than literal atmospheric descent, the subsequent phrase *fī ẓulumātin thalāth* ("within three darknesses") employs macroscopic, observable natural imagery rather than cellular histology.

In Classical Arabic philology, the root *ẓ-l-m* denotes obscurity, absence of light, or concealment. As documented in Ibn Manẓūr’s classical lexicon *Lisān al-ʿArab* (entry *ẓ-l-m*), the plural *ẓulumāt* signifies nested enclosures or obscure environments. The phrase poetically depicts the hidden, lightless interior of the pregnant maternal abdomen—a standard rhetorical motif throughout ancient Near Eastern literature emphasizing that God shapes the infant within the unseen interior of the mother's body.

---

### 2. Anatomical & Historical Empirical Analysis & Comparison Table

The hypothesis that [Quran 39:6](quran://39/6) anticipates modern embryology diverges from both contemporary anatomical classification and the historical record of ancient medicine:

| Layer / Feature | Modern Concordist Claim | Classical Exegetical & Ancient Anatomical Context ([Quran 39:6](quran://39/6)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Visibility to the Naked Eye** | Proposed microscopic knowledge of three cellular membrane barriers invisible without modern surgical instruments and microscopes. | Gross macroscopic structures visible to ancient herdsmen, slaughterers, and midwives when examining pregnant livestock or assisting births (belly, womb, afterbirth sac). |
| **Number of Histological Layers** | Exactly three distinct anatomical layers enclose the fetus: abdominal wall, uterine wall, and amniochorionic membrane. | Multiple distinct histological and anatomical layers: skin, Camper's fascia, Scarpa's fascia, anterior rectus sheath, rectus abdominis muscle, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, parietal peritoneum, perimetrium, myometrium, decidua basalis/capsularis, chorion laeve, and amnion. |
| **Classical Exegetical Definition** | Proposed early Islamic recognition of modern clinical obstetrical envelopes. | Consistently defined in early *tafsīr* as the maternal belly (*al-baṭn*), the muscular womb (*al-raḥim*), and the expelled placenta/fetal caul (*al-mashīmah* / *al-salā*). |
| **Pre-Islamic Medical Precedents** | Knowledge of protective fetal coverings originated uniquely in 7th-century Arabia. | Detailed dissection and systematic Greek nomenclature for the abdominal wall (*epigastrion*), uterus (*mētra*), and three fetal membranes (*chorion*, *allantois*, *amnios*) documented by Galen (2nd century AD) and Soranus (early 2nd century AD). |
| **Rabbinic & Pastoral Precedents** | Enclosure of the embryo was unknown prior to the 7th century AD. | The Babylonian Talmud (*b. Niddah* 25a–26a, c. AD 500) and Arabian camel breeders routinely identified the fetal sac (*shefir* / *al-sābīʾāʾ*) and placenta (*shilyah* / *al-mashīmah*) inside the uterus (*reḥem*) and belly (*meʿayim*). |

#### Taxonomic Stratification of the Maternal and Fetal Envelopes
In modern surgical obstetrics, entering the gravid uterus during a Caesarean section requires traversing numerous distinct anatomical and histological boundaries:
1. **Cutaneous and Subcutaneous Layers:** Maternal epidermis and dermis.
2. **Superficial Fascia:** Camper's fatty fascia and Scarpa's membranous fascia.
3. **Musculoaponeurotic Wall:** Anterior rectus sheath, rectus abdominis muscle, and associated aponeuroses.
4. **Peritoneal Envelopes:** Transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal connective tissue, and parietal peritoneum.
5. **Uterine Wall:** Perimetrium (outer serosa), myometrium (composed of three distinct muscular strata: outer longitudinal, middle crisscrossing figure-of-eight fibers, and inner circular fibers), and endometrium/decidua.
6. **Maternal-Fetal Boundary:** Decidua capsularis and decidua parietalis.
7. **Fetal Membranes:** Chorion laeve (consisting of syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, and extraembryonic somatic mesoderm) and amnion (consisting of amniotic epithelium, basement membrane, compact layer, fibroblast layer, and spongy intermediate layer).

To propose that modern anatomy identifies strictly "three layers" requires consolidating more than a dozen independent histological and surgical planes into three broad macroscopic categories while omitting intermediate structures. If, alternatively, the correlation is restricted solely to the fetal membranes, human anatomy features two primary fetal membranes (the chorion and the amnion), whereas classical mammalian anatomy identifies three (chorion, allantois, and amnion)—a triad already established by Greek anatomists five centuries before the 7th century AD.

---

### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr)

Early Muslim commentators did not interpret [Quran 39:6](quran://39/6) as a reference to microscopic membranes or clinical surgical layers. Rather, they interpreted the verse through ordinary macroscopic observations of mammalian anatomy and birth.

In [Tafsir al-Tabari 39:6](tabari://39/6), the foundational exegete Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī (d. 310 AH / AD 923) assembled the primary narrations from the Companions and Successors (*Salaf*):

> **Interpretation of the Three Darknesses in al-Ṭabarī:**
> *"And His saying: {in three darknesses}, meaning: in the darkness of the belly (ẓulmat al-baṭn), the darkness of the womb (ẓulmat al-raḥim), and the darkness of the placenta (ẓulmat al-mashīmah). And the people of interpretation have spoken similarly to what we have said regarding that."* ([Tafsir al-Tabari 39:6](tabari://39/6))

Al-Ṭabarī records chains of transmission confirming this identical definition across the premier authorities of early Quranic exegesis:
* **ʿIkrimah (client of Ibn ʿAbbās):** *"The three darknesses: the belly, the womb, and the placenta (*al-baṭn, wa-l-raḥim, wa-l-mashīmah*)."*
* **Ibn ʿAbbās:** *"By the three darknesses it means: the belly of his mother, the womb, and the placenta."*
* **Mujāhid ibn Jabr:** *"The belly, the womb, and the placenta."*
* **Qatādah ibn Diʿāmah:** *"The placenta, the womb, and the belly."*
* **Al-Suddī:** *"The darkness of the placenta, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the belly."*
* **Ibn Zayd:** *"The placenta is in the womb, and the womb is in the belly."*
* **Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim:** *"The womb, the placenta, and the belly; and the placenta (*al-mashīmah*) is what is upon the child when he comes out, and in animals it is the amniotic sac (*al-salā*)."*

Similarly, in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 39:6](ibnkathir://39/6), Ismāʿīl ibn Kathīr (d. 774 AH / AD 1373) affirms this universal consensus:

> *"And His saying: {in three darknesses} means, in the darkness of the womb, the darkness of the placenta—which is like a covering and protection for the child—and the darkness of the belly. This was the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Abū Mālik, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, al-Suddī, Ibn Zayd, and others."* ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 39:6](ibnkathir://39/6))

#### The Second Early Exegetical View: Loins, Belly, and Womb
In addition to the majority view, classical commentators such as Abū ʿUbaydah Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā (d. 209 AH / AD 824), al-Qurṭubī (*al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān*), and Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī (*Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb*) documented an alternative early interpretation:
1. The darkness of the father's loins (*ẓulmat al-ṣulb*),
2. The darkness of the mother's belly (*ẓulmat al-baṭn*), and
3. The darkness of the mother's womb (*ẓulmat al-raḥim*).

This secondary tradition demonstrates that classical scholars viewed the phrase as an idiomatic depiction of the progressive stages through which reproductive fluids travel from generation to birth, rather than a rigid boundary map of maternal abdominal histology.

#### Macroscopic Pastoral Realities: The Afterbirth (*al-Mashīmah*, *al-Salā*, and *al-Sābīʾāʾ*)
The gloss provided by al-Ḍaḥḥāk in [Tafsir al-Tabari 39:6](tabari://39/6) is particularly informative: *"and the placenta (*al-mashīmah*) is what is upon the child when he comes out, and in animals it is the amniotic sac (*al-salā*)."*

In pastoral nomadic societies, the birth of animals was an everyday occurrence. Domesticated camels, sheep, goats, and cows frequently give birth to offspring encased in an intact, translucent amniotic sac—a phenomenon known in veterinary medicine and traditional obstetrics as being born "in a caul." The expelled afterbirth—consisting of the placenta and its fibrous membranes—is called *al-salā* (السَّلَى) in Classical Arabic when referring to livestock, and *al-mashīmah* (المَشِيمَة), *al-gharbiy* (الغَرْبِيّ), or *al-sābīʾāʾ* (السَّابِيَاء) when referring to human beings (attested in pre-Islamic poetry and compiled in *Lisān al-ʿArab*). Bedouin herdsmen, animal slaughterers, and tribal midwives observed these three nested structures continuously:
1. The external abdomen/belly (*al-baṭn*),
2. The thick muscular womb/uterus (*al-raḥim*), and
3. The membranous fetal sac/afterbirth (*al-mashīmah* / *al-salā*).

Consequently, observing that a fetus resides within an afterbirth membrane, situated within a muscular womb inside the maternal abdomen, required only ordinary macroscopic observation rather than microscopic instrumentation.

---

### 4. Verbatim Pre-Islamic Greek, Roman, and Talmudic Obstetrical Precedents

Centuries before the 7th century AD, ancient Mediterranean, Hellenistic, Roman, and Rabbinic medical traditions had systematically investigated and documented the maternal abdomen, the uterine cavity, and the membranes enclosing the mammalian fetus.

#### 1. Galen of Pergamon (AD 129–c. 216)
Galen, the preeminent medical authority of the Roman Empire whose treatises dominated Byzantine and Near Eastern medicine for over a millennium, detailed the anatomy of the pregnant uterus and fetal membranes in multiple major works:
* In ***On the Anatomy of the Uterus*** (*De Uteri Dissectione*, Ch. 10, ed. Kühn II.902–908), Galen provides surgical dissection instructions on pregnant mammals (sheep, goats, and cows), explicitly describing:
  1. The outer abdominal wall (*epigastrion*),
  2. The muscular uterus (*mētra* / *hystera*), and
  3. The three distinct protective envelopes surrounding the fetus: the **chorion** (*to chorion*, vascular outer membrane), the **allantois** (*allantoīdēs chitōn*, sausage-shaped membrane collecting urine), and the **amnion** (*to amnion*, innermost transparent sac holding fluid).
* In ***On the Usefulness of the Parts of the Body*** (*De Usu Partium*, Book XV, Chs. 4–5, 2nd century AD), Galen explains the physiological function of these three membranes, demonstrating how nature protects the delicate embryo through concentric protective layers:
  > *"Nature has enclosed the fetus within membranes... The innermost of these is called the amnion, which contains the moist liquid that cushions the child; surrounding this is the allantoic membrane; and outermost of all is the chorion, which attaches to the vessels of the womb."* (*De Usu Partium* XV.4, ed. Kühn IV.222–226)

Galen’s detailed schema of three fetal membranes enclosing the fetus within the womb was translated into Syriac by Sergius of Reshaina (d. AD 536) and formed the core curriculum of the medical academies of Alexandria, Nisibis, and Gondeshapur, which were active across the Near East in the 6th and 7th centuries AD.

#### 2. Soranus of Ephesus (Early 2nd Century AD)
Soranus of Ephesus, practicing in Rome during the reigns of Trajan and Hadrian, authored a foundational obstetrical treatise of antiquity, the ***Gynecology*** (*Gynaecia*, Book I, Chs. 6–18 & Book I, Ch. 57):
* Soranus details the anatomy of the female abdominal wall, the structure and orifices of the uterus (*mētra*), the placenta, and the surrounding fetal membranes (*hymenes*).
* He describes how the fetus is suspended inside the fluid-filled amniotic sac (*amnios*) and chorion (*chorion*), and instructs midwives on how to open the caul if an infant is born with its head enclosed in the membranous sac (*Gynaecia* II.14).
* Soranus’s obstetrical handbook was subsequently adapted into Latin by Caelius Aurelianus (5th century AD) and Muscio (6th century AD), serving as a standard reference for midwives throughout Late Antiquity.

#### 3. Hippocrates (5th Century BC) and Aristotle (4th Century BC)
Centuries before the Roman era, Classical Greek natural philosophers had described the membranes enclosing the developing embryo:
* **Hippocrates (*On the Nature of the Child* / *De Natura Pueri*, §§ 13–16, 5th century BC):** The Hippocratic author explains that as the seed develops inside the womb, a membrane grows around it like a thin rind around a loaf of bread, becoming thicker and developing multiple protective coverings (*chitōnes*) filled with amniotic fluid.
* **Aristotle (*Historia Animalium* VI.3, VII.7–8, 586a–b, 4th century BC):** Aristotle details the dissection of pregnant animals, noting that all viviparous quadrupeds and human beings possess an outer membrane called the *chorion* and an inner membrane containing fluid called the *amnion*, situated inside the maternal uterus (*hystera*).

#### 4. Babylonian Talmud (Compiled c. AD 500) and Arabian Pastoral Husbandry
In Late Antique Mesopotamia and the Arabian borderlands, Jewish scholars discussed fetal membranes in extensive legal and anatomical detail. In the Babylonian Talmud, tractate **Niddah 25a–26a**, the sages examine the status of miscarriages based on the physical appearance of the expelled gestational sac:
* The Talmud distinguishes between the **fetal sac / amnion** (*shefir*, שפיר), the **placenta** (*shilyah*, שליא), the **womb** (*reḥem*, רחם), and the **maternal belly** (*meʿayim*, מעים).
* The rabbis discuss an embryo enclosed within a *shefir* filled with water, blood, or tissue, noting that an intact sac may be expelled with the embryo visible inside—an exact parallel to the Hellenistic *amnion* and the Arabic *mashīmah*.

Furthermore, Bedouin society in pre-Islamic Arabia was thoroughly pastoral. Sheep, goats, and camels were slaughtered regularly for sustenance and hospitality, while pregnant animals were frequently slaughtered during times of food scarcity or ritual sacrifice. Every herdsman who dressed the carcass of a pregnant camel or ewe cut directly through:
1. The abdominal wall (*al-baṭn*),
2. The gravid uterine horn (*al-raḥim*), and
3. The fluid-filled amniotic and chorionic sac (*al-salā* / *al-mashīmah*).

Accordingly, familiarity with three macroscopic envelopes surrounding a developing fetus reflects millennia of continuous animal husbandry, livestock processing, and pre-modern obstetrical practice across the ancient Near East and Mediterranean.

---

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Modern Harmonizations

Modern concordist literature proposes two primary alternative readings to correlate [Quran 39:6](quran://39/6) with contemporary embryology; both encounter substantial anatomical, philological, and historiographical difficulties:

#### 1. Hypothesis A: The Three Darknesses as Clinical Surgical Planes
Keith L. Moore proposed that the three darknesses represent the anterior abdominal wall, the uterine wall, and the amniochorionic membrane.
* *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment (Histological Stratification):* As detailed in Section 2, the human abdominal wall alone comprises epidermis, dermis, superficial fascia (Camper's and Scarpa's layers), deep musculoaponeurotic strata (rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis), transversalis fascia, and parietal peritoneum, while the uterine wall comprises the perimetrium, three-layered myometrium, and endometrium/decidua. Consolidating these numerous histological strata into two units (abdominal wall and uterine wall) while counting the amniochorionic membrane as a third unit represents a post-hoc taxonomic grouping rather than an objective histological enumeration.
* *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment (Embryological Differentiation of Fetal Membranes):* Within clinical embryology, the chorion and amnion are two anatomically and developmentally distinct membranes derived from separate embryological lineages (trophoblast and extraembryonic somatic mesoderm versus epiblast/ectoderm). Partitioning the maternal-fetal anatomy into "belly, womb, and amniotic sac" reproduces the classical macroscopic triad rather than a microscopic histological classification.

#### 2. Hypothesis B: The Three Darknesses as Three Microscopic Fetal Membranes
A secondary harmonization proposes that the verse refers specifically to three fetal membranes: the amnion, the chorion, and the decidua capsularis.
* *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment (Philological and Exegetical Context):* [Quran 39:6](quran://39/6) explicitly frames the process macrosomatically: *"He creates you in the bellies of your mothers (*fī buṭūni ummahātikum*), creation after creation, in three darknesses."* The text situates gestation within the maternal abdomen (*buṭūn*) rather than enumerating microscopic membranes. As documented in [Tafsir al-Tabari 39:6](tabari://39/6) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 39:6](ibnkathir://39/6), early Islamic exegetes uniformly identified *al-baṭn* (the belly) and *al-raḥim* (the womb) as two of the three darknesses.
* *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment (Graeco-Roman Historiographical Precedent):* Even if the triad were interpreted strictly as three fetal membranes, a three-membrane model (*chorion*, *allantois*, and *amnion*) had already been systematically described five centuries earlier by Galen in *De Uteri Dissectione* (Ch. 10) and *De Usu Partium* (XV.4–5) and transmitted into Syriac medical curricula across the Late Antique Near East.

86:6.classification_explanation: Modern concordist commentators propose that [Quran 86:6](quran://86/6)–[86:7](quran://86/7) depicts modern embryology, interpreting the "gushing fluid" as a reference to embryonic gonads migrating from the upper posterior abdominal wall, or to the testicular neurovascular bundle originating near the lumbar spine. However, classical Arabic lexicography (*Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*, *Lisān al-ʿArab*), classical exegesis ([Tafsir al-Tabari 86:6](tabari://86/6), [Tafsir al-Tabari 86:7](tabari://86/7), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 86:6](ibnkathir://86/6), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 86:7](ibnkathir://86/7)), and the comparative history of Greco-Arabic medicine demonstrate that the text reflects the standard Late Antique encephalomyelogenic reproductive theory. First formulated in the Hippocratic corpus (*De Genitura*, 5th century BC) and Plato (*Timaeus*, 4th century BC), this ancient doctrine taught that ejaculated semen originates from the brain and descends down the spinal marrow (*al-ṣulb*) and thoracic ribs (*al-tarāʾib*) before exiting the body.
86:6.summary: In classical Arabic and early tafsīr (Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ṭabarī, and Ibn Kathīr), Quran 86:6–7 states that ejaculated seminal fluid (*māʾ dāfiq*) emerges from between a man's backbone (*al-ṣulb*) and a woman's upper chest or ribs where a necklace rests (*al-tarāʾib*). Biologically, however, sperm and semen are produced entirely in the scrotal testes and lower pelvic glands, never emerging from the spine or rib cage, while embryonic gonads do not secrete gushing fluid. Rather than describing modern embryology, the verse reflects the widespread Late Antique medical theory of Hippocrates, Plato, and Galen, which taught that seed descends down the spinal marrow and torso to mix with female fluid. The sections below present the full lexical, anatomical, exegetical, and historical evidence.
86:6.refutation:
Textual, philological, anatomical, and historical evidence indicates that [Quran 86:6](quran://86/6)–[86:7](quran://86/7) does not describe modern embryology. Instead, the statement that reproductive fluid (*māʾ dāfiq*) emerges from *"between the backbone and the ribs"* reflects the prevailing Late Antique encephalomyelogenic reproductive theory—originating in the Hippocratic corpus and Greek biology—combined with the classical Arabian exegetical view that conception results from commingling a man's spinal fluid with a woman's thoracic fluid.

---

### 1. Context of the Claim & Classical Arabic Philology (al-Ṣulb and al-Tarāʾib)

In Sūrat al-Ṭāriq ([Quran 86:5](quran://86/5)–[86:7](quran://86/7)), humanity is directed to consider its origin as an indicator of divine resurrection ([Quran 86:8](quran://86/8)):

> *"So let man observe from what he was created. He was created from a gushing fluid (`khuliqa min māʾin dāfiq`), emerging from between the backbone and the ribs (`yakhruju min bayni al-ṣulbi wa-l-tarāʾib`)."* ([Quran 86:5](quran://86/5)–[86:7](quran://86/7))

Classical Arabic lexicography and syntax define each term precisely:

* **`Māʾ dāfiq` (مَاء دَافِق):** The noun `māʾ` (fluid) is qualified by the active participle `dāfiq` (from *d-f-q*, to pour forth with force or spurt). In [Tafsir al-Tabari 86:6](tabari://86/6), al-Ṭabarī explains that `dāfiq` is an active participle (*fāʿil*) carrying the passive sense of `madfūq` (*"spurted/poured-forth water"*) according to the linguistic convention of the Ḥijāz. As recorded by al-Farāhīdī (*Kitāb al-ʿAyn*), al-Jawharī (*al-Ṣiḥāḥ*), Ibn Manẓūr (*Lisān al-ʿArab*), and Lane's *Arabic-English Lexicon*, `māʾ dāfiq` specifically designates ejaculated seminal fluid discharged in spurts. Syntactically, `yakhruju` (*"it emerges"*) is an adjectival clause (`ṣifah`) whose antecedent is `māʾin dāfiq` (*"a gushing fluid"*) in verse 6.
* **`Al-Ṣulb` (الصُّلْب):** In classical Arabic, `al-ṣulb` denotes the vertebral column, spine, or loins of a man (cf. [Quran 4:23](quran://4/23) *"from your loins"* [`min aṣlābikum`]).
* **`Al-Tarāʾib` (التَّرَائِب):** Plural of `tarībah` (تَرِيبَة). Classical lexicographers unanimously define `al-tarāʾib` as the upper chest, clavicles, or upper ribs of a woman where a necklace rests (`mawḍiʿ al-qilādah min al-ṣadr`). Al-Farāhīdī defines it in *Kitāb al-ʿAyn* as *"the bones of the chest where the necklace hangs."* Ibn Manẓūr in *Lisān al-ʿArab* confirms that philologists identify `al-tarāʾib` with the female chest, collarbones, and upper ribs.

This usage is attested across classical Arabic poetry. In his *Muʿallaqah* (v. 31, cited in *Lisān al-ʿArab*, root `t-r-b`, and al-Zawzanī's *Sharḥ al-Muʿallaqāt*), Imruʾ al-Qays (6th century AD) describes the chest of his beloved:
> *"Slender-waisted, fair-skinned, not flabby of belly; her breastbones are polished like a mirror."*
> (`مُهَفْهَفَةٌ بَيْضَاءُ غَيْرُ مُفَاضَةٍ ... تَرَائِبُهَا مَصْقُولَةٌ كَالسَّجَنْجَلِ` — *muhafhafatun bayḍāʾu ghayru mufāḍatin / tarāʾibuhā maṣqūlatun ka-al-sajanjali*)

Similarly, [Tafsir al-Tabari 86:7](tabari://86/7) records the poetic *shāhid* of al-Muthaqqab al-ʿAbdī (*"And from gold that is polished upon a breastbone [`tarīb`], like the color of ivory, having no wrinkles"*) and a second classical verse:
> *"And saffron upon her chest-bones shining, with it are the upper breasts and the upper chest."*
> (`وَالزَّعْفَرَانُ عَلَى تَرَائِبِهَا شَرِقًا / بِهِ اللَّبَّاتُ والنَّحْرُ` — *wa-l-zaʿfarānu ʿalā tarāʾibihā shariqan / bihi al-labbātu wa-l-naḥr*)

The Arabic text of [Quran 86:6](quran://86/6)–[86:7](quran://86/7) thus denotes an ejaculated fluid emerging from between the male spine and female chest or ribs.

---

### 2. Anatomical & Physiological Empirical & Textual Analysis

Modern reproductive anatomy establishes that seminal fluid and spermatozoa do not originate, form, or emerge from between the thoracic spine and the ribs:

1. **Spermatogenesis Occurs Exclusively in Scrotal Testes:** Spermatozoa are produced in the seminiferous tubules of the testes, located outside the abdominal cavity in the scrotum to maintain a temperature 2°C to 3°C below core body temperature (34.4°C vs. 37°C). If testes remained in the thoracic or abdominal cavity between spine and ribs, thermal inhibition would result in complete azoospermia.
2. **Seminal Fluid is Produced by Pelvic Accessory Glands:** The fluid volume of semen is secreted entirely within the lesser pelvis, inferior to the diaphragm and rib cage:
   * **Seminal Vesicles (65%–70% of volume):** Located posterior to the urinary bladder in the pelvis, secreting alkaline fluid rich in fructose and prostaglandins.
   * **Prostate Gland (25%–30% of volume):** Located directly inferior to the urinary bladder, secreting proteolytic enzymes (PSA), citric acid, and zinc.
   * **Bulbourethral (Cowper's) Glands (1% of volume):** Located in the deep perineal pouch inferior to the prostate, producing pre-ejaculatory lubricating mucoproteins.
3. **Ejaculatory Pathway is Exclusively Pelvic and Perineal:** During ejaculation, spermatozoa travel from the epididymis via the vas deferens into the prostatic ejaculatory ducts, exiting through the penile urethra. At no point does reproductive fluid pass through or emerge from the thoracic spine (*al-ṣulb*) or ribs (*al-tarāʾib*).

| Anatomical Feature | Modern Reproductive Anatomy & Physiology | Quranic & Classical Exegetical Account ([Quran 86:6](quran://86/6)–[86:7](quran://86/7)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Site of Fluid Production** | Produced by scrotal testes and pelvic accessory glands (seminal vesicles and prostate gland). | Stated to emerge from between the backbone (*al-ṣulb*) and the ribs/breastbone (*al-tarāʾib*). |
| **Grammatical Subject of Ejection** | Ejaculated seminal fluid (*māʾ dāfiq*) expelled through the pelvic and penile urethral canal. | Singular masculine verb *yakhruju* ("it emerges"), syntactically modifying the gushing fluid (*māʾ*). |
| **Location Relative to Rib Cage** | Entirely pelvic and perineal; situated inferior to the diaphragm and thoracic skeletal cage. | Localized between the vertebral column and the thoracic ribs/clavicles (*al-tarāʾib*). |
| **Female Reproductive Contribution** | Single microscopic ovum released from the pelvic ovary into the fallopian tube; no thoracic fluid. | Classical exegesis identifies *al-tarāʾib* as the woman's yellow fluid emerging from her chest. |

---

### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr)

Classical commentators on [Quran 86:6](quran://86/6)–[86:7](quran://86/7) did not interpret the passage in terms of modern embryology. Instead, early authorities explained the text through the dual-fluid reproductive model of 7th-century Arabia:

* **Consensus of the Salaf:** In [Tafsir al-Tabari 86:6](tabari://86/6)–[86:7](tabari://86/7) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 86:6](ibnkathir://86/6)–[86:7](ibnkathir://86/7), the earliest authorities—including Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Qatādah, and Sufyān al-Thawrī—recorded that *al-ṣulb* refers to the backbone of the man, and *al-tarāʾib* refers to the upper chest, collarbones, or ribs of the woman where her necklace hangs (`mawḍiʿ al-qilādah`).
* **Ibn ʿAbbās's Two-Parental Fluid Model:** Ibn Abī Ḥātim (cited in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 86:7](ibnkathir://86/7)) transmits the specific chain of Shabīb ibn Bishr from ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbās:
  > *"Proceeding from between the backbone and the ribs: The backbone of the man and the ribs of the woman. It (the woman's fluid) is yellow and fine in texture. The child will not be born except from both of them."*
  In [Tafsir al-Tabari 86:7](tabari://86/7), al-Ṭabarī documents parallel narrations from Ibn ʿAbbās via ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī (*"Al-Tarāʾib is the place of the necklace"*) and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah (*"From between the breasts of the woman"*), as well as from ʿIkrimah via ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Nuʿmān (*"The spine of the man, and the ribs of the woman"*), and Sufyān al-Thawrī (*"Above the breasts"*). This corresponds to the canonical hadith in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* (hadith 315): *"The fluid of the man is white and thick, while the fluid of the woman is yellow and thin. Whichever of them prevails or comes first, the child will resemble that parent."*
* **Al-Ṭabarī's Philological Conclusion:** In [Tafsir al-Tabari 86:7](tabari://86/7), Imām al-Ṭabarī concludes:
  > *"The correct statement regarding that in our view is the statement of those who said: It is the place of the necklace on the woman, where it rests upon her chest; because that is what is well-known in the speech of the Arabs, and their poetry has come with it."*
* **Secondary Exegetical View:** In [Tafsir al-Tabari 86:7](tabari://86/7), reports narrated specifically from Qatādah gloss the phrase as *"between his [the man's] backbone and his upper chest (`naḥr`),"* alongside Maʿmar ibn Abī Ḥabībah al-Madīnī (*"It is the extract of the heart [`ʿuṣārat al-qalb`], and from it the child is produced"*). In this reading, both structures belong to the male, describing semen as descending through the torso along the spine.
* **Syntactic Corroboration in Verse 8:** That the Salaf understood the emerging entity to be ejaculated semen rather than embryonic gonads or an infant is documented in [Tafsir al-Tabari 86:8](tabari://86/8). Explicating the subsequent verse—*"Surely He is able to bring it back"* (`innahu ʿalā rajʿihi la-qādir`)—ʿIkrimah explains that God is able to return the emitted fluid *"into his backbone"* (`fī ṣulbihi`), while Mujāhid explains it as returning the drop of fluid *"into the urethra"* (`fī al-iḥlīl`). Early Muslim authorities consistently identified the subject of emergence as ejaculated fluid (`al-māʾ`).

---

### 4. Verbatim Pre-Islamic Greek, Syriac, and Near Eastern Medical Precedents

The concept that reproductive fluid originates in or descends along the spinal column and chest represents the encephalomyelogenic (brain-spine) doctrine of seed articulated by Greek medical authors, translated into Syriac and taught across the Late Antique Near East:

1. **Hippocratic Corpus (*De Genitura* §§ 1–2 & *Airs, Waters, Places* § 22, 5th Century BC):** In *On Generation* (*De Genitura* §§ 1–2, c. 420 BC), the Hippocratic author details the encephalomyelogenic theory:
   > *"The seed of man comes from all the humor in the body, the strongest part being separated off... It is carried from the brain into the loins and the whole body, but especially into the spinal marrow (`nōtiaios myelos`); and from the spinal marrow passages lead to the kidneys and along the torso to the testicles and penis."* (*De Genitura*, § 1)
   In § 2, the treatise adds that severing veins behind the ears causes sterility because it interrupts the channel conveying seed from the brain down the spine—a view repeated in *Airs, Waters, Places* (§ 22) regarding Scythian men.
2. **Plato (*Timaeus* 77d, 91a–b, 4th Century BC):** In *Timaeus* (91a–b), Plato identifies the spinal marrow (`myelos`) running down the vertebral column (`rhabdos`) as the animated conduit of reproductive seed (`sperma`), which exits through the reproductive tract.
3. **Galen of Pergamon (*De Semine* I–II, 2nd Century AD):** While Galen (*De Semine* I.12–16, II.1) recognized the role of the testes, he maintained that seminal fluid is derived from arterial and venous blood descending via the great vessels alongside the spine and loins (*para tēn rhachin*), infused with vital *pneuma* supplied from the brain and spinal cord. In contrast to Aristotle's single-seed model, Galen (*De Semine* II.1–4) advanced the **two-seed (dual-fluid) doctrine**—asserting that the female secretes a thinner reproductive fluid (*sperma*) that commingles with the thicker male fluid inside the womb—paralleling Ibn ʿAbbās's exegetical synthesis under [Quran 86:6](quran://86/6)–[86:7](quran://86/7) and the canonical tradition in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* (hadith 315).
4. **Diogenes of Apollonia & Alcmaeon of Croton (5th Century BC):** Alcmaeon held that semen is a direct secretion of the brain, while Diogenes maintained that semen is refined blood carried from the heart and lungs through thoracic vessels along the ribs and backbone to the reproductive organs. These doctrines were translated into Syriac (e.g., Sergius of Reshaina, d. AD 536) and taught at centers such as the Academy of Gondeshapur, training physicians including al-Ḥārith ibn Kaladah who practiced in 7th-century Mecca.
5. **Biblical and Ancient Near Eastern Idiom of the "Loins":** Semitic literature located reproductive seed in the paternal "loins" (*ḥălāṣayim* in Hebrew, *osphys* in Greek, *aṣlāb* in Arabic):
   * **[Genesis 35:11](bible://gn/35/11):** *"Kings shall come from your loins."*
   * **[1 Kings 8:19](bible://1kgs/8/19):** *"Your son, who shall come from your loins, he shall build the temple."*
   * **[Hebrews 7:10](bible://heb/7/10):** *"For he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him."*
   In conjunction with Greek physiological theories, the concept of seed emanating from the spine and torso was standard medical doctrine in Late Antiquity.

---

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Modern Harmonizations

Concordist commentators propose four primary alternative readings to harmonize [Quran 86:6](quran://86/6)–[86:7](quran://86/7) with modern anatomy; each diverges from classical Arabic syntax, early exegesis, and empirical findings:

1. **Secondary Harmonization #1: The Embryonic Gonadal Migration Hypothesis:**
   * *Concordist Hypothesis:* Commentators propose that the verse describes embryonic development at weeks 5–7, when primordial gonads originate near the mesonephric kidneys between the spine and lower ribs before descending into the scrotum or pelvis prior to birth.
   * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment (Grammatical, Philological & Embryological):* Syntactically, the grammatical subject of `yakhruju` (*"it emerges"*) in [Quran 86:7](quran://86/7) is `māʾin dāfiq` (*"a gushing fluid"*) in [Quran 86:6](quran://86/6). Undifferentiated fetal gonads are cellular organs rather than a "fluid" (*māʾ*), and their retroperitoneal descent does not involve a "gushing" or "spurting" motion (*dāfiq*). Physiologically, embryonic and fetal gonads do not secrete seminal fluid; spermatogenesis and seminal fluid production begin only at puberty, more than a decade after testicular descent is complete. Anatomically, the genital ridge develops retroperitoneally at the T10–L2 vertebral levels, whereas in classical Arabic lexicography (*Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, *Lisān al-ʿArab*), `al-tarāʾib` designates the upper chest, clavicles, or upper four ribs where a necklace rests (`mawḍiʿ al-qilādah`), rather than the lower abdominal wall.
2. **Secondary Harmonization #2: The Emerging Infant Hypothesis (Childbirth):**
   * *Concordist Hypothesis:* Commentators suggest that `yakhruju` refers to the newborn infant (`al-insān` from [Quran 86:5](quran://86/5)) emerging from the mother's body during parturition, treating verse 6 as a parenthetical clause (*jumlah muʿtariḍah*).
   * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment (Syntactic & Obstetrical):* In classical Arabic grammar, an unmarked imperfect verb clause (`yakhruju...`) immediately following an indefinite noun phrase (`māʾin dāfiq`) functions as an adjectival clause (`ṣifah`), governed by the syntactic principle *al-jumal baʿda al-nakirāt ṣifāt* ("clauses following indefinite nouns are adjectives"). As documented in [Tafsir al-Tabari 86:7](tabari://86/7)–[86:8](tabari://86/8) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 86:7](ibnkathir://86/7), early exegetes parsed `yakhruju` as modifying the fluid—an interpretation corroborated by ʿIkrimah (`fī ṣulbihi`) and Mujāhid (`fī al-iḥlīl`) under [Tafsir al-Tabari 86:8](tabari://86/8). From an obstetrical standpoint, during parturition the fetus traverses the birth canal within the *true bony pelvis*, bounded posteriorly by the sacrum and anteriorly by the pubic symphysis, rather than emerging from the maternal ribs (*tarāʾib*) or thoracic spine.
3. **Secondary Harmonization #3: The Testicular Neurovascular Bundle Hypothesis:**
   * *Concordist Hypothesis:* Commentators suggest that because the testicular arteries branch from the abdominal aorta at L2, the testicular sympathetic plexus originates from T10–L1 spinal segments, and the venous and lymphatic networks drain to the para-aortic region, the verse describes the neurovascular supply of the testes.
   * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment (Physiological & Anatomical):* In systemic anatomy, the vascular, lymphatic, and autonomic supply of an organ is distinct from the site of secretion and the excretory pathway of its exocrine product. While the gonadal arteries branch from the abdominal aorta at L2, sympathetic nerves arise from T10–L1, and the pampiniform venous plexus and lymphatics drain toward para-aortic nodes near the renal region, all pelvic and peripheral organs receive vascular and neural supply from proximal axial structures without their secretions being described as emerging from the axial skeleton. Textually, [Quran 86:6](quran://86/6)–[86:7](quran://86/7) states that the secreted fluid itself (`māʾ dāfiq`), rather than its arterial supply or autonomic innervation, emerges from between *al-ṣulb* and *al-tarāʾib*.
4. **Secondary Harmonization #4: The Pelvic Bones Hypothesis (Equating Tarāʾib with the Pubic Symphysis):**
   * *Concordist Hypothesis:* A fourth alternative reading proposes that `al-ṣulb` refers to the sacrum and `al-tarāʾib` refers to the pubic bone (symphysis pubis), situating the prostate and seminal vesicles between them within the pelvis.
   * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment (Lexical & Exegetical):* Classical Arabic anatomical nomenclature possesses dedicated terms for the pubic region and pubic bone, specifically `al-ʿānah` (العَانَة) and `al-shafah`, which are never conflated with `al-tarāʾib`. Foundational lexicons (*Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*, *Lisān al-ʿArab*) and early tafsīr corpora ([Tafsir al-Tabari 86:7](tabari://86/7), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 86:7](ibnkathir://86/7)) establish that `al-tarāʾib` refers exclusively to the upper chest, clavicles, or upper ribs where a necklace rests.
