### 4. Pre-Islamic Philosophical & Near Eastern Precedents

Concordist literature frequently posits that pre-modern natural philosophy uniformly regarded the atom as devoid of smaller constituents, and that subdivision below the atomic or visible threshold was unattested prior to modern physics. Historical documentation demonstrates, however, that both atomic theory and the conceptual division of matter below the atomic or visible threshold were extensively formulated in Greco-Roman and Indian philosophy more than a millennium before the rise of Islam.

#### Pre-Islamic Greek and Roman Atomism: Epicurus and Lucretius

While Leucippus and Democritus (5th century BC) pioneered classical atomism by positing indivisible particles (*atoma*), later atomists explicitly addressed the internal structure of atoms:

* **Epicurus (341–270 BC), *Letter to Herodotus* (§§ 58–59):** Epicurus recognized that for an atom to have shape, size, and weight, it must possess spatial parts. He formulated the theory of the *elachista* ("minimal parts"):
  > *"We must also consider that the atom has minimal parts (elachista moria) that are indivisible and without parts of their own... These minimal parts serve as the primary units of measure for the atom."* (Epicurus, *Letter to Herodotus*, §§ 58–59)
* **Lucretius (c. 99–55 BC), *De Rerum Natura* (I.599–634):** In his Latin philosophical treatise *On the Nature of Things*, the Roman atomist Lucretius explicitly articulated the existence of constituent parts within the atom:
  > *"Furthermore, since there is a crowning peak [extremity] of that body which our senses can no longer perceive, that peak certainly exists without parts and is endowed with the least possible nature... It is a part of the atom, first and single, and other like parts in order fill up the nature of the prime body in a close-packed mass."* (*De Rerum Natura*, Book I, lines 599–605)
  Thus, over 700 years before the 7th century AD, Greco-Roman atomists explicitly posited constituent sub-parts smaller than the physical atom.

#### Aristotle and Stoic Infinite Divisibility

In contrast to atomism, Aristotle (384–322 BC) in *Physics* (Book VI, chapters 1–2, 231a–233b) and Stoic philosophers such as Chrysippus (c. 280–206 BC) rejected indivisible units altogether, proposing the continuum theory:
* Aristotle argued that every continuous magnitude is divisible *ad infinitum* (*eis apeiron tomē*). Under Aristotelian physics—which formed the standard curriculum of Late Antique philosophical schools in Alexandria, Antioch, and Nisibis—it was a foundational axiom that for any material quantity, there is perpetually **"something smaller than that"** (*elasson toutou*).

#### Ancient Indian Atomism: The *Vaiśeṣika* and *Abhidharma* Schools

In ancient India, the *Vaiśeṣika* school founded by the philosopher Kaṇāda (*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra*, c. 6th–2nd century BC) and subsequent Buddhist *Abhidharma* traditions formulated a hierarchical taxonomy of microscopic particles:

1. **The Sunbeam Dust Mote (*Trasareṇu* or *Truṭi*):** Directly analogous to the Classical Arabic *dharrah* or *habāʾ*, Indian philosophers defined the *trasareṇu* as the smallest particle visible to the naked human eye floating in a sunbeam passing through a window lattice.
2. **Sub-Units of the Mote:** Kaṇāda stated that this visible sunbeam dust mote is composite, consisting of three binary dyads (*dvyaṇukas*).
3. **The Ultimate Particle (*Paramāṇu*):** Each dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is further composed of two ultimate constituent particles (*paramāṇus*).
Thus, Indian natural philosophy systematically divided the visible sunbeam dust mote into two distinct tiers of sub-visible constituent particles more than a thousand years before the Quran.

#### Pre-Islamic Biblical and Near Eastern Omniscience Parallels

The theological motif of divine omniscience encompassing the weight of the smallest creature or dust speck is widely attested in Jewish and Christian scripture:

* **[Matthew 10:29](bible://mt/10/29)–[Matthew 10:30](bible://mt/10/30):** *"Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered."*
* **[Matthew 13:31](bible://mt/13/31)–[Matthew 13:32](bible://mt/13/32):** *"The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field; it is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants..."*
* **[Isaiah 40:15](bible://is/40/15):** *"Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are regarded as a speck of dust on the scales (kedeq me'oznayim nihshāvū); behold, He takes up the isles as a very little thing."*
* **[Isaiah 40:12](bible://is/40/12):** *"Who has measured the waters in the hollow of His hand, and marked off the heavens with a span, and enclosed the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance?"*

The imagery in [Quran 10:61](quran://10/61) of weighing the smallest dust speck or ant aligns directly with these ancient Near Eastern metaphors of divine balance and omniscience.

### 5. Evaluation of Secondary Concordist Proposals

Several secondary arguments have been advanced in modern concordist literature to support an atomic reading of [Quran 10:61](quran://10/61). Each can be evaluated against historical lexicography and comparative philology:

* **Proposal 1: Lexical Continuity with Modern Scientific Arabic:** Proponents suggest that because modern Arabic scientific textbooks employ *dharrah* for the chemical atom, the Quranic occurrence carries the same denotation.
  * *Primary-Source & Philological Assessment:* This reasoning conflates diachronic semantic shift with original historical usage. In historical linguistics, terms frequently undergo technical specialization over centuries; for instance, in 17th-century English, the noun "computer" denoted a human clerk performing arithmetic calculations by hand, and projecting modern silicon microprocessor technology onto a 17th-century occurrence of the word would constitute a diachronic anachronism. Analogously, interpreting the 7th-century Arabic *dharrah* as a chemical or nuclear atom on the basis of 19th- and 20th-century *Nahḍah* translation conventions overlooks the documented semantic history of the term.
* **Proposal 2: The Spatial Formula ("In the Earth or in the Sky"):** Concordist commentators argue that because small red ants inhabit the ground, the phrase *"in the earth or in the sky"* (*fī al-arḍi wa-lā fī al-samāʾ*) indicates that *dharrah* cannot denote an ant and must instead denote an atom distributed throughout cosmic space.
  * *Primary-Source & Philological Assessment:* Both lexicographical evidence and comparative Semitic rhetoric address this syntactic construction:
    1. *Airborne Dust Specks:* As documented in *Kitāb al-ʿAyn* and *Lisān al-ʿArab*, *dharrah* equally denotes fine dust motes (*habāʾ*) suspended in sunbeams in the air.
    2. *Semitic Merism of Totality:* The pairing of "earth and sky" functions in Classical Arabic and broader Semitic literature as a polar merism signifying universal totality—that is, anywhere in existence. The Quran employs this identical spatial merism in [Quran 31:16](quran://31/16) with reference to a mustard seed: *"even if it should be the weight of a mustard seed and should be within a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth, God will bring it forth."* Just as the mention of "the heavens" in [Quran 31:16](quran://31/16) does not imply that botanical mustard seeds populate outer space, the parallel clause in [Quran 10:61](quran://10/61) expresses the universality of divine omniscience across all realms.
* **Proposal 3: Conceptual Novelty of Sub-Unit Divisibility:** A third concordist reading suggests that even if *dharrah* denotes a generic minute particle, the assertion that entities exist "smaller than that" was conceptually unprecedented in antiquity.
  * *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* As documented in Section 4, both continuous infinite divisibility (Aristotle, Stoic physics) and explicit sub-atomic or sub-mote particle hierarchies (Epicurus's *minimae partes*, and the Indian *Vaiśeṣika* progression from the visible sunbeam mote *trasareṇu* $\rightarrow$ *dvyaṇuka* $\rightarrow$ *paramāṇu*) were established doctrines in ancient natural philosophy more than a millennium prior to the 7th century AD. Furthermore, because *dharrah* in 7th-century Hijazi usage denoted a small ant or visible dust speck, noting that a constituent part—such as an ant's head or leg, as cited by Ibn ʿAbbās in [Tafsir al-Tabari 4:40](tabari://4/40), or a smaller fraction of dust—is "smaller than a *dharrah*" reflects direct macroscopic observation.

12:43.refutation:
Philological, archaeological, numismatic, and Late Antique literary evidence demonstrates that the Quran's use of *al-Malik* ("the King") in [Quran 12:43](quran://12/43) does not reflect miraculous historical foresight or an Egyptological correction of the Hebrew Bible. In classical Arabic grammar and early Islamic exegesis, *Firʿawn* is treated strictly as an indeclinable foreign personal proper name (*ʿalam aʿjamī*) designating Moses's specific royal antagonist, rather than an institutional dynastic title. Consequently, any other monarch in the narrative naturally defaults to the common Arabic noun *malik* ("king") or *al-Malik* ("the King"). Furthermore, the Quranic Joseph narrative incorporates prominent chronological anachronisms—most notably the sale of Joseph for counted silver Hellenistic coins (*darāhim maʿdūdah*, [Quran 12:20](quran://12/20)) more than a millennium before the invention of coinage—while the alternation between "the King" and "Pharaoh" was already standard in the Hebrew Bible ([Genesis 40:1](bible://gn/40/1), [Genesis 41:46](bible://gn/41/46)) and pre-Islamic Syriac liturgical homilies on Joseph (*Mimrē d-Yausep*).

Concordists attempt to correlate this textual feature with modern Egyptological epigraphy:
1. The Ancient Egyptian word *pr-ꜥꜣ* (literally "Great House"), which originally designated the royal palace, palace precinct, or royal administration during the Old and Middle Kingdoms, only began to be applied metonymically to the person of the monarch during the 18th Dynasty of the New Kingdom (specifically under Thutmose III, c. 1479–1425 BC, or Akhenaten, c. 1353–1336 BC).
2. Concordists argue that the Hebrew Bible's use of "Pharaoh" during the era of Abraham ([Genesis 12:15](bible://gn/12/15)) and Joseph (conventionally dated to the Middle Kingdom, c. 2000–1700 BC, or the Second Intermediate Period / Hyksos 15th Dynasty, c. 1650–1550 BC; e.g., [Genesis 41:1](bible://gn/41/1)) represents an anachronistic historical inaccuracy, which the Quran allegedly corrected by terming Joseph's ruler *al-Malik*.
3. Alternatively, other concordist authors claim that Joseph lived under the Semitic Hyksos rulers of the 15th Dynasty, who allegedly were foreign rulers who did not assume traditional Egyptian royal titles.

#### The Philological Category Error: `Firʿawn` as a Personal Proper Name

This concordist argument rests on a philological misapprehension of classical Arabic grammar and internal Quranic syntax. In classical Arabic and the Quranic text, **`Firʿawn` (`فِرْعَوْن`) is treated strictly as an indeclinable foreign personal proper name (*ʿalam aʿjamī mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf*)**, rather than as an institutional or dynastic title:

1. **Morphological Classification in Classical Arabic Grammar:** In the seminal linguistic work of Sībawayh (d. c. AD 796), *al-Kitāb* (Vol. 3), and subsequent authorities such as Ibn ʿAqīl (*Sharḥ Ibn ʿAqīl ʿalā Alfiyyat Ibn Mālik*), *Firʿawn* is explicitly classified among the non-Arabic proper nouns (*al-asmāʾ al-aʿjamiyyah*). It is treated as a diptote (*mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf*), prevented from receiving nunation (*tanwīn*) and inflected with *fatḥah* in genitive positions, strictly due to two combining morphological causes (*ʿillatān*): *al-ʿalamiyyah* (designating a specific unique personal individual) and *al-ʿujmah* (non-Arabic foreign linguistic origin).
2. **Total Absence of the Definite Article Across All 74 Quranic Occurrences:** Across all 74 occurrences of *Firʿawn* in the Quran, it never once takes the Arabic definite article (*al-*); the form `*al-Firʿawn*` is completely unattested in the Quranic corpus. In contrast, genuine institutional, royal, and official titles in the Quran consistently carry the definite article:
   - *al-Malik* ("the King", [Quran 12:43](quran://12/43), [Quran 12:72](quran://12/72))
   - *al-ʿAzīz* ("the Chief / Governor", [Quran 12:30](quran://12/30), [Quran 12:51](quran://12/51))
   - *al-Nabī* ("the Prophet", [Quran 8:64](quran://8/64))
   - *al-Rasūl* ("the Messenger", [Quran 4:59](quran://4/59))
3. **Parallels with Other Personal Proper Names:** The Quran treats *Firʿawn* syntactically and narratively in the same manner as other personal proper names of ancient figures: *Ibrāhīm*, *Ismāʿīl*, *Hāmān*, and *Qārūn*. Just as the Quran treats the ethnic/geographic descriptor *al-Sāmirī* ([Quran 20:85](quran://20/85)) or the Mesopotamian/Persian ministerial name *Hāmān* ([Quran 28:38](quran://28/38), [Quran 40:36](quran://40/36)) as personal proper names of specific individuals, the Quranic text treats *Firʿawn* as the specific personal name of the individual monarch confronting Moses.
4. **Default Usage of `Malik` and `Mulk` for Other Sovereigns:** Because *Firʿawn* was regarded as the unique personal name of that specific Mosaic antagonist, the text does not apply it to a different monarch in the Joseph narrative. Any other monarch in the Quran—whether the sovereign in Joseph's story (*al-Malik*, [Quran 12:43](quran://12/43)), the king Ṭālūt/Saul appointed over Israel (*malik*, [Quran 2:246](quran://2/246), [Quran 2:247](quran://2/247)), or the ruler encountered by al-Khiḍr during Moses's journey (*malik*, [Quran 18:79](quran://18/79))—is naturally designated by the ordinary Arabic common noun *malik* ("king"), just as the rule of the sovereign who debated Abraham ([Quran 2:258](quran://2/258)) and the reign of David ([Quran 2:251](quran://2/251)) are described using the cognate verbal noun *al-mulk* ("the kingship / sovereignty"; alongside *khalīfah*, "ruler / vicegerent," for David in [Quran 38:26](quran://38/26)).

Therefore, referring to Joseph's ruler as *al-Malik* in Surah 12 is a grammatical consequence of classical Arabic syntax treating *Firʿawn* as Moses's opponent's personal proper name, rather than an awareness of New Kingdom epigraphy.

### 2. Egyptological, Numismatic & Internal Textual Analysis

The hypothesis of Egyptological precision in Surah 12 can be evaluated against the material culture, numismatics, and internal chronology of the text alongside the epigraphic record:

| Narrative / Historical Feature | Modern Concordist Assertion | Archaeological, Epigraphic, Numismatic & Textual Evidence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hyksos Royal Titulary** | Hyksos rulers of Joseph's era were foreign Semites who were only called "King" and did not use Pharaonic royal titles. | Epigraphic monuments of 15th-Dynasty Hyksos kings (Khyan, Apophis) at Avaris confirm they adopted the complete fivefold Pharaonic royal protocol: *nsw-bjtj* ("King of Upper and Lower Egypt"), *sꜣ-Rꜥ* ("Son of Ra"), and royal cartouches. |
| **Monetary Currency (Quran 12:20)** | Surah 12 reflects second-millennium BC Egyptian historical reality without chronological anachronisms. | [Quran 12:20](quran://12/20) depicts Joseph sold for counted silver coins (*darāhim maʿdūdah*, from Greek *drachmē*), whereas minted coinage was invented c. 630–600 BC in Lydia—over a millennium after Joseph. [Genesis 37:28](bible://gn/37/28) accurately specifies weighed silver. |
| **Lifespan of Moses's Monarch** | The Quran accurately portrays ancient Egyptian dynastic succession and historical chronology. | The Quran depicts the same individual *Firʿawn* ruling from Moses's infancy to the Exodus decades later ([Quran 26:18](quran://26/18), [Quran 28:8](quran://28/8)), diverging from [Exodus 2:23](bible://ex/2/23) where the king of Egypt dies during Moses's exile. |
| **Method of Judicial Execution** | The Quran reflects authentic Middle and New Kingdom Egyptian penal practices. | [Quran 12:41](quran://12/41) and [Quran 20:71](quran://20/71) describe execution by crucifixion (*taṣlīb*), a Persian and Roman penal method introduced centuries later. Middle/New Kingdom Egypt utilized decapitation and suspension on a wooden pole ([Genesis 40:19](bible://gn/40/19)). |
| **Royal Nomenclature in Historiography** | Genesis committed a historical inaccuracy by calling Joseph's ruler "Pharaoh", which the Quran corrected to *al-Malik*. | Genesis and Exodus repeatedly designate the monarch *melekh Miṣrayim* ("the king of Egypt", [Genesis 39:20](bible://gn/39/20), [Genesis 40:1](bible://gn/40/1), [Exodus 1:8](bible://ex/1/8)), while pre-Islamic Syriac homilies (*Mimrē d-Yausep*) standardly used *malkā* ("the King") for Joseph's sovereign. |

#### Detailed Analysis of Primary Archaeological and Historical Evidence

1. **The Hyksos Adopted Full Egyptian Pharaonic Titulary:**
   - Concordist authors frequently assert that Joseph lived under the Semitic Hyksos (15th Dynasty, c. 1650–1550 BC), who allegedly were Asiatic rulers not considered "Pharaohs" and not using Egyptian royal titles.
   - Archaeological excavations at Tell el-Dab'a (ancient Avaris) directed by Manfred Bietak, alongside epigraphic discoveries across Egypt and the Levant, diverge directly from this hypothesis. The major 15th-Dynasty Hyksos rulers—most notably King Khyan (c. 1610 BC) and King Apophis / Apepi (c. 1575–1540 BC)—thoroughly Egyptianized their court and officially adopted the traditional Fivefold Pharaonic Titulary.
   - Inscriptions on monumental stone stelae, granite lintels, scarabs, and cylinder seals demonstrate that Hyksos kings enclosed their throne names in royal cartouches (*šenw*) and adopted the classic Pharaonic royal titles: *nsw-bjtj* ("King of Upper and Lower Egypt"), *sꜣ-Rꜥ* ("Son of Ra"), and *nṯr nfr* ("The Good God"). On an offering table dedicated to Setekh/Seth found at Avaris, Apophis is styled with the complete royal titulary of the ancient native Egyptian monarchs.
   - Moreover, native Egyptian Middle Kingdom texts (such as 12th Dynasty Papyrus Berlin 10016, dating to the reign of Sesostris III / Amenemhat III, c. 1850 BC) already applied the term *pr-ꜥꜣ* ("Great House") directly to the royal palace and palace administration.

2. **Numismatic Anachronism: *Darāhim Maʿdūdah* (Counted Silver Coins) in [Quran 12:20](quran://12/20):**
   - In [Quran 12:20](quran://12/20), the Quran recounts that Joseph was sold into Egypt for: *wa-sharawhu bi-thamanin bakhsin darāhima maʿdūdatin* ("And they sold him for a low price, a few counted dirhams [silver coins]").
   - In historical reality, **minted coinage was non-existent during the Middle and Late Bronze Ages (c. 2000–1200 BC)**. The world's earliest minted coins were not invented until approximately 630–600 BC in Lydia (western Anatolia) under the Mermnad dynasty (King Alyattes and King Croesus), spreading to the Persian Empire and the Greek world during the 6th and 5th centuries BC.
   - Coinage was not introduced into Egypt until the late Achaemenid Persian and Ptolemaic periods (post-525 BC and especially after Alexander's conquest in 332 BC). During the era conventionally assigned to Joseph (c. 1800–1550 BC), monetary transactions in Egypt and Canaan were conducted exclusively by weighing uncoined raw metal pieces or *Hacksilber* against stone balance weights (such as the Egyptian *deben* and *kite*, or the Canaanite *shekel*).
   - Furthermore, the Arabic word *dirham* (`دِرْهَم`) is a direct linguistic loanword via Sasanian Middle Persian (*dram*) from the Ancient Greek silver coin **`drachmē`** (`δραχμή`). The accompanying Quranic modifier *maʿdūdah* ("counted out by number") confirms that these were discrete minted coin units rather than weighed bullion (*mawzūnah*).
   - In contrast, [Genesis 37:28](bible://gn/37/28) records: *"and they sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty [shekels of] silver."* The Hebrew text uses uncoined weighed silver (*kesep*), the standard historical medium of exchange in the Bronze Age Near East. The depiction of merchants paying for Joseph in counted Greek-derived *drachma* coins reflects the monetary economy of Late Antiquity rather than second-millennium BC Egypt.

3. **Single-Ruler Anachronism Across Moses's Lifespan:**
   - In the Quran, the exact same individual *Firʿawn* who adopts Moses as an infant from the Nile ([Quran 28:8](quran://28/8)–[28:9](quran://28/9)) is still reigning when Moses flees to Midian, stays for many years, returns as an adult prophet, confronts the court with signs, and pursues the Israelites into the Red Sea ([Quran 26:18](quran://26/18)–[26:19](quran://26/19), [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38)). In [Quran 26:18](quran://26/18), Pharaoh explicitly reminds Moses: *qāla a-lam nurabbika fīnā walīdan wa-labithta fīnā min ʿumurika sinīn* ("He said: Did we not bring you up among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life?").
   - Moses was an infant at his adoption, spent his youth in the palace, fled to Midian for at least eight to ten years ([Quran 28:27](quran://28/27)), and returned as an elderly man—spanning 60 to 80 years. In historical New Kingdom Egypt, no single Pharaoh had a reign matching this lifespan across the Exodus era (Ramesses II reigned 66 years, but Moses's lifespan exceeds this, and Ramesses II did not drown in the Red Sea; his successor Merneptah reigned only 10 years).
   - In contrast, the Hebrew Bible explicitly preserves the change of monarchs: [Exodus 2:23](bible://ex/2/23) records: *"Now it came about in the course of those many days that the king of Egypt died, and the sons of Israel sighed because of the bondage."* Moses returns to confront a *different* king (the Pharaoh of the Exodus), whereas the Quran portrays an identical, unchanging sovereign throughout Moses's life.

4. **The Anachronism of Crucifixion (*Taṣlīb*):**
   - In [Quran 12:41](quran://12/41), Joseph interprets the dream of the royal baker: *wa-ammā al-ākharu fa-yuṣlabu fa-taʾkulu al-ṭayru min raʾsihi* ("And as for the other, he will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head"). Similarly, in [Quran 7:124](quran://7/124) and [Quran 26:49](quran://26/49), Pharaoh threatens his sorcerers with mass crucifixion (*la-uṣallibannakum ajmaʿīn*), and in [Quran 20:71](quran://20/71) specifically with crucifixion on palm trunks (*wa-la-uṣallibannakum fī judhūʿi al-nakhl*).
   - Capital punishment by crucifixion on a wooden frame or cross was developed centuries later by the Neo-Assyrians, Persians, and Romans (c. 6th century BC to 1st century AD). Ancient Egyptians of the Middle and New Kingdoms executed criminals by decapitation, strangulation, or burning, and occasionally displayed executed bodies by hanging them on wooden stakes or trees.
   - In contrast, [Genesis 40:19](bible://gn/40/19) reflects authentic Egyptian practice: *"Yet within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head from you and hang you on a tree [or wooden stake], and the birds will eat your flesh from you."* Genesis specifies decapitation followed by exposure on a tree, whereas the Quran employs the late Roman-era penal term *yuṣlabu* ("he will be crucified").

5. **Alternation of *Melekh* ("King") and *Pharaoh* in Biblical Historiography:**
   - The Hebrew Bible does not exclusively use "Pharaoh" for Joseph's ruler. Genesis itself repeatedly refers to the Egyptian monarch as *melekh Miṣrayim* ("the king of Egypt", [Genesis 39:20](bible://gn/39/20), [Genesis 40:1](bible://gn/40/1), [Genesis 40:5](bible://gn/40/5), [Genesis 41:46](bible://gn/41/46)), in parallel with the Exodus narrative ([Exodus 1:8](bible://ex/1/8), [Exodus 1:15](bible://ex/1/15), [Exodus 2:23](bible://ex/2/23), [Exodus 3:19](bible://ex/3/19)).
   - Ancient Semitic writers utilized "Pharaoh" alongside "King" as an intelligible cultural designation for any Egyptian ruler, much as modern historians write about "the Roman Emperor" Augustus or "the Russian Tsar" Peter the Great.

### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr)

Classical Muslim exegetes and historians did not interpret the word *al-Malik* in [Quran 12:43](quran://12/43) as an Egyptological indicator of dynastic titles or hieroglyphic vocabulary. Instead, they understood both the king of Joseph's time and the Pharaoh of Moses's time through the lens of pre-Islamic Arabian genealogical lore, explicitly identifying both rulers as **Amalekite Arabs (*ʿAmālīq*)**:

#### Exegetical Commentary on Quran 12:43

In [Tafsir al-Tabari 12:43](tabari://12/43), Abu Ja'far Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī provides the traditional identification of the king:
> **{وَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ إِنِّي أَرَىٰ سَبْعَ بَقَرَاتٍ سِمَانٍ يَأْكُلُهُنَّ سَبْعٌ عِجَافٌ}**
> *"Abu Ja'far said: He means by His saying: And the king of Egypt said: 'I see in a dream seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean cows.' ... Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Isḥāq, who said: Then the king, **al-Rayyān ibn al-Walīd**, saw his vision which he saw, and it startled him."* ([Tafsir al-Tabari 12:43](tabari://12/43))

Similarly, Ismāʿīl ibn Kathīr records in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 12:43](ibnkathir://12/43):
> *"This dream of the King of Egypt was something that Allah the Exalted decreed to be the reason for Yusuf's (peace be upon him) release from prison in a state of honor and dignity. This is because the King saw this dream, and it startled him; he wondered about it and what its interpretation could be. Thus, he gathered the priests, the diviners, the leading figures of his state, and his commanders, and recounted to them what he had seen."* ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 12:43](ibnkathir://12/43))

#### The Amalekite Genealogies of Joseph's King and Moses's Pharaoh

In their historical chronicles (*Taʾrīkh al-Rusul wa-al-Mulūk*, Vol. 1, pp. 177–178; *al-Bidāyah wa-al-Nihāyah*, Vol. 1), both al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr trace the full genealogy of Joseph's sovereign:
- His name was **al-Rayyān ibn al-Walīd ibn Tharwān ibn Arāshah ibn Qārān ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿImlīq ibn Lāwudh ibn Sām ibn Nūḥ**—identifying him as a member of the ancient Arabian tribe of **ʿImlīq (the Amalekites)**.
- Furthermore, classical historians record that the *Firʿawn* of Moses was also an Amalekite Arab named **al-Walīd ibn Muṣʿab** (or Qābūs ibn Muṣʿab), stating that he was directly related to al-Rayyān ibn al-Walīd from the same Amalekite dynasty.
- Early Islamic historical tradition did not distinguish Ancient Egyptian dynastic shifts, Old vs. Middle vs. New Kingdoms, or the evolution of the hieroglyphic title *pr-ꜥꜣ*. To early Muslim scholars, the monarchs of Egypt were ancient Amalekite Arab kings who bore Arabic patronymics.

#### Direct Continuity Between Joseph and Moses's Pharaoh in the Quran

Moreover, in [Quran 40:28](quran://40/28)–[40:34](quran://40/34), the Quran portrays a believer from the household of Pharaoh (*rajulun muʾminun min āli Firʿawn*) who addresses Pharaoh's court by declaring:
> **{وَلَقَدْ جَاءَكُمْ يُوسُفُ مِن قَبْلُ بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ فَمَا زِلْتُمْ فِي شَكٍّ مِّمَّا جَاءَكُم بِهِ}**
> *"And Joseph had already come to you before with clear proofs, yet you ceased not to be in doubt of that which he brought you..."* ([Quran 40:34](quran://40/34))

This passage demonstrates that the Quran views Joseph and the court of Moses's Pharaoh (*āl Firʿawn*) in direct generational and institutional continuity, explicitly addressing Pharaoh's people as the same corporate entity that had received Joseph.

### 4. Verbatim Pre-Islamic Biblical, Septuagint & Syriac Precedents

The distinction between "the King" and "Pharaoh" was not an innovation of the 7th-century AD Quranic text. The alternation between "King" (*melekh* / *basileus*) and "Pharaoh" (*parʿōh* / *Pharaō*) was firmly established in pre-Islamic biblical literature and Late Antique Christian homilies:

#### Biblical and Septuagint Alternation of Titles

1. **[Genesis 39:20](bible://gn/39/20):** *"So Joseph’s master took him and put him into the jail, the place where the king's prisoners were confined"* (Hebrew: `ʾăsîrê ham-melekh`; Septuagint Greek: `τοῦ βασιλέως`).
2. **[Genesis 40:1](bible://gn/40/1):** *"Then it came about after these things, the cupbearer and the baker for the king of Egypt offended their lord, the king of Egypt"* (Hebrew: `melekh Miṣrayim`; Septuagint Greek: `τῷ βασιλεῖ Αἰγύπτου`).
3. **[Genesis 40:5](bible://gn/40/5):** *"Then the cupbearer and the baker for the king of Egypt, who were confined in jail, both had a dream the same night"* (Hebrew: `melekh Miṣrayim`; Septuagint Greek: `βασιλέως Αἰγύπτου`).
4. **[Genesis 41:46](bible://gn/41/46):** *"Now Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh, king of Egypt [melekh Miṣrayim, LXX: βασιλέως Αἰγύπτου], and Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh and went through all the land of Egypt."*
5. **[Exodus 1:8](bible://ex/1/8):** *"Now a new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph"* (Hebrew: `melekh-ḥādāsh ʿal-Miṣrāyim`; Septuagint Greek: `βασιλεὺς ἕτερος ἐπʼ Αἴγυπτον`).
6. **[Exodus 1:15](bible://ex/1/15):** *"Then the king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives..."* (Hebrew: `melekh Miṣrayim`; Septuagint Greek: `ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Αἰγυπτίων`).
7. **[Acts 7:10](bible://act/7/10):** *"...and granted him favor and wisdom in the sight of Pharaoh, king of Egypt [Pharaō basileōs Aigyptou], and he made him governor over Egypt and all his household."*
8. **[Acts 7:18](bible://act/7/18):** *"until another king arose over Egypt who did not know about Joseph"* (`basileus heteros ep' Aigypton`).

#### Syriac Christian Homilies on Joseph (*Mimrē d-Yausep*, 4th–6th Century AD)

In Late Antiquity, the narrative of Joseph was among the most prominent and widely performed liturgical traditions across the Syriac-speaking Near East. Prominent Syriac poets and theologians—including the homiletic corpus attributed to Ephrem the Syrian (d. AD 373), Narsai of Edessa (d. c. AD 502), and Balai (5th century AD)—composed extensive metrical homilies (*mimrē*) on the life of Joseph (*Mimrē d-Yausep*).

As documented by Syriac scholars Witold Witakowski (*"The Story of Joseph in Syriac Literature"*, 1999) and Joseph P. Amar (*A Metrical Homily on Holy Mar Joseph by Mar Narsai*, 2000), alongside Sidney Griffith (*The Bible in Arabic*, Princeton University Press, 2013) and Gabriel Said Reynolds (*The Qur'an and the Bible*, Yale University Press, 2018):
- These Syriac liturgical traditions standardly referred to the ruler of Egypt in the Joseph narrative simply as **`malkā` (`ܡܠܟܐ`)**—the exact Northwest Semitic and Aramaic/Syriac cognate of Arabic **`al-malik`** ("the King").
- In the Syriac *Mimrē*, the monarch of Joseph's dream is repeatedly referred to as *malkā d-Meṣrēn* ("the King of Egypt") or simply *malkā*, whereas *Peraʿōn* ("Pharaoh") was reserved as the iconic name of the ruler in the Exodus narrative.
- Thus, the practice of designating Joseph's monarch simply as "the King" while designating Moses's opponent as "Pharaoh" was firmly established across the Christian, Jewish, and Aramaic/Syriac literary milieu of the pre-Islamic Near East centuries before the compilation of the Quran.

---

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Modern Harmonizations

Modern concordist writers propose three primary secondary harmonizations regarding these historical and philological findings:

1. **Secondary Harmonization of the Numismatic Anachronism (*Darāhim Maʿdūdah*) in [Quran 12:20](quran://12/20):**
   - *Concordist Assertion:* Proponents claim that "dirham" in [Quran 12:20](quran://12/20) is merely a dynamic translation or generic term for weighed silver pieces (*shekels*).
   - *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* This alternative reading is not supported by the Arabic text of [Quran 12:20](quran://12/20) or classical lexicography. The verse does not say *bi-thamanin min fiḍḍah* ("for a price of silver"), but specifically *darāhima maʿdūdatin*. In Arabic grammar, the passive participle *maʿdūdah* ("counted out one by one by number") stands in direct semantic opposition to *mawzūnah* ("weighed out by balance scales").
   - Classical exegetes in [Tafsir al-Tabari 12:20](tabari://12/20) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 12:20](ibnkathir://12/20) explicitly confirm this distinction: al-Ṭabarī cites the earliest authorities (Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Mujāhid) specifying that Joseph was purchased for twenty or twenty-two counted silver coins, explicitly stating that *maʿdūdah* was used because anything under forty pieces was counted out individually rather than weighed on scales. The reference to counted Greek-derived *drachma* coins in a Bronze Age Egyptian setting constitutes a documented chronological anachronism.

2. **The Claim That *al-ʿAzīz* Represents an Ancient Egyptian Official Title:**
   - *Concordist Assertion:* Writers suggest that *al-ʿAzīz* in [Quran 12:30](quran://12/30) and [Quran 12:51](quran://12/51) preserves an authentic ancient Egyptian court title.
   - *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* In [Genesis 39:1](bible://gn/39/1), Joseph's master is named **Potiphar**, which Egyptologists confirm is the authentic Egyptian personal name **`pꜣ-dj-pꜣ-Rꜥ`** (*"He whom Ra has given"*), together with his authentic military title *sar haṭ-ṭabbāḥîm* (captain of the bodyguard).
   - In contrast, the Quran omits this Egyptian personal name and substitutes the native Arabic descriptor **`al-ʿAzīz`** ("the Mighty / Noble One"). Rather than representing an Egyptian loanword, *al-ʿAzīz* derives from a common Arabic root (*ʿ-z-z*) used throughout Arabic literature. The Quran applies this exact same title to Joseph himself once he achieves prominence ([Quran 12:78](quran://12/78), [Quran 12:88](quran://12/88)), and repeatedly employs *al-ʿAzīz* as one of the attributes of God ([Quran 2:129](quran://2/129), [Quran 59:23](quran://59/23)).

3. **Oral Homiletic Transmission vs. Epigraphic Innovation:**
   - *Concordist Assertion:* Concordists argue that 7th-century Arabians could not have known the titular distinction without divine revelation.
   - *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* As demonstrated by the pre-Islamic biblical text ([Genesis 39:20](bible://gn/39/20), [Genesis 40:1](bible://gn/40/1), [Genesis 40:5](bible://gn/40/5), [Genesis 41:46](bible://gn/41/46)) and the widespread performance of Syriac Christian homilies on Joseph (*malkā* in the *Mimrē d-Yausep*), "the King" was the standard oral and homiletic designation circulating in the Arabian Peninsula and the Levant during Late Antiquity. The Quran's narrative choices align directly with this regional literary tradition, combined with its grammatical treatment of *Firʿawn* as an individual personal proper name.

10:92.classification_explanation: First popularized in AD 1976 by French physician Maurice Bucaille (*La Bible, le Coran et la Science*) and widely repeated in modern concordist literature, this reading interprets [Quran 10:92](quran://10/92) (*fa-l-yawma nunajjīka bi-badanika*) as a prediction of modern museum preservation. Grammatically and lexically, the temporal marker *al-yawma* ('today') and root *n-j-w* (*al-najwah*, an elevated coastal mound) designate an immediate physical event witnessed on the shore by the crossing Israelites, as documented by early exegetes in [Tafsir al-Tabari 10:92](tabari://10/92) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 10:92](ibnkathir://10/92), where *bi-badanika* denotes a lifeless corpse (*jasad bi-lā rūḥ*) or armor-clad torso cast ashore to resolve doubts regarding Pharaoh's death. Furthermore, paleopathological CT scans (G. Elliot Smith AD 1912; Sahar Saleem & Zahi Hawass AD 2016) indicate that both candidate pharaohs died of advanced cardiovascular disease and age-related pathology and were preserved through standard New Kingdom natron desiccation, while the narrative motif of Pharaoh's corpse washed ashore parallels pre-Islamic Jewish Midrashic traditions (*b. Pesachim* 118b; *b. Arakhin* 15a) on [Exodus 14:30](bible://ex/14/30).
10:92.summary: In classical Arabic and early Islamic commentaries (al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr), [Quran 10:92](quran://10/92) does not predict a modern museum discovery; instead, it states that *on that very day* (*al-yawma*), the sea cast Pharaoh's lifeless, armor-clad corpse onto a raised coastal bank (*najwah*) so the doubting Israelites could see that he had died. Forensically, CT scans of Ramesses II and Merneptah show that both kings died in old age from natural vascular and skeletal disease rather than drowning, and their bodies survived through standard 70-day Egyptian natron embalming. Historically, the motif of the sea casting Pharaoh's drowned corpse ashore for skeptical Israelites to witness parallels a pre-Islamic Jewish tradition in [Exodus 14:30](bible://ex/14/30) and the Babylonian Talmud (*b. Pesachim* 118b).
10:92.refutation:
The hypothesis that [Quran 10:92](quran://10/92) predicts the late-19th-century archaeological discovery and museum exhibition of Pharaoh's mummified body is inconsistent with classical Arabic lexicography, early Islamic exegesis (*tafsīr*), forensic paleopathology, and the documentary history of the ancient Near East. Within its immediate narrative and grammatical context, the verse addresses the conclusion of the Exodus sea crossing: Pharaoh's lifeless corpse was cast by the sea onto an elevated coastal mound on that day so that the departing Israelites could visually verify that the pursuing monarch had perished. Furthermore, this narrative sequence—including the doubts of the Israelites and the divine command to the sea to eject Pharaoh's corpse onto the shore—parallels an established pre-Islamic Jewish rabbinic tradition documented centuries earlier in the Babylonian Talmud (*b. Pesachim* 118b; *b. Arakhin* 15a) and the *Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael* on [Exodus 14:30](bible://ex/14/30).

---

### 1. Context of Claim & Classical Arabic Philology

In modern concordist literature, this interpretation was formulated by French gastroenterologist **Maurice Bucaille** (AD 1920–1998). In *La Bible, le Coran et la Science* (AD 1976) and *Les Momies des Pharaons et la Médecine* (AD 1987), Bucaille proposed that whereas the biblical text implied that Pharaoh's body was lost at sea, [Quran 10:92](quran://10/92) preserved a historical prediction fulfilled when 19th-century Egyptologists excavated the royal caches at Thebes:

> *"فَالْيَوْمَ نُنَجِّيكَ بِبَدَنِكَ لِتَكُونَ لِمَنْ خَلْفَكَ آيَةً ۚ وَإِنَّ كَثِيرًا مِّنَ النَّاسِ عَنْ آيَاتِنَا لَغَافِلُونَ"*  
> *"So today We will save you in your body, that you may be a sign for those after you. Yet surely many of the people are indeed oblivious of Our signs."* ([Quran 10:92](quran://10/92))

Bucaille and subsequent writers (such as Zakir Naik) argued that this verse anticipated the AD 1881 discovery of the Royal Cache at Deir el-Bahari (DB320) containing Ramesses II, or the AD 1898 discovery of the tomb of Amenhotep II (KV35) containing Merneptah, whose mummies are now housed in the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Cairo.

However, a philological analysis of the Arabic text in light of classical Arabic lexicons (*Kitāb al-ʿAyn* of al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* of al-Jawharī, *Lisān al-ʿArab* of Ibn Manẓūr, and Edward William Lane's *Arabic-English Lexicon*, Book I, pp. 167, 2772–2773) indicates that this modern concordist reading diverges from the classical syntax and lexicon of the verse:

1. **The Temporal Marker `Fa-l-yawma` (`فَالْيَوْمَ` — "So TODAY"):**  
   The verse begins with the connective particle *fa-* prefixed to the definite temporal adverb *al-yawma* ("today", "on this day"). In Arabic grammar, *al-yawma* denotes immediate temporal coincidence with the ongoing narrative event—namely, the day of the Red Sea crossing described in [Quran 10:90](quran://10/90). It specifies that the casting ashore of Pharaoh's body occurred *on that very day* on the seashore, directly following his drowning in [Quran 10:90](quran://10/90)–[Quran 10:91](quran://10/91). Interpreting a temporal adverb meaning "today" as an event deferred for 3,100 years (until the late 19th century AD) is inconsistent with the standard temporal syntax of classical Arabic.

2. **The Verbal Root of `Nunajjīka` (`نُنَجِّيكَ` — From *al-Najwah*, "Elevated Ground"):**  
   While popular translations render *nunajjīka* generally as "We save you" or "We deliver you," classical lexicographers and early exegetes noted that the verb derives from the root *n-j-w*, which fundamentally signifies elevation and separation. As Edward William Lane records (*Arabic-English Lexicon*, p. 2772), *al-najwah* (النَّجْوَةُ) is *"a place of elevation, rising above the surrounding water or torrent."*  
   In [Tafsir al-Tabari 10:92](tabari://10/92), the early Quranic commentator Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī (d. AD 923) defines the verbal phrase explicitly:  
   *"يَقُولُ تَعَالَى ذِكْرُهُ لِفِرْعَوْنَ: الْيَوْمَ نَجْعَلُكَ عَلَى نَجْوَةٍ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ بِبَدَنِكَ، يَنْظُرُ إِلَيْكَ هَالِكًا مَنْ كَذَّبَ بِهَلَاكِكَ"*  
   *("The Exalted says in His remembrance to Pharaoh: Today We place you upon an elevated ground (najwah) of the earth with your body, so that those who denied your destruction may look at you in your ruined state.")*  
   The verb does not denote preserving the corpse from natural decay across millennia; it describes the physical action of the sea casting the submerged body up onto a high coastal sandbank so it would not remain submerged beneath the waves.

3. **The Lexical Meaning of `Bi-badanika` (`بِبَدَنِكَ`):**  
   In classical Arabic lexicography and the consensus of the earliest exegetes (*al-Salaf*), the noun *badan* (بَدَن) in this verse carries two primary technical senses, neither of which refers to artificial embalming or mummification:
   * **A Lifeless Corpse Without a Soul (`jasad lā rūḥa fīhi`):** As recorded in both [Tafsir al-Tabari 10:92](tabari://10/92) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 10:92](ibnkathir://10/92), early authorities—including Mujāhid ibn Jabr (d. AD 722), al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (d. AD 728), and ʿAbdullāh ibn Shaddād—glossed *bi-badanika* as *bi-jasadika* ("with your physical corpse"), specifically *jasadan bi-lā rūḥ* ("a body devoid of spirit"), while Qays ibn ʿUbbād and Ibn Jurayj in [Tafsir al-Tabari 10:92](tabari://10/92) add that his corpse was cast ashore *ka-annahu thawrun aḥmar* ("as if he were a red bull"). In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 10:92](ibnkathir://10/92), Ibn Shaddād clarified that it meant *sawiyyan ṣaḥīḥan, ay: lam yatamazzaq li-yataḥaqqaqūhu wa-yaʿrifūhu* ("intact and whole, meaning not torn to pieces, so that they could verify and recognize him").
   * **A Coat of Mail or Hauberk Armor (`dirʿ qaṣīrah`):** In classical Arabic, *badan* also designates a short coat of mail or cuirass that covers the torso (*badan*) of a warrior (Lane, *Lexicon*, p. 167; *Lisān al-ʿArab*, root *b-d-n*). In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 10:92](ibnkathir://10/92), Ibn Kathīr records from Ibn ʿAbbās and others of the *Salaf* that Pharaoh's corpse was cast ashore *wa-ʿalayhi dirʿuhu al-maʿrūfatu bihi* (`وَعَلَيْهِ دِرْعُهُ الْمَعْرُوفَةُ بِهِ`, "wearing his well-known armor"), and cites Abū Ṣakhr's gloss of *bi-badanika* as *bi-dirʿika* (`بِدِرْعِكَ`, "with your armor"), enabling the Israelites to recognize the monarch from a distance.

4. **The Target Audience: `Li-takūna li-man khalfaka āyatan` (`لِتَكُونَ لِمَنْ خَلْفَكَ آيَةً`):**  
   Classical commentators explain that *man khalfaka* ("those behind you" or "those after you") refers directly to the Children of Israel standing on the seashore after having crossed the parted waters. Having experienced generations of subjugation under Pharaoh's rule, segments of the community doubted Moses when he announced that the king had perished. The corpse was therefore exposed to them *on that day* to provide immediate visual verification of his death. A body sealed inside a subterranean tomb for over 3,000 years would not have been visible to the audience standing on the shore.

### 2. Egyptological, Forensic & Textual Analysis (With Markdown Comparison Table)

Evaluating the concordist correlation against modern Egyptology requires examining New Kingdom mortuary customs, archaeological stratigraphy, and the paleopathology of the royal mummies.

| Forensic & Historical Feature | Modern Concordist Assertion (Bucaille / Naik) | Archaeological & Paleopathological Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cause of Preservation** | Bodily preservation is a unique sign reserved for the Exodus Pharaoh who drowned in the sea. | **Routine New Kingdom Embalming:** Royal pharaohs were preserved through artificial 70-day natron desiccation, evisceration, and resin wrapping. Dozens of intact royal mummies were preserved by the same method. |
| **Paleopathology of Ramesses II** (r. 1279–1213 BC, DB320) | Identified as the Pharaoh of the Exodus who drowned at sea while pursuing Moses. | **Advanced Senility & Natural Death:** CT and radiographic scans show he died at ~90 years of age from severe ankylosing spondylitis, advanced vascular arteriosclerosis, and severe mandibular osteomyelitis, with no drowning pathology. |
| **Paleopathology of Merneptah** (r. 1213–1203 BC, KV35) | Identified as exhibiting salt encrustation from seawater and lethal cranial trauma from waves. | **Elderly Cardiovascular Disease & Natron Salt:** Died at ~60–70 years of age from severe aortic atherosclerosis; cranial openings were cut post-mortem by ancient embalmers or tomb robbers; skin salts are standard natron embalming salts. |
| **Audience Visibility** (*Li-man khalfaka āyatan*) | Pharaoh's preserved mummy was foretold to be displayed for modern museum visitors across the world. | **Three Millennia of Subterranean Burial:** Both mummies were entombed in rock-cut crypts in the Valley of the Kings, re-cached c. 1000 BC in DB320 and KV35, and remained unseen for over 3,000 years until AD 1881/1898. |
| **Internal Quranic Account of Drowning** | The Quran states Pharaoh was saved from drowning, diverging from the biblical account. | **Quran Explicitly Describes Drowning:** [Quran 28:40](quran://28/40) states *"We cast them into the sea"*, [Quran 43:55](quran://43/55) states *"We drowned them all"*, and [Quran 10:90](quran://10/90) confirms drowning overtook him. |

#### Detailed Analysis of the Egyptological and Forensic Data

* **1. Routine Egyptian Mummification vs. Post-Immersion Preservation:**  
  A central premise of the modern concordist reading is that the physical survival of a New Kingdom royal body represents a singular historical anomaly. In archaeological terms, however, artificial corporeal preservation was the standard funerary protocol for ancient Egyptian royalty. When Gaston Maspero unbandaged the Deir el-Bahari cache (DB320) in AD 1881 and Victor Loret entered KV35 in AD 1898, they did not recover a single isolated body. They documented the intact mummies of much of the New Kingdom royal lineage: **Seqenenre Tao, Ahmose I, Amenhotep I, Thutmose I, Thutmose II, Thutmose III, Thutmose IV, Amenhotep II, Amenhotep III, Seti I, Ramesses I, Ramesses II, Ramesses III, Merneptah, Seti II, and Siptah**, alongside royal women such as **Hatshepsut** and **Queen Tiye**.  
  Each of these bodies survived because ancient mortuary priests removed their internal organs (lungs, liver, stomach, and intestines, which were stored separately in canopic jars), treated the cranial cavity with heated tree resins, and desiccated the cadaver by packing it in dry **natron salt** (a natural evaporite composed of hydrated sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate) for seventy days before wrapping it in linen bandages. Because New Kingdom funerary priests applied this identical desiccation protocol across the 18th, 19th, and 20th Dynasties, the survival of any individual royal mummy reflects standard Egyptian mortuary technology rather than a unique post-immersion preservation event.

* **2. Forensic Paleopathology of Ramesses II (r. 1279–1213 BC, DB320):**  
  Frequently identified in popular literature and early concordist works as the Pharaoh of the Exodus, Ramesses II's mummy was recovered from DB320. Detailed anatomical studies—beginning with Sir Grafton Elliot Smith (*The Royal Mummies*, AD 1912), continuing through the multidisciplinary Parisian examination at the Musée de l'Homme (AD 1976–1977, directed by Lionel Balout and C. Roubet), and culminating in high-resolution computed tomography (CT) scans by Zahi Hawass and Sahar Saleem (*Scanning the Pharaohs: CT Imaging of the New Kingdom Royal Mummies*, American University in Cairo Press, AD 2016, pp. 153–165)—demonstrate that Ramesses II died of age-related pathology rather than drowning:
  * Ramesses II reigned for 66 years and died at the advanced age of approximately **90 years old**.
  * The CT scans revealed severe **ankylosing spondylitis** (diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis), fusing his cervical and thoracic vertebrae into a rigid, permanently flexed posture that restricted mobility.
  * His cardiovascular system exhibited widespread **arteriosclerosis**, with heavily calcified plaques obstructing his femoral and iliac arteries.
  * His dentition showed severe periodontal disease, extensive tooth loss, periapical abscesses, and chronic osteomyelitis of the mandible that likely contributed to systemic sepsis.  
  Ramesses II died of chronic degenerative conditions associated with advanced age at Pi-Ramesses, showing no pathological indicators of asphyxiation, pulmonary edema, water aspiration, or maritime trauma.

* **3. Forensic Paleopathology of Merneptah (r. 1213–1203 BC, KV35):**  
  Because Ramesses II's advanced age was difficult to reconcile with battlefield pursuit, Maurice Bucaille focused on Ramesses II's thirteenth son and successor, **Merneptah** (r. 1213–1203 BC), discovered in KV35 in AD 1898. Bucaille suggested that Merneptah exhibited forensic indicators of drowning, citing an opening in the skull and white salt deposits on the mummy's skin. Modern paleopathological and chemical analyses do not support this interpretation:
  * Grafton Elliot Smith conducted the primary anatomical examination (*The Royal Mummies*, AD 1912, pp. 65–70) and recorded that Merneptah was an elderly man of approximately **60 to 70 years of age**, affected by obesity, calcified **aortic atherosclerosis**, and degenerative joint disease.
  * Regarding the defect in Merneptah's skull, Elliot Smith established that this cranial opening was produced **post-mortem** by ancient embalmers or by tomb robbers who cut through the occipital bone to extract funerary amulets in antiquity, rather than representing ante-mortem trauma from waves or combat.
  * Regarding the white deposits on Merneptah's skin, chemical analysis identifies them not as marine sodium chloride (sea salt) from the Red Sea, but as **natron salts** (*hydrated sodium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate, and sodium sulfate*), the standard chemical dehydrating agent in which Egyptian royal bodies were packed during mummification. Comparable white natron efflorescence is documented on other royal mummies, including Thutmose IV and Amenhotep III.
  * High-resolution CT imaging by Hawass and Saleem (AD 2016, pp. 177–183) confirmed that Merneptah died of natural cardiovascular complications associated with severe atherosclerotic disease, with no evidence of ante-mortem immersion trauma.

* **4. Subterranean Concealment vs. Public Sign (*Āyah*):**  
  The concordist interpretation proposes that [Quran 10:92](quran://10/92) designated Pharaoh's preserved body as an enduring visible sign (*āyah*) for subsequent generations. Historically, however, both Ramesses II and Merneptah were interred in subterranean rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings (KV7 and KV8). During the 21st Dynasty (c. 1000 BC), High Priests of Amun transferred the royal mummies from their original tombs, re-wrapped them, and sealed them inside the caches of DB320 and KV35.  
  For more than **3,000 years**, from c. 1000 BC until AD 1881 and AD 1898, these bodies remained in subterranean concealment, unseen by any population in Egypt, Arabia, or the wider Near East.

* **5. Internal Quranic Account of Drowning:**  
  Modern concordist literature frequently suggests that the Quran diverges from the biblical account by denying that Pharaoh drowned. Throughout the Quranic corpus, however, Pharaoh's death is consistently described as drowning:
  * *"فَأَخَذْنَاهُ وَجُنُودَهُ فَنَبَذْنَاهُمْ فِي الْيَمِّ ۖ فَانظُرْ كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الظَّالِمِينَ"* — *"So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea. Look, then, what was the end of the wrongdoers!"* ([Quran 28:40](quran://28/40))
  * *"فَلَمَّا آسَفُونَا انتَقَمْنَا مِنْهُمْ فَأَغْرَقْنَاهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ"* — *"So when they provoked Us, We took vengeance on them and drowned them all."* ([Quran 43:55](quran://43/55))
  * In [Quran 10:90](quran://10/90), the text states: *"حَتَّىٰ إِذَا أَدْرَكَهُ الْغَرَقُ قَالَ آمَنتُ"* — *"until, when the drowning overtook him, he said: 'I believe...'"*  
  The Quranic text does not state that Pharaoh survived immersion; rather, it states that his drowned, lifeless corpse was cast by the waves onto the shore.

### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr)

When foundational classical commentators analyzed [Quran 10:92](quran://10/92), they preserved a consistent body of early traditions (*āthār*) explaining the historical setting of the verse. None of these authorities interpreted the verse as a reference to future archaeological excavations or Egyptian embalming.

#### The Exegesis of al-Ṭabarī (d. AD 923)

In [Tafsir al-Tabari 10:92](tabari://10/92), Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭabarī compiles over a dozen chains of transmission (*asānīd*) from the Companions and Successors:

1. **The Doubts of the Children of Israel:**  
   Al-Ṭabarī records via multiple transmissions (from Qays ibn ʿUbbād, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, and Mujāhid) that because Pharaoh had ruled with absolute authority and claimed divinity (*"I am your Lord Most High"*, [Quran 79:24](quran://79/24)), some among the Israelites doubted that he had actually died in the sea:
   * **Narration 17868:** Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā reported from Qays ibn ʿUbbād: *"The Children of Israel said to Moses: 'Pharaoh did not die!' So Allah brought him out to them, that they might look at him, like a red bull."*
   * **Narration 17869:** Qays ibn ʿUbbād narrated: *"When the sea closed over them, the Children of Israel said: 'Pharaoh did not die, and he could never die!' So Allah heard their denial of His Prophet. So he was thrown onto the shore as if he were a red bull, where the Children of Israel could see him."*
   * **Narration 17874:** Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: *"When Moses crossed the sea with all those who were with him, the sea met together over them... So the companions of Moses said: 'We fear that Pharaoh has not drowned, and we do not believe in his destruction!' Thus Moses supplicated his Lord, and He brought him out, and the sea cast him aside, until they were certain of his destruction."*
   * **Narration 17875:** Qatādah stated: *"Factions of the Children of Israel denied that, so Allah cast him onto the shore of the sea for them to look at him."*

2. **The Exegetical Clarification of `Bi-badanika`:**  
   Al-Ṭabarī addresses a specific linguistic and theological question discussed by early scholars:
   > *"فَإِنْ قَالَ قَائِلٌ: وَمَا وَجْهُ قَوْلِهِ: {بِبَدَنِكَ}؟ وَهَلْ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُنَجِّيَهُ بِغَيْرِ بَدَنِهِ، فَيَحْتَاجَ الْكَلَامُ إِلَى أَنْ يُقَالَ فِيهِ {بِبَدَنِكَ}؟  
   > قِيلَ: كَانَ جَائِزًا أَنْ يُنَجِّيَهُ بِهَيْئَتِهِ حَيًّا كَمَا دَخَلَ الْبَحْرَ. فَلَمَّا كَانَ جَائِزًا ذَلِكَ قِيلَ: {فَالْيَوْمَ نُنَجِّيكَ بِبَدَنِكَ}، لِيُعْلَمَ أَنَّهُ يُنَجِّيهِ بِالْبَدَنِ بِغَيْرِ رُوحٍ، وَلَكِنْ مَيِّتًا."*  
   > *("If a questioner asks: What is the meaning of His saying: {with your body}? And is it possible that He would deliver him without his body, such that the speech would require it to be said {with your body}?  
   > It is said: It would have been possible for Him to deliver him in his state alive, just as he entered the sea. But since that was possible, it was said: {Today We deliver you with your body}, to make it known that He delivers him with the body without a soul, but rather dead.")* ([Tafsir al-Tabari 10:92](tabari://10/92))

#### The Exegesis of Ibn Kathīr (d. AD 1373)

In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 10:92](ibnkathir://10/92), ʿImād al-Dīn Ismāʿīl ibn Kathīr summarizes the consensus of early scholarship:
> *"وَقَوْلُهُ: {فَالْيَوْمَ نُنَجِّيكَ بِبَدَنِكَ لِتَكُونَ لِمَنْ خَلْفَكَ آيَةً} قَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ وَغَيْرُهُ مِنَ السَّلَفِ: إِنَّ بَعْضَ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ شَكُّوا فِي مَوْتِ فِرْعَوْنَ، فَأَمَرَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى الْبَحْرَ أَنْ يُلْقِيَهُ بِجَسَدِهِ بِلَا رُوحٍ، وَعَلَيْهِ دِرْعُهُ الْمَعْرُوفَةُ بِهِ عَلَى نَجْوَةٍ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ وَهُوَ الْمَكَانُ الْمُرْتَفِعُ، لِيَتَحَقَّقُوا مَوْتَهُ وَهَلَاكَهُ؛ وَلِهَذَا قَالَ تَعَالَى: {فَالْيَوْمَ نُنَجِّيكَ} أَيْ: نَرْفَعُكَ عَلَى نَشَزٍ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ، {بِبَدَنِكَ} قَالَ مُجَاهِدٌ: بِجَسَدِكَ. وَقَالَ الْحَسَنُ: بِجِسْمٍ لَا رُوحَ فِيهِ. وَقَالَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ شَدَّادٍ: سَوِيًّا صَحِيحًا، أَيْ: لَمْ يَتَمَزَّقْ لِيَتَحَقَّقُوهُ وَيَعْرِفُوهُ. وَقَالَ أَبُو صَخْرٍ: بِدِرْعِكَ. وَكُلُّ هَذِهِ الْأَقْوَالِ لَا مُنَافَاةَ بَيْنَهَا..."*  
> *("Regarding Allah's statement: {So this day We shall deliver your body that you may be a sign to those who come after you}: Ibn ʿAbbās and others from among the Salaf said: 'Some of the Children of Israel doubted the death of Pharaoh, so Allah commanded the sea to throw his body—whole, without a soul, wearing his known armor—onto an elevated place of the earth (najwah), so that they could verify his death and destruction.' For this reason Allah said: {So this day We shall deliver you}, meaning: We raise you upon an elevated knoll of the land; {with your body}, Mujāhid said: 'With your physical corpse.' Al-Ḥasan said: 'With a body that has no soul in it.' ʿAbdullāh ibn Shaddād said: 'Intact and whole, meaning it was not torn apart, so that they could verify and recognize it.' Abū Ṣakhr said: 'With your armor.' And all of these sayings do not contradict one another...")* ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 10:92](ibnkathir://10/92))

Ibn Kathīr connects the drowning of Pharaoh directly to the Jewish practice of fasting on the 10th of Muharram (ʿĀshūrāʾ), citing the hadith in *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* in which the Prophet Muhammad learned from the Jews of Medina that Moses prevailed over Pharaoh on that day. Both al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr show that classical exegetes understood [Quran 10:92](quran://10/92) strictly as an immediate event witnessed on the seashore by the ancient Israelites.

### 4. Verbatim Pre-Islamic Biblical & Rabbinic Precedent

The thematic correspondence between [Quran 10:92](quran://10/92) and classical *tafsīr* on one hand, and pre-Islamic Jewish literature on the other, is closely documented. The narrative sequence—the crossing of the sea, the Israelites' doubt that Pharaoh was dead, the divine command to the sea to cast the body onto the shore, and the sight of the lifeless corpse on an elevated bank—is recorded in Jewish scripture and rabbinic commentaries compiled centuries before the rise of Islam.

#### 1. The Hebrew Bible: Exodus 14:30

The foundational scriptural text is [Exodus 14:30](bible://ex/14/30):

> *"וַיּוֹשַׁע יְהוָה בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל מִיַּד מִצְרָיִם וַיַּרְא יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת־מִצְרַיִם מֵת עַל־שְׂפַת הַיָּם׃"*  
> *"Thus the Lord saved Israel that day (`bay-yôm ha-hūʾ`) from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore (`ʿal-śəp̄at hay-yām`)."* ([Exodus 14:30](bible://ex/14/30))

Several direct linguistic parallels are evident:
* Hebrew **`bay-yôm ha-hūʾ`** ("on that day") corresponds semantically to Quranic **`fa-l-yawma`** ("so today / on this day").
* Hebrew **`way-yarʾ yiśrāʾēl ... mēt ʿal-śəp̄at hay-yām`** ("and Israel saw [them] dead on the seashore") describes the same narrative event recounted in [Quran 10:92](quran://10/92) and glossed in [Tafsir al-Tabari 10:92](tabari://10/92) by al-Ṭabarī (`يَنْظُرُ إِلَيْكَ هَالِكًا مَنْ كَذَّبَ بِهَلَاكِكَ`, *yanẓuru ilayka hālikan man kadhdhaba bi-halākika*) and by Qatādah in Narration 17875 (`فَقَذَفَهُ اللَّهُ عَلَى سَاحِلِ الْبَحْرِ يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَيْهِ`, *fa-qadhafahu Allāhu ʿalā sāḥil al-baḥr yanẓurūna ilayhi*).

#### 2. The Babylonian Talmud: b. Pesachim 118b & b. Arakhin 15a (Compiled c. AD 500)

Why did the sea cast Pharaoh and his army up onto the dry land? In the Babylonian Talmud (*Talmud Bavli*, redacted c. AD 500), **Rav Huna** and **Rabbah bar Mari** preserve the tradition (expounding [Psalm 106:7](bible://ps/106/7) and [Exodus 14:30](bible://ex/14/30)) explaining that the Israelites doubted that the Egyptians had drowned, prompting God to command the Prince of the Sea (*Sar shel Yam*) to eject the corpses onto the dry shore:

In ***b. Pesachim* 118b** and ***b. Arakhin* 15a**, the Talmud records verbatim:

> *"אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ הַדּוֹר מִקְּטַנֵּי אֲמָנָה הָיוּ, וּכְדִמְפָרֵשׁ רַבָּה בַּר מָרִי: מַאי דִּכְתִיב 'וַיַּמְרוּ עַל יָם בְּיַם סוּף'? מְלַמֵּד שֶׁבְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה מָרְדוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאָמְרוּ: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאָנוּ עוֹלִים מִצַּד אֶחָד, כָּךְ מִצְרִיִּים עוֹלִים מִצַּד אַחֵר. אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְשַׂר שֶׁל יָם: פְּלוֹט אוֹתָם לַיַּבָּשָׁה. אָמַר לְפָנָיו: רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, כְּלוּם יֵשׁ עֶבֶד שֶׁנּוֹתֵן לוֹ רַבּוֹ מַתָּנָה וְחוֹזֵר וְנוֹטֵל הֵימֶנּוּ? אָמַר לוֹ: אֶתֵּן לְךָ אֶחָד וּמֶחֱצָה שֶׁבָּהֶן... מִיָּד פְּלָטָן הַיָּם לַיַּבָּשָׁה, וּבָאוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל וְרָאוּ אוֹתָן, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: וַיַּרְא יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת־מִצְרַיִם מֵת עַל־שְׂפַת הַיָּם."*  
> *"Rav Huna said: The Israelites of that generation were of little faith, as Rabbah bar Mari expounded: What is the meaning of what is written, 'Yet they rebelled at the sea, at the Red Sea' ([Psalm 106:7](bible://ps/106/7))? This teaches that at that hour the Israelites rebelled and said: 'Just as we are ascending from one side [of the sea], so the Egyptians are ascending from another side!'  
> The Holy One, blessed be He, said to the Prince of the Sea (`Sar shel Yam`): **'Spit them out onto the dry land!'**  
> He said before Him: 'Master of the Universe, is there any servant whose master gives him a gift and then takes it back from him?'  
> He said to him: 'I will give you one and a half times their number...'  
> Immediately, **the sea spat them out onto the dry land**, and Israel came and saw them, as it is stated: 'And Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore' ([Exodus 14:30](bible://ex/14/30))."*

This Talmudic passage exhibits the same narrative structure found in [Quran 10:92](quran://10/92) and its classical *tafsīr*:
1. The Israelites express skepticism that the pursuing Egyptians had actually drowned.
2. God issues a command to the sea to cast the corpses out of the water onto dry land.
3. The corpses are ejected onto the coastal shore so that the Israelites can visually confirm their physical death.

#### 3. Tannaite Midrash: Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael (2nd–3rd Century AD)

The halakhic and aggadic commentary *Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael* (*Tractate Beshallaḥ*, Parashah 7 on [Exodus 14:30](bible://ex/14/30), ed. Horovitz-Rabin p. 114; ed. Lauterbach Vol. 1, pp. 252–253), compiled in Roman Palestine during the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD, enumerates four reasons why Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore (`מפני ארבעה דברים ראו ישראל את מצרים מת על שפת הים`):
1. *"So that the Israelites should not say: 'Just as we have come up on this side, so the Egyptians have come up on another side and will pursue after us'"* (`שלא יהו ישראל אומרים כשם שעלינו אנו מצד זה כך עלו הם מצד אחר וירדפו אחרינו`);
2. So that the Egyptians would not say that the Israelites had also drowned in the sea;
3. So that the Israelites might take their spoil (`שיקחו ישראל את הביזה`, studded with gold, silver, and armor);
4. *"So that the Israelites might set their eyes upon them, recognize them, and reprove them"* (`שיתנו ישראל עיניהם בהם ויכירום ויוכיחו אותם`).

Furthermore, in *Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael* (*Tractate Shirata*, Ch. 7 on [Exodus 15:11](bible://ex/15/11)), the 2nd–3rd century AD Tannaite tradition records the motif of Pharaoh making a last-minute confession of faith while drowning in the sea—paralleling [Quran 10:90](quran://10/90)–[Quran 10:92](quran://10/92).

#### 4. Distinction Between Pre-Islamic Tannaitic/Talmudic Sources and Post-Islamic Geonic Midrashim

In later, post-Islamic Geonic and medieval rabbinic works—such as *Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer* (Chapter 42, redacted c. 8th–9th century AD) and *Midrash Wayosha* (redacted c. 11th century AD)—the earlier Talmudic tradition was homiletically expanded into a narrative in which Pharaoh survived the drowning alive and later ruled Nineveh as an enduring sign (*ot*). Notably, [Quran 10:92](quran://10/92) and early Islamic *tafsīr* ([Tafsir al-Tabari 10:92](tabari://10/92), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 10:92](ibnkathir://10/92)) align with the **earlier, pre-Islamic Tannaitic and Talmudic stage** (*Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael*, 2nd–3rd century AD; *b. Pesachim* 118b and *b. Arakhin* 15a, c. AD 500), in which Pharaoh's **lifeless corpse** (`بِالْبَدَنِ بِغَيْرِ رُوحٍ، وَلَكِنْ مَيِّتًا`) is cast ashore onto elevated ground so the doubting Israelites can verify his death on that day.

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Modern Harmonizations

Modern concordist literature proposes three primary arguments in support of Bucaille's thesis, each of which can be evaluated against historical, philological, and forensic evidence:

* **Concordist Argument 1: Salt Crystals and Skeletal Trauma Indicate Merneptah Drowned at Sea.**  
  *Concordist Hypothesis:* Proponents argue that because Merneptah's skin bore white salt encrustations and his skeleton exhibited cranial damage, he perished by drowning in the Red Sea as proposed by Bucaille.  
  *Forensic & Paleopathological Assessment:* This interpretation conflates marine sodium chloride with the mineral salts used in Egyptian mummification. As documented by Alfred Lucas and J.R. Harris (*Ancient Egyptian Materials and Industries*, 4th ed., Edward Arnold, AD 1962, pp. 298–303), the white efflorescence found on Egyptian mummies is **natron** (*wāḥāt al-naṭrūn*), the hydrated sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate desiccation compound mined from the Wadi Natrun deposits. Every preserved pharaoh in KV35 and DB320 was packed in natron salt for roughly seventy days. Natron residue on a New Kingdom royal mummy therefore represents the standard chemical dehydrating medium of Egyptian embalming rather than maritime seawater encrustation. Furthermore, the CT imaging published by Hawass and Saleem (AD 2016) demonstrated that the cranial defect on Merneptah was cut post-mortem by ancient embalmers or tomb robbers, while the monarch died of advanced atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease at an elderly age.

* **Concordist Argument 2: Ancient Knowledge of Mummification Was Unknown Until Champollion Deciphered Hieroglyphs in AD 1822.**  
  *Concordist Hypothesis:* Proponents suggest that 7th-century inhabitants of the Near East could not have known that Egyptian pharaohs were bodily preserved, rendering [Quran 10:92](quran://10/92) an anticipation of modern archaeology.  
  *Historical & Historiographical Assessment:* Knowledge of Egyptian mummification remained continuous across the classical, Late Antique, and medieval Near East. Classical Greek and Roman historians whose works circulated throughout the Mediterranean described Egyptian embalming in technical detail centuries before the 7th century AD:
  * **Herodotus** (*Histories*, Book II, chapters 85–88, written c. 440 BC) provided a step-by-step account of Egyptian mummification, describing the extraction of the brain through the nostrils, the removal of internal viscera, and the 70-day desiccation in natron salt.
  * **Diodorus Siculus** (*Bibliotheca Historica*, Book I, chapter 91, written c. 60–30 BC) documented the embalming guilds of Egypt, their anatomical incisions, and the preservation of the physical features so that *"every member of the body is preserved so perfectly that the hairs of the eyebrows and eyelashes remain intact."*  
  Moreover, throughout the Byzantine and Islamic eras, the trade in *mūmiyāʾ* (preserved Egyptian remains used in Galenic and medieval pharmacology) was widely documented across the Near East by medical writers such as Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna) and Ibn al-Bayṭār.

* **Concordist Argument 3: The Quran Clarified a Biblical Omission Regarding Pharaoh's Corpse.**  
  *Concordist Hypothesis:* Proponents cite [Exodus 14:28](bible://ex/14/28) (*"there remained not so much as one of them"*) to argue that the Hebrew Bible implied Pharaoh's body vanished without trace, whereas the Quran specified that his corpse was preserved.  
  *Philological & Textual Assessment:* This reading overlooks the standard usage of the biblical Hebrew idiom. In Semitic syntax, the clause in [Exodus 14:28](bible://ex/14/28) (*lōʾ nišʾar bāhem ʿad-ʾeḥād*) signifies that not a single living survivor remained among the military force—denoting total loss of life rather than the disappearance of physical corpses. Two verses later, the narrative explicitly states: *"and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore"* ([Exodus 14:30](bible://ex/14/30)). Consequently, [Quran 10:92](quran://10/92) parallels the existing biblical and Midrashic narrative in which the drowned corpses of Pharaoh and his forces were cast ashore on that day for the Israelites to witness.

### 1. Context of the Claim & Origin in Modern Concordism (Maurice Bucaille)

In the Quran, **Haman** (*Hāmān*, هامان) appears six times—[Quran 28:6](quran://28/6), [Quran 28:8](quran://28/8), [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38), [Quran 29:39](quran://29/39), [Quran 40:24](quran://40/24), and [Quran 40:36](quran://40/36)—as Pharaoh's chief court minister in Egypt during the life of Moses. Pharaoh commands Haman to kindle a fire upon clay to bake bricks ([Quran 28:38](quran://28/38)) and construct a lofty tower (*ṣarḥ*) so that Pharaoh may reach the *"ropes of the heavens"* (*asbāb al-samāwāt*, glossed by early exegetes in [Tafsir al-Tabari 40:37](tabari://40/37) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 40:37](ibnkathir://40/37) as the physical gates or pathways of the sky) and look upon the God of Moses ([Quran 40:36](quran://40/36)–[40:37](quran://40/37); see also [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 40:36](ibnkathir://40/36) and [Tafsir al-Tabari 40:36](tabari://40/36)).

Historically, biblical and Near Eastern historians noted a major chronological divergence:
* In the Hebrew Bible, **Haman the Agagite** is the chief minister of the Achaemenid Persian king Ahasuerus (Xerxes I, r. 486–465 BC) in the imperial capital of Susa ([Esther 3:1](bible://est/3/1))—living roughly 800 to 1,000 years after the New Kingdom Egyptian setting of the Exodus ([Exodus 5:1](bible://ex/5/1)).
* Furthermore, [Quran 29:39](quran://29/39) and [Quran 40:24](quran://40/24) group **Pharaoh**, **Haman**, and **Qārūn** (the Israelite Levite **Korah** of the post-Exodus Sinai wilderness rebellion in [Numbers 16:1](bible://nm/16/1)) into a single Egyptian ruling front rejecting Moses, leading classical commentators such as [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 29:39](ibnkathir://29/39) to state that *"Fir'awn, the king of Egypt at the time of Musa, and his minister Haman were two Coptics."*

#### Origin of the Modern Hypothesis (Maurice Bucaille, AD 1995)

The hypothesis that Egyptology corroborates the Quranic Haman was introduced in AD 1995 by **Maurice Bucaille** (1920–1998) in his book *Moïse et Pharaon* (*Moses and Pharaoh: The Hebrews in Egypt*):

1. **Medical Background and "Bucaillism":** Bucaille was a French medical doctor (gastroenterologist), not a trained Egyptologist, Semitic philologist, or historian of antiquity. After being appointed family physician to King Faisal of Saudi Arabia in AD 1973 and treating members of Egyptian President Anwar Sadat's family, he was granted access to inspect royal mummies in Cairo and published *La Bible, le Coran et la Science* (*The Bible, The Qur'an and Science*, AD 1976), founding the modern concordist genre that historians of science term *"Bucaillism"* (Leif Stenberg, *The Islamization of Science*, 1996, pp. 219–225). Contrary to widespread popular accounts stating that he converted to Islam upon examining Pharaoh's mummy, Bucaille never publicly converted to Islam—explicitly answering *"No"* when asked directly at public lectures in Tunisia (AD 1976) and Morocco (early 1980s), and maintaining the public posture of a Christian Western physician evaluating the Quran from the outside.
2. **How Bucaille Located the Name:** Because Bucaille could not read Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, he recounts in *Moïse et Pharaon* that he wrote down the Arabic consonants of *"Haman"* (`h-m-n`, هامان) and showed them to a French Egyptologist while withholding that the name came from the Quran—telling the specialist instead that he had seen the name in a *"7th-century AD Arab manuscript"* relating to Egyptian history.
3. **The Lexicon Lookup:** The specialist referred Bucaille to German Egyptologist Hermann Ranke's dictionary of Egyptian personal names (*Die Ägyptischen Personennamen*, AD 1935) and Walter Wreszinski's AD 1906 catalog of the Vienna Hofmuseum (now the Kunsthistorisches Museum). Searching the transliterated index without formal training in Egyptian phonology or Ranke's German apparatus, Bucaille argued that:
   * Ranke's lexicon listed a New Kingdom official named **"Haman"**;
   * Wreszinski's Vienna catalog recorded a monument where this individual held the title **"Chief of the workers in the stone-quarries"** and was an **"intimate of Pharaoh"**; and
   * Because knowledge of hieroglyphs died out by the 4th century AD and was only deciphered by Jean-François Champollion in AD 1822, [Quran 40:36](quran://40/36) preserved historical knowledge inaccessible in the 7th century AD.

### 2. Archaeological, Epigraphic, and Linguistic Analysis

Direct examination of the Vienna artifact (**Kunsthistorisches Museum, Inv. Nr. ÄS 109**), Walter Wreszinski's AD 1906 publication (*Aegyptische Inschriften aus dem K.K. Hof-Museum in Wien*, p. 130, Inschrift I 15), and Hermann Ranke's AD 1935 lexicon (*Die Ägyptischen Personennamen*, Vol. I, p. 240, nos. 25–26) demonstrates that the epigraphic record diverges from each component of the proposed identification:

| Claimed Detail | Actual Archaeological & Epigraphic Record |
| --- | --- |
| **Name on Artifact:** "Haman" (*Hāmān*) | **`ḥmn-ḥ (?)`**, an abbreviated writing of **`ḥmn-ḥtp`** (*Ḥemen-ḥotep*), meaning *"The falcon-god Hemen is satisfied/gracious."* |
| **Phonetic Match:** Matches Arabic/Hebrew *Hāmān* | **Linguistically incompatible.** Begins with Egyptian pharyngeal `ḥ` (**ح**) rather than glottal `h` (**ه**), and lacks long *ā* vowels. |
| **Title & Role:** Royal master brick-builder | **`ḥrj kꜣwtjw n jmn`** — *"Chief of the stone-quarry workers of [the temple estate of] Amun."* |
| **Relation to Pharaoh:** "Intimate of Pharaoh" | **Zero mention of Pharaoh.** The object is a private tomb doorjamb (*Türpfosten*) for a temple quarry supervisor. |

#### Detailed Breakdown of the Primary Evidence

* **Truncation of the Hieroglyphic Name (`ḥmn-ḥ (?)` = `ḥmn-ḥtp`):** In Ranke's lexicon (Vol. I, p. 240, entry no. 25), the name on the Vienna doorjamb is transliterated as **`ḥmn-ḥ (?)`**. It is written with five hieroglyphic signs: the first three spell `ḥmn`—the name of **Hemen**, an Upper Egyptian falcon deity worshipped at Hefat (modern el-Mo'alla)—and the final two spell `-ḥ`. In his German footnote to entry 25 (*"Abkürzung des folgenden Namens?"*), Ranke explicitly notes that this is an abbreviated spelling of entry no. 26 immediately below it: **`ḥmn-ḥtp`** (*Ḥemen-ḥotep*, *"Hemen is satisfied"*). Bucaille omitted the final `-ḥ` (`-ḥtp`) element (40% of the written hieroglyphs) and treated a truncated theophoric prefix as a standalone personal name.
* **Phonetic Incompatibility (`ḥ` ح vs. `h` ه):** Both Ancient Egyptian and Semitic languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, and Arabic) strictly distinguish between two separate *"h"* consonants:
  * Quranic Arabic **Hāmān** (هامان) and Biblical Hebrew **Hāmān** (הָמָן, from Old Persian/Elamite) begin with the voiceless glottal fricative **`h`** (Arabic *hāʾ* **ه** / Hebrew *he* **ה**, corresponding to Egyptian reed-shelter sign Gardiner O4).
  * The Egyptian divine name **`ḥmn`** (*Ḥemen*) begins with the voiceless pharyngeal fricative **`ḥ`** (Gardiner V28, twisted flax wick, corresponding to Semitic/Arabic *ḥāʾ* **ح**).
  * In documented New Kingdom transcriptions between Egyptian and Northwest Semitic, `ḥ` and `h` were kept strictly distinct. Had an Arabic name derived from *Ḥemen*, it would begin with **ح** (*Ḥ-m-n*), not **ه** (*Hāmān*), and Egyptian `ḥmn-ḥtp` lacks both long *ā* vowels.
* **Epigraphic Context of the Monument, Title, and Construction Material:**
  * The artifact in Vienna (**Inv. Nr. ÄS 109**) is not an imperial stela or royal chronicle; it is a limestone **doorjamb** (*Türpfosten*) from a private 19th-Dynasty tomb gateway.
  * Wreszinski (AD 1906, p. 130) rendered the German title as *"Oberster der Steinbrucharbeiter"* ("Chief of the stone-quarry workers"), while the untranslated hieroglyphs immediately following it read **`n jmn`** (*"of Amun"*), giving the full title **`ḥrj kꜣwtjw n jmn`** (*"Chief of the stone-quarry workers of [the temple estate of] Amun"*).
  * The word *"Pharaoh"* does not appear anywhere on the monument; describing him as an *"intimate of Pharaoh"* is an unattested modern addition not present in the hieroglyphic text. Furthermore, *Ḥemen-ḥotep* supervised stonecutters for the priesthood of Amun, whereas [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38) depicts Haman firing **kiln-baked clay bricks**—the characteristic building technique of Mesopotamia ([Genesis 11:3](bible://gn/11/3)), in contrast to New Kingdom Egypt, where monumental architecture was built from quarried stone and sun-dried mudbrick ([Exodus 5:7](bible://ex/5/7)).
