### 3. Late Antique Literary Parallels Behind Quran 40:36 and 28:38

Historians of Near Eastern literature and Quranic studies—most thoroughly **Adam Silverstein** (*"Haman's Transition from the Jāhiliyya to Islam"*, *Jerusalem Studies in Arabic and Islam* 34, 2008, pp. 285–308) and **Gabriel Said Reynolds** (*The Qur'an and the Bible: Text and Commentary*, Yale University Press, 2018, pp. 600–602, 697–698)—have traced the textual pedigree of [Quran 40:36](quran://40/36) and [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38). The Quranic narrative synthesizes three widely circulated Late Antique Near Eastern traditions:

#### A. The *Story of Ahiqar* and Tobit 14:10 (How Haman Entered Pharaoh's Court to Build a Sky-Tower)

The literary link explaining why Haman appears in Egypt building an impossible tower into the sky for Pharaoh is the **Story of Ahiqar**—an Aramaic wisdom narrative originating in the 5th century BC that circulated across the Near East in Aramaic, Syriac, Greek, Armenian, and Arabic:

1. **Pharaoh's Sky-Tower Demand:** In the *Story of Ahiqar*, the **Pharaoh of Egypt** sends a challenge to King Esarhaddon of Assyria: *"Send me a man who will build me a castle (or tower) between heaven and earth."*
2. **From Nadan to Aman / Haman ([Tobit 14:10](bible://tb/14/10)):** In the Aramaic narrative, the wise vizier Ahiqar has a treacherous nephew and court rival named *Nadan*. However, in the deuterocanonical Book of Tobit—which explicitly summarizes the Ahiqar narrative in [Tobit 14:10](bible://tb/14/10)—and in related Greek and Syriac transmissions, Ahiqar's nephew is named **Aman / Haman** (Greek: `Ἁμάν` / `Ἀμάν`: *"Remember, my son, how Aman handled Achiacharus [Ahiqar] that brought him up... but Aman fell into the snare, and perished"*).
3. **Bricks and Clay Mortar in Pharaoh's Court:** In the *Story of Ahiqar*, Ahiqar travels to Pharaoh's court in Egypt to answer the sky-tower demand. To demonstrate the impossibility of Pharaoh's request to build a tower between heaven and earth, Ahiqar trains boys to fly upward on eagles carrying **bricks and clay mortar**, shouting down to Pharaoh's masons to bring up more building materials until Pharaoh acknowledges that the task is impossible.

#### B. The *Book of Esther* and Rabbinic Homiletic Triads (Pharaoh, Haman, and Korah)

* In [Esther 3:1](bible://est/3/1)–[3:6](bible://est/3/6) and [Esther 7:6](bible://est/7/6)–[7:10](bible://est/7/10), Haman is the quintessential royal vizier who plots to destroy the Israelites.
* In Late Antique Jewish homilies and Midrashic texts (such as *Midrash Tehillim*, *Numbers Rabbah*, and Talmudic literature), preachers routinely paired **Pharaoh**, **Haman**, and **Korah** (*Qārūn*) together as typological equivalents—three prominent adversaries of Israel across history.
* The Quran reflects this homiletic triad in [Quran 29:39](quran://29/39) and [Quran 40:24](quran://40/24), which group *"Pharaoh, Haman, and Qārūn (Korah)"* together as contemporaries opposing Moses. Notably, several classical Islamic historians and scholars—including al-Ṭabarī (in his *Taʾrīkh* when recounting the Persian king Ahasuerus and Esther), al-Maqdisī, and al-Bīrūnī (*al-Āthār al-bāqiya*)—recognized the figure of Haman in the Jewish Purim/Esther tradition.

#### C. Genesis 11:3–4 (The Mesopotamian Tower of Babel Formula)

Pharaoh's command to Haman in [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38) and [Quran 40:36](quran://40/36)–[40:37](quran://40/37) mirrors the Mesopotamian Tower of Babel formula in [Genesis 11:3-4](bible://gn/11/3):
* **[Genesis 11:3-4](bible://gn/11/3):** *"Come, let us make bricks, and burn them thoroughly [with fire]... Come, let us build ourselves a city, and a tower with its top in the heavens."*
* **[Quran 28:38](quran://28/38) & [Quran 40:36-37](quran://40/36):** *"So light a fire for me, Haman, on the clay, and make a tower (ṣarḥ) for me, so that I may reach the ropes—the ropes of the heavens—and look upon the God of Moses."*
* In Late Antique Jewish and Syriac commentary on Babel (including Philo of Alexandria, *3 Baruch*, and rabbinic traditions surrounding Nimrod), the builders of the Tower of Babel baked bricks specifically to climb into the heavens and inspect or wage war against God—a motif transferred onto Pharaoh in the Quranic narrative (cf. [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 40:36](ibnkathir://40/36), [Tafsir al-Tabari 40:37](tabari://40/37)).

### 4. Scholarly Evaluation of Secondary Harmonizations

* **Secondary Concordist Harmonizations:** Recognizing the philological difficulties with Bucaille's reading of `ḥmn-ḥtp`, secondary concordist writers frequently advance three alternative readings: (1) that *"Haman"* in [Quran 40:36](quran://40/36) is an Arabicized rendering of an Egyptian high-priestly title (*ḥm-nṯr tpy n jmn*, *"First Prophet/High Priest of Amun"*) or theophoric compound (*ḥm-jmn*, *"Servant of Amun"*); (2) that the Quranic Haman was simply an otherwise unattested Egyptian official who happened to share the same name as the Persian vizier of [Esther 3:1](bible://est/3/1); or (3) that Pharaoh's command to build a tower to reach the *"ropes of the heavens"* ([Quran 40:36](quran://40/36)–[40:37](quran://40/37)) was merely rhetorical sarcasm rather than a literal Babel-like tower.
* **Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:** Each of these proposals encounters substantial philological, grammatical, and literary difficulties:
  1. **Title vs. Proper Name (`ḥm-nṯr` and `jmn`):** In Arabic grammar, the Quran treats *Hāmān* (هامان) strictly as an uninflected foreign proper noun (diptote) without the definite article *al-*—in contrast to genuine titles in the Quranic Egypt narratives such as *al-ʿAzīz* ([Quran 12:30](quran://12/30)). Phonetically, the Egyptian priestly title *ḥm-nṯr* (*"servant of the god"*, translated as `προφήτης` in Greek decrees) begins with pharyngeal `ḥ` (**ح**) rather than glottal `h` (**ه**) and contracted in Demotic and Coptic into **`ϩⲟⲛⲧ`** (*hont*, making *ḥm-nṯr n jmn* *"Hont-en-Amoun"*), while the divine name *Jmn* (Amun) begins with an initial glottal stop/aleph (`j` / `ʾ`) that was transcribed into Semitic with *aleph* (**א** / **أ**)—as attested in Biblical Hebrew **ʾĀmôn** (אָמוֹן) in [Jeremiah 46:25](bible://jer/46/25) and [Nahum 3:8](bible://na/3/8)—never Semitic *Hāmān*.
  2. **Literal Hubris vs. Rhetorical Sarcasm:** [Quran 40:37](quran://40/37) explicitly characterizes Pharaoh's tower command as an *"evil deed"* (*sūʾu ʿamalihi*) and a *"plot"* (*kayd*) that ended in ruin, and classical exegetes ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 40:36](ibnkathir://40/36), [Tafsir al-Tabari 40:37](tabari://40/37)) consistently understood it as an actual baked-brick architectural project. Moreover, whether Pharaoh's demand is read as literal architectural hubris or royal mockery, it still relies on the Mesopotamian motif of firing clay bricks ([Quran 28:38](quran://28/38)) to build a sky-tower.
  3. **Composite Literary Footprint:** Coincidental homonymy does not account for why the Quranic Haman is simultaneously grouped in a triad with **Pharaoh** and **Korah** ([Quran 29:39](quran://29/39), [Quran 40:24](quran://40/24)) *and* tasked with baking clay bricks to build a sky-tower in Egypt ([Quran 28:38](quran://28/38), [Quran 40:36](quran://40/36))—a specific combination of name, setting, construction material, and motif explained by the Late Antique confluence of the *Story of Ahiqar* ([Tobit 14:10](bible://tb/14/10)), *Esther* ([Esther 3:1](bible://est/3/1)), and *Genesis* ([Genesis 11:3-4](bible://gn/11/3)).

Philological, historical, and embryological evidence does not support the claim that [Quran 76:2](quran://76/2) anticipates cellular fertilization or genetics. Rather than describing the microscopic fusion of a secondary oocyte and a spermatozoon to form a diploid zygote, the phrase *nuṭfatin amshāj* ("mingled drop") articulates the pre-modern Mediterranean physiological doctrine that human generation results from the macroscopic blending of male and female sexual fluids. In classical Arabic philology, early exegesis ([Tafsir al-Tabari 76:2](tabari://76/2), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 76:2](ibnkathir://76/2)), and canonical prophetic hadith ([Sahih Muslim 315a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:315a), [Sahih Muslim 311](https://sunnah.com/muslim:311)), *nuṭfah amshāj* is explicitly defined as the mutual mingling of male "white water" and female "yellow water"—a reproductive model identical in structure and anatomical tissue distribution to the classical Greek treatises of the Hippocratic Corpus (c. 420 BC), Galen of Pergamon (2nd century AD), and the Babylonian Talmud (c. AD 500).

### 1. Context of the Claim & Classical Arabic Philology (Nuṭfah Amshāj)

In [Quran 76:2](quran://76/2), the text describes human generation:

> *"Indeed, We created man from a drop, a mixture (nuṭfatin amshājin) to test him, and We made him hearing and seeing."* (`innā khalaqnā al-insāna min nuṭfatin amshājin nabtalīhi fa-jaʿalnāhu samīʿan baṣīrā`)

Modern concordist writers—notably French physician Maurice Bucaille (*The Bible, The Qur'an and Science*, AD 1976, pp. 200–205) and Canadian anatomist Keith L. Moore (*The Developing Human with Islamic Additions*, AD 1982; Commission on Scientific Signs in the Quran and Sunnah, Makkah, AD 1986)—propose that this verse describes the single-celled diploid zygote formed when a microscopic spermatozoon penetrates a female ovum. Concordist commentators argue that because the mammalian ovum was only identified microscopically by Karl Ernst von Baer in AD 1827 (following Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's AD 1677 observation of spermatozoa), the Quranic "mingled drop" reflects pre-modern knowledge of gamete fusion and chromosome combination.

#### Classical Arabic Root and Morphological Analysis

Lexical analysis of classical Arabic authorities—al-Farāhīdī's *Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, Ibn Fāris's *Maqāyīs al-Lughah*, Ibn Manẓūr's *Lisān al-ʿArab*, al-Zabīdī's *Tāj al-ʿArūs*, and E. W. Lane's *Arabic-English Lexicon* (p. 2806)—demonstrates that this modern reading diverges from the historical semantics of the terms:

1. ***Nuṭfah* (`n-ṭ-f`, نطفة):** Denotes a small quantity of dribbling liquid (*al-māʾ al-qalīl*), such as water trickling from a leather water-skin (*shannah*) or well bucket. In reproductive contexts, it signifies a drop of emitted seminal fluid (*māʾ al-rajul*). The Quran consistently equates *nuṭfah* with macroscopic ejaculated semen: [Quran 53:45](quran://53/45)–[53:46](quran://53/46) (*min nuṭfatin idhā tumnā*, "from a drop when it is emitted/ejaculated") and [Quran 75:37](quran://75/37) (*alam yaku nuṭfatan min maniyyin yumnā*, "was he not a drop of emitted semen?").
2. ***Amshāj* (`m-sh-j`, أمشاج):** Broken plural of *mashīj* (مَشِيج) or *mashj* (مَشْج), signifying mixed liquids or streaks of differing colors (*al-akhlāṭ*). In [Tafsir al-Tabari 76:2](tabari://76/2), al-Ṭabarī cites the classical Arab *rajaz* poet Ruʾbah ibn al-ʿAjjāj (*"in mixed blood"* / *fī damin amshāji*) and the *mukhaḍram* poet Abū Dhuʾayb al-Hudhalī (*"stirred with a mixture"* / *sīṭa bihi mashīju*).
3. **Grammatical Agreement (*Naʿt*):** Classical grammarians (al-Farrāʾ, *Maʿānī al-Qurʾān*; al-Zajjāj; Ibn Manẓūr) explain that the plural adjective *amshāj* qualifies the singular noun *nuṭfah* because *nuṭfah* functions as a collective noun for mingled constituent fluids (*akhlāṭ*), or because every portion of the drop is mixed with another.

#### Lexical Comparison with Gamete Biology

In classical usage, *nuṭfatin amshāj* denotes a macroscopic fluid mixture. In biological terms, the human female gamete (secondary oocyte) is not an emitted fluid drop (*nuṭfah* / *māʾ*). It is an immobile, solitary cellular gamete (`~0.1 mm` / 100–120 microns) produced in the ovary and retained within the fallopian tube. Women do not emit or ejaculate an ovum as a liquid secretion during intercourse.

---

### 2. Empirical Embryological Analysis & Comparative Overview

In modern human embryology and genetics (Schoenwolf et al., *Larsen's Human Embryology*, 5th ed., Elsevier, AD 2014, pp. 13–24; Gilbert & Barresi, *Developmental Biology*, 11th ed., Sinauer, AD 2016, pp. 115–140; Carlson, *Human Embryology and Developmental Biology*, 6th ed., Elsevier, AD 2019, pp. 23–38), human generation operates through cellular gametogenesis and syngamy rather than bulk liquid mixing:

| Biological Feature | Modern Cellular Embryology & Genetics | Quranic & Classical Exegetical Model ([Quran 76:2](quran://76/2)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Female Contribution** | A single microscopic cellular gamete (secondary oocyte, `~0.1 mm`) containing 23 maternal chromosomes, surrounded by the zona pellucida and corona radiata. | Macroscopic 'thin yellow water' (*māʾ al-marʾah*) or menstrual blood expelled/emitted during intercourse and pooled in the womb. |
| **Site & Mechanism of Union** | Cellular fertilization in the fallopian ampulla: a single sperm penetrates the zona pellucida and fuses membranes; seminal plasma is filtered at the cervix. | Macroscopic intermingling (*ikhtilāṭ / imtizāj*) of bulk male semen and female fluid inside the uterine cavity. |
| **Formation of Tissues & Organs** | Every somatic cell contains an identical diploid set of 46 chromosomes (23 paternal + 23 maternal); differential gene expression directs tissue specialization. | Paternal fluid produces bones, nerves, sinews, and nails; maternal fluid produces skin, flesh, hair, and blood. |
| **Determination of Sex & Resemblance** | Sex is determined strictly by the paternal sex chromosome (X or Y) of the fertilizing sperm; resemblance involves complex polygenic and epigenetic factors. | Resemblance and sex are determined by which parental fluid 'prevails' (*ʿalā*) or 'precedes' (*sabaqa*) the other during intercourse. |

#### Detailed Breakdown of the Embryological Evidence

1. **Seminal Fluid Filtration vs. Ampullary Fertilization:** Seminal plasma remains in the vagina and is filtered out at the cervix. Only motile spermatozoa swim into the fallopian tubes, where a single spermatozoon fertilizes the secondary oocyte. Bulk male fluid does not mix with female secretions inside the fallopian tube.
2. **Absence of Tissue Partitioning:** Somatic cells inherit equal genetic material from both parents. The classical model in which paternal fluid forms bones and sinews while maternal fluid forms flesh and blood is inconsistent with empirical findings in developmental genetics.
3. **Paternal Chromosomal Sex Determination:** Fetal sex is determined entirely by whether the fertilizing sperm carries an X or Y chromosome. Fluid volume, speed, or parental 'precedence' does not influence chromosomal sex determination.

### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr) and Canonical Ḥadīth

Early Islamic authorities consistently interpreted [Quran 76:2](quran://76/2) in reference to macroscopic bodily secretions rather than microscopic gametes. In [Tafsir al-Tabari 76:2](tabari://76/2) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 76:2](ibnkathir://76/2), the foundational exegetes define *nuṭfah amshāj* through the mixing of macroscopic bodily fluids:

- **Exegetical Consensus in al-Ṭabarī:** In [Tafsir al-Tabari 76:2](tabari://76/2), al-Ṭabarī records multiple authoritative transmission chains defining *amshāj* as the physical mixing of male and female fluids:
  - **Ibn ʿAbbās:** Narrated via ʿAṭiyyah and al-Suddī: *"The fluid of the woman and the fluid of the man mix together"* (`māʾu al-marʾati wa-māʾu al-rajuli yamshujān / yakhtaliṭān`).
  - **ʿIkrimah:** Narrated via Ibn al-Aṣbahānī: *"The fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman, one of them mixes with the other"* (`māʾu al-rajuli wa-māʾu al-marʾati yumshaju aḥaduhumā bi-l-ākhar`).
  - **Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas:** *"When the fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman meet, it is amshāj (a mixture)"* (`idhā ijtamaʿa māʾu al-rajuli wa-māʾu al-marʾati fa-huwa amshāj`).
  - **Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī & Mujāhid:** Al-Ḥasan stated: *"The fluid of the woman is mixed with the fluid of the man."* Mujāhid affirmed: *"Allah created the child from the fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman."*
  - **Color and Precedence Traditions in al-Ṭabarī:** Al-Ṭabarī documents Mujāhid's reports regarding fluid colors and resemblance: *"Whichever of the two fluids precedes, the child resembles his paternal uncles or maternal uncles"* (`ayyu al-māʾayni sabaqa ashbaha ʿalayhi aʿmāmahu wa-akhwālahu`), and *"The fluid of the man is white and red, and the fluid of the woman is red and green."* He also records Qatādah's report that *amshāj* means *"the fluid and the blood mixed"* (`ikhtalaṭa al-māʾu wa-al-dam`), as well as Ibn Masʿūd's and Zayd ibn Aslam's gloss that *amshāj* refers to the veins (*ʿurūquhā*) within the drop.
- **Al-Ṭabarī's Exegetical Conclusion:** Al-Ṭabarī evaluates and sets aside the view that *amshāj* refers to the successive developmental stages (*aṭwār*), colors, or veins, identifying two-fluid mingling as the primary lexical meaning:
  > *"The statement most resembling correctness is the statement of the one who said: The meaning of that {from a drop, a mixture} is the fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman, because Allah described the drop as being a mixture (amshāj), and if it transitions and becomes a clinging clot (ʿalaqah), it has transformed from the meaning of a drop (nuṭfah), so how can it be a drop that is a mixture while it is a clinging clot?"* ([Tafsir al-Tabari 76:2](tabari://76/2))
- **Ibn Kathīr's Affirmation:** In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 76:2](ibnkathir://76/2), Ibn Kathīr confirms: *"Ibn ʿAbbās said concerning Allah's statement {from a drop, a mixture}: 'This means the fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman when they meet and mix.'... And likewise ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas all said: 'Amshāj is the mixing of the man's fluid with the woman's fluid.'"*
- **The Anatomical Tissue Division Tradition in Classical Exegesis:** The specific anatomical division assigning bones and sinews to the male fluid and flesh and blood to the female fluid was documented across early Hadith and Tafsīr compendia:
  - Recorded by **ʿAbd al-Razzāq** (*al-Muṣannaf*), **Ibn Abī Ḥātim** (*Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm*), **Ibn al-Mundhir**, and **al-Ṭabarānī** from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd on [Quran 76:2](quran://76/2).
  - Preserved in standard classical exegesis by **al-Qurṭubī** (*al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān*, on 76:2: *"The bones, sinews, and strength come from the man's fluid, while the flesh, blood, and hair come from the woman's fluid"*), **al-Baghawī** (*Maʿālim al-Tanzīl*, on 76:2 and 86:6–7), and **al-Suyūṭī** (*al-Durr al-Manthūr*, on 76:2).

#### Canonical Ḥadīth Foundations

This two-fluid physiology is anchored in canonical prophetic traditions:

1. **[Sahih Muslim 315a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:315a) (Hadith of Thawbān on the Jewish Rabbi's Question):** When a Jewish scholar (*ḥabr min aḥbār al-Yahūd*) questioned Muhammad regarding human reproduction (*"jiʾtu asʾaluka ʿan al-walad"*), Muhammad replied verbatim:
   > مَاءُ الرَّجُلِ أَبْيَضُ وَمَاءُ الْمَرْأَةِ أَصْفَرُ فَإِذَا اجْتَمَعَا فَعَلَا مَنِيُّ الرَّجُلِ مَنِيَّ الْمَرْأَةِ أَذْكَرَا بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ وَإِذَا عَلَا مَنِيُّ الْمَرْأَةِ مَنِيَّ الرَّجُلِ آنَثَا بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ
   > 
   > *"The water of the man is white and the water of the woman is yellow. When they meet (`fa-idhā ijtamaʿā`), and the semen of the man (`maniyyu al-rajuli`) rises above/prevails over the semen of the woman (`maniyya al-marʾati`), they produce a male child (`adhkarā`) by Allah's permission; and when the semen of the woman rises above/prevails over the semen of the man, they produce a female child (`ānathā`) by Allah's permission."* (`māʾu al-rajuli abyaḍu wa-māʾu al-marʾati aṣfaru, fa-idhā ijtamaʿā fa-ʿalā maniyyu al-rajuli maniyya al-marʾati adhkarā bi-idhni Allāhi, wa-idhā ʿalā maniyyu al-marʾati maniyya al-rajuli ānathā bi-idhni Allāh`)
   
   Crucially, this canonical text uses the exact phrase *fa-idhā ijtamaʿā* ("when they meet/mingle") that mirrors Ibn ʿAbbās's and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas's exegetical gloss on [Quran 76:2](quran://76/2), explicitly designates the female yellow fluid as *maniyy al-marʾah* ("the woman's semen"), and states that fetal sex (*adhkarā* vs. *ānathā*) is determined by which fluid rises above the other.

2. **[Sahih Muslim 311](https://sunnah.com/muslim:311) (Hadith of Umm Sulaym):** When Umm Sulaym asked whether a woman who experiences a wet dream must perform ritual purification (*ghusl*) and then bashfully asked whether a woman actually experiences such emission (*"wa-hal yakūnu hādhā?"*), Muhammad replied verbatim:
   > نَعَمْ فَمِنْ أَيْنَ يَكُونُ الشَّبَهُ إِنَّ مَاءَ الرَّجُلِ غَلِيظٌ أَبْيَضُ وَمَاءَ الْمَرْأَةِ رَقِيقٌ أَصْفَرُ فَمِنْ أَيِّهِمَا عَلَا أَوْ سَبَقَ يَكُونُ مِنْهُ الشَّبَهُ
   > 
   > *"Yes; otherwise from where does the resemblance come? Indeed, the water of the man is thick and white, and the water of the woman is thin and yellow; so from whichever of the two rises above or precedes, the resemblance is from it."* (`naʿam fa-min ayna yakūnu al-shabahu? inna māʾa al-rajuli ghalīẓun abyaḍu wa-māʾa al-marʾati raqīqun aṣfaru, fa-min ayyihimā ʿalā aw sabaqa yakūnu minhu al-shabahu`)

3. **[Sahih al-Bukhari 3329](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3329):** Responding to ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām regarding parental resemblance, Muhammad stated: *"As for the resemblance of the child: if a man has sexual intercourse with his wife and his water precedes her water, the child resembles him; and if her water precedes his water, the child resembles her."*

---

### 4. Verbatim Pre-Islamic Greek, Syriac, and Talmudic Precedents

Every element of the Quranic and early Islamic model of *nuṭfah amshāj*—the dual emission of parental fluids, their mixing *in utero*, fluid precedence governing sex/resemblance, and the division of bones vs. flesh—was established Late Antique medical and rabbinic doctrine:

1. **Hippocratic Corpus (*De Genitura*, §§ 4–7; *De Natura Pueri*, § 12; c. 420–400 BC):**
   - Established the 'two-seed theory' (*semen duplex*): both male and female emit reproductive seed (*gonē*) during intercourse.
   - *De Genitura* § 5: *'When the seed from both partners has fallen into the uterus, it stays there and mixes together... The two seeds mix together (`symmignyetai`).'*
   - *De Genitura* §§ 6–8: Teaches that whichever parental seed is greater in volume or potency determines fetal sex and parental resemblance.
2. **Galen of Pergamon (*De Semine*, Book I, Chs. 5–8; Book II, Chs. 1–4; ed. Kühn, IV.512–625; c. AD 160–180):**
   - Maintained that female semen from the ovaries mixes in the uterus with thicker male semen. The male seed forms the 'spermatic parts' (bones, sinews, nerves, membranes), while maternal blood forms the fleshy organs (*sarx*).
   - **Syriac and Arab Transmission:** Galen's works were translated into Syriac by Sergius of Reshaina (d. AD 536). Galenic medicine was taught at the Academy of Gundeshapur. Early Arab physicians—notably **al-Ḥārith ibn Kalada al-Thaqafī** (d. c. AD 634) of Ṭāʾif—studied at Gundeshapur, demonstrating direct regional transmission of Galenic embryology into pre-Islamic Arabia.
3. **Aristotle (*De Generatione Animalium* I.19–20, 727a–729a; 4th century BC) & [Wisdom 7:2](bible://ws/7/2):**

His father sows the white substance, from which come the child's bones, sinews, nails, the brain in his head, and the white of his eye; his mother sows the red substance, from which come his skin, flesh, hair, blood, and the dark of his eye. And the Holy One, blessed be He, gives him the spirit, the soul, the features of the face, sight of the eyes, hearing of the ears...'*

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Modern Harmonizations

Concordist commentators propose three primary secondary harmonizations to support a modern embryological reading:

1. **Harmonization 1: 'Amshāj refers to chromosomes or genetic traits mingling in the zygote':**
   - *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* In classical Arabic grammar, *amshāj* is an adjectival modifier of the macroscopic fluid droplet *nuṭfah* (*nuṭfatin amshājin*). In Quranic chronology ([Quran 23:13](quran://23/13)–[23:14](quran://23/14), [Quran 22:5](quran://22/5)), the *nuṭfah* remains in the womb before becoming a clinging clot (*ʿalaqah*). Chromosomes are sub-cellular macromolecular complexes (`~2–10 µm`) within a cell nucleus, not liquid droplets. Furthermore, chromosomes do not blend into a homogeneous liquid mixture; maternal and paternal homologous chromosomes remain distinct structural entities. Reinterpreting liquid mingling as chromosomal pairing represents an anachronistic reading.
2. **Harmonization 2: 'Nuṭfah denotes an individual gamete, and Ibn ʿAbbās anticipates modern sperm in al-Ṭabarī':**
   - *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* In [Tafsir al-Tabari 76:2](tabari://76/2), al-Ṭabarī records a report from Ibn ʿAbbās via ʿAṭāʾ: *"Man was only created from a small amount of the drop (`al-shayʾ al-qalīl min al-nuṭfah`). Do you not see that when a child is silenced, you see from him something like drool (`al-rīr`)? And the son of Adam was only created from something like that from the drop, a mixture."* Modern concordists frequently pair this report with [Sahih Muslim 1438k](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1438k) (*"Not from all the fluid is the child created"*) to argue that early Islam taught that only a single microscopic sperm cell conceives a child.
   - However, primary contextual analysis indicates otherwise:
     1. Ibn ʿAbbās explicitly defines the scale of this *"small amount"* macroscopically by comparing it directly to infant drool or spittle (*mithla al-rīr*) seen dribbling down a baby's chin—a visible macroscopic liquid measure (`~0.5–1.0 mL`) observable by the naked eye, rather than an unobservable `50 µm` spermatozoon.
     2. In [Sahih Muslim 1438k](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1438k), Muhammad's statement addresses *ʿazl* (coitus interruptus), explaining to companions that withdrawal does not reliably prevent pregnancy because a visible residual droplet of semen still induces conception.
     3. The Quran consistently defines *nuṭfah* as macroscopic ejaculated semen: [Quran 53:45](quran://53/45)–[53:46](quran://53/46) (*min nuṭfatin idhā tumnā*, 'from a drop when it is emitted/ejaculated') and [Quran 75:37](quran://75/37) (*alam yaku nuṭfatan min maniyyin yumnā*, 'was he not a drop of emitted semen?'). Moreover, female sexual lubrication ('thin yellow water' in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 315a) consists of Bartholin gland secretions and vaginal transudates containing no ova. The microscopic oocyte is released internally into the fallopian tube and is never expelled externally during intercourse.
3. **Harmonization 3: 'The bone/flesh division in classical sources is fallible human commentary, not the Quran':**
   - *Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:* The phrase *nuṭfatin amshāj* belongs to a specific Late Antique physiological context. Muhammad himself articulated the two-fluid doctrine in [Sahih Muslim 315a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:315a) and [Sahih Muslim 311](https://sunnah.com/muslim:311), specifying the white and yellow fluids and stating that fluid dominance determines sex and resemblance. The tissue division between paternal bones and maternal flesh is recorded in canonical hadith (*Musnad Aḥmad* 4206) and classical exegesis (al-Qurṭubī, al-Baghawī, al-Suyūṭī). The Quranic vocabulary aligns with the standard Hippocratic-Galenic and Talmudic medical consensus of the Late Antique Mediterranean world, rather than modern 19th- or 20th-century cellular biology.

Textual, historical, and embryological evidence does not support the claim that [Quran 96:2](quran://96/2) anticipates modern developmental biology. The assertion that the Arabic noun *ʿalaq* (عَلَق) encodes an implanted blastocyst, an aquatic leech, or an early vascular network relies on semantic overextension, retrospective harmonization, and the dehistoricization of 7th-century Arabian lexical usage. Classical Arabic lexicons, canonical Hadith collections, and classical Quranic commentaries ([Tafsir al-Tabari 96:2](tabari://96/2), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 96:2](ibnkathir://96/2)) demonstrate that *ʿalaq* and its unit noun *ʿalaqah* were universally understood as thick, congealed blood (*al-dam al-jāmid*). Rather than representing an unprecedented anatomical disclosure, this terminology reflects the established ancient Near Eastern and Greco-Roman medical frameworks that modeled embryonic generation as the coagulation of male semen with retained maternal menstrual blood.

### 1. Context of the Claim & Classical Arabic Philology (ʿAlaq / ʿAlaqah)

According to Islamic tradition, [Quran 96:1](quran://96/1)–[96:2](quran://96/2) (*iqraʾ bi-smi rabbika al-ladhī khalaq, khalaqa al-insāna min ʿalaq*) represents the inaugural revelation delivered to Muhammad in the cave of Hira, declaring that God *"created the human from a clot [ʿalaq]."*

In late-20th-century concordism—originated by Maurice Bucaille (*La Bible, le Coran et la Science*, AD 1976) and expanded by Keith L. Moore alongside Zaghloul El-Naggar (*The Developing Human with Islamic Additions*, AD 1986)—writers reinterpreted *ʿalaq* to propose advanced embryological foreknowledge. Moore asserted that the single word *ʿalaq* conveys three distinct meanings simultaneously:
1. An aquatic **"leech"** (*Hirudo medicinalis*), proposing that a 24-day human embryo visually resembles an aquatic leech;
2. A **"suspended thing"**, describing the blastocyst hanging in the chorionic cavity by the connecting stalk (days 7–14); and
3. A **"blood clot"**, proposing that stagnant blood in early vessels gives the conceptus a clot-like appearance.

In his AD 1986 paper (*Journal of the Islamic Medical Association of North America* / *JIMA* 18:15–16), Keith L. Moore noted that Aristotle had already described the embryo forming from a coagulated clot of menstrual blood in the 4th century BC. Following academic scrutiny, the *"Islamic Additions"* co-authored with Abdul Majeed al-Zindani were omitted from subsequent standard international editions of *The Developing Human*.

#### Philological Analysis of the Root *ʿ-l-q*

This threefold concordist reading conflates etymological derivation with contextual semantic designation. The triliteral root `ʿ-l-q` (ع-ل-ق) denotes adhering, clinging, sticking, or hanging. Because multiple physical objects exhibit adherence, distinct nouns were derived from this root:
* An aquatic leech is called an *ʿalaqah* (collective *ʿalaq*) because it clings to animal skin to suck blood (*dūdah fī al-māʾ tamuṣṣu al-dam*).
* Congealed red blood is called *ʿalaqah* (collective *ʿalaq*) because, before drying, it sticks and adheres to hands or vessels due to its viscous moisture (*li-luṣūqi-hi wa-ghilẓi-hi*).
* This represents standard linguistic polysemy: English *"bat"* designates both a nocturnal flying mammal and a wooden baseball club. An English speaker stating *"a bat flew into the cave"* does not intend a baseball club, nor does the sentence carry both meanings simultaneously.

#### Classical Lexica on *ʿAlaq* in Human Generation

In classical Arabic lexicography, when *ʿalaq* or *ʿalaqah* is used in human reproduction, it denotes **exclusively** thick, congealed blood (*al-dam al-ʿabīṭ al-jāmid*):
* **Al-Farāhīdī (d. AD 786), *Kitāb al-ʿAyn*:** The earliest Arabic dictionary defines *al-ʿalaqah* s.v. `ʿ-l-q`: *"A piece of thick, congealed blood"* (*qiṭʿat dam jāmidah*).
* **Ibn Fāris (d. AD 1004), *Maqāyīs al-Lughah* (Vol. 4, p. 125, s.v. `علق`):** Explains that the root `ʿ-l-q` denotes hanging or attachment (*ināṭat al-shayʾ bi-l-shayʾ*), and under it defines: *"al-ʿalaq is congealed blood [al-dam al-jāmid], and a piece of it is ʿalaqah"* (`والعَلَقُ: الدَّمُ الجامِد، والقطعة منه عَلَقَة`).
* **Al-Jawharī (d. AD 1003), *al-Ṣiḥḥāḥ*:** Explicitly defines *al-ʿalaq* as *al-dam al-jāmid* ("congealed blood"), unit noun *ʿalaqah*.
* **Ibn Manẓūr (d. AD 1312), *Lisān al-ʿArab* (Vol. 10, pp. 261–267, citing Ibn Sīdah's *al-Muḥkam*):** Records: *"al-ʿAlaq is congealed blood before it dries... and al-ʿalaqah is a thick piece of blood, which is the stage from which the child is formed after the drop [nuṭfah]."* Ibn Manẓūr explicitly distinguishes this obstetric usage from the aquatic worm (*dūdah fī al-māʾ*).
* **Lane's *Arabic-English Lexicon* (AD 1863, Bk. I, p. 2129):** In [Quran 96:2](quran://96/2), *ʿalaq* signifies *"clotted blood; a piece of thick, or thick and moist, coagulated blood."*
* **Al-Zamakhsharī (d. AD 1144), *al-Kashshāf* on [Quran 96:2](quran://96/2):** Explains that *ʿalaq* is the plural of *ʿalaqah*, which is *"moist, congealed blood"* (*dam jāmid raṭb*), used here because *al-insān* is a collective noun for mankind.

At no point in classical Arabic lexicography or pre-Islamic literature was the human embryo described as being created from an "aquatic leech" or an "implanted blastocyst".

### 2. Empirical Embryological & Comparative Analysis

Findings from modern developmental biology diverge from the threefold concordist reading of *ʿalaq* in [Quran 96:2](quran://96/2):

| Claimed Meaning of *ʿAlaq* | Concordist Assertion | Empirical Embryological & Textual Assessment ([Quran 96:2](quran://96/2)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **"Congealed Blood Clot" (*Dam Jāmid*)** | Keith L. Moore asserts that the conceptus resembles a blood clot because primitive blood pools in early embryonic vessels before dynamic circulation begins. | Living human embryos never pass through a stage of congealed or clotted blood. Vasculogenesis occurs synchronously with early cardiogenesis, and embryonic blood circulates continuously from day 21–22 onward. Clotting in vivo only occurs in pathological conditions or following embryonic demise. |
| **"Suspended / Clinging Structure" (Implantation)** | Maurice Bucaille and modern commentators assert that *ʿalaq* refers to the blastocyst attaching and clinging to the endometrial wall via its connecting stalk during implantation at days 6–12. | An implanting blastocyst is a microscopic, hollow sphere of cells measuring 0.1 to 0.2 millimeters, below the threshold of unaided human vision. Moreover, in canonical Islamic chronology ([Sahih al-Bukhari 3208](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3208)), the *ʿalaqah* stage begins on Day 40, long after blastocyst implantation is completed. |
| **"Leech-Like Organism" (*Dūdat al-Māʾ*)** | Concordist commentators present side-by-side photographic comparisons of a 24-day human embryo and an aquatic leech (*Hirudo medicinalis*), asserting that the dorsal curvature and somites visually mirror a leech. | A day-24 embryo measures approximately 2 to 3 millimeters and is in the neural fold and somite stage, which concordist writers elsewhere identify as the *muḍghah* ("chewed lump") stage. Furthermore, the human conceptus in its amniotic fluid never feeds like an ectoparasite: fetal and maternal blood never mix across the placental syncytiotrophoblast barrier, and gas/nutrient transfer occurs entirely via molecular diffusion. |
| **"Stagnant Intravascular Pooling"** | Proponents claim that blood in primitive vascular channels during week 3 is stationary and unclotted, giving the embryo an external appearance identical to clotted blood. | Embryonic erythroblasts and blood islands within the yolk sac and intraembryonic mesoderm do not form a stagnant, macroscopic clot. Blood cells develop within endothelial tubes and begin circulating the moment the primitive tubular heart initiates peristaltic contractions at 21–22 days, precluding any static clot phase. |

#### Detailed Breakdown of the Embryological Evidence

1. **Absence of a Clot Stage:** In human biology, blood is a mesodermal derivative appearing in the third gestational week. Inside the living embryo, intravascular blood remains strictly fluid; in vivo coagulation causes microvascular thrombosis and immediate embryonic demise.
2. **Microscopic Blastocyst vs. Macroscopic Observational Perception:** Implantation occurs between days 6 and 10 post-fertilization. During this window, the conceptus is a microscopic sphere measuring 0.1–0.2 mm, containing zero blood and zero pigmentation. The Quranic and Hadith presentation of *ʿalaqah*, by contrast, represents a macroscopic object observable in spontaneous first-trimester miscarriages.
3. **Morphological and Physiological Divergence from Hirudinea (Leeches):** The visual comparison relies on selective, highly magnified micrographs cropped and oriented at a specific angle. An aquatic leech is an adult segmented ectoparasite with an open coelom and jaws adapted to ingest host blood. In contrast, the human embryo is enclosed within its amniotic sac; fetal and maternal blood never intermingle across the placental barrier, and nutrient exchange occurs across chorionic villi through molecular diffusion.

### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr) and Canonical Ḥadīth

Classical Islamic scholarship confirms that early Muslim exegetes understood [Quran 96:2](quran://96/2) strictly as creation from a piece of congealed red blood, without reference to leeches or microscopic blastocysts:

* **[Tafsir al-Tabari 96:2](tabari://96/2):** The foundational exegete Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī (d. AD 923) provides the exact philological and semantic gloss:
  > `ثم بين الذي خلق فقال: ( خَلَقَ الإنْسَانَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ ) يعني: من الدم، وقال: من علق؛ والمراد به من علقة، لأنه ذهب إلى الجمع، كما يقال: شجرة وشجر، وقصَبة وَقصَب، وكذلك علقة وعَلَق. وإنما قال: من علق والإنسان في لفظ واحد، لأنه في معنى جمع، وإن كان في لفظ واحد، فلذلك قيل: من عَلَق.`
  > *"Then He clarified that which He created, saying: (creates the human from a clot), meaning: from blood [yaʿnī: min al-dam]. And He said: 'from ʿalaq'; and what is intended by it is 'from an ʿalaqah' (a single clot), because He used the plural form, just as it is said: shajarah (a tree) and shajar (trees), and qaṣabah (a reed) and qaṣab (reeds), and likewise ʿalaqah (a clot) and ʿalaq (clots). And He only said: 'from ʿalaq' while 'the human' (al-insān) is in a singular wording, because it carries the meaning of a plural, even though it is in a singular wording; for this reason, it was said: 'from ʿalaq'."*
* **[Tafsir Ibn Kathir 96:2](ibnkathir://96/2):** Ismāʿīl ibn Kathīr (d. AD 1373) explains concisely: *"(creates the human from a clot): Drawing attention to the beginning of man's creation from a dangling clot [ʿalaqah]."*
* **Parallel Exegetical Formulations Across the Corpus:** In every parallel passage describing embryonic formation, classical commentaries define *ʿalaqah* explicitly as blood:
  * In **[Tafsir al-Tabari 23:13](tabari://23/13)** (covering the opening clauses of [Quran 23:14](quran://23/14)), al-Ṭabarī explains: *"And His statement: 'Then We made the drop into a clot', He says: Then We transformed the drop that We placed in a secure dwelling place into a clot [ʿalaqah], and it is a piece of blood [wa-hiya al-qiṭʿah min al-dam]. 'then We made the clot into a little lump of flesh', He says: So We made that blood [dhālika al-dam] into a little lump of flesh, and it is a piece of flesh."*
  * In **[Tafsir al-Tabari 75:38](tabari://75/38)**, al-Ṭabarī writes: *"And His statement: {Then he was a clot,} He, exalted is His remembrance, says: then he was blood [daman] after he was a drop of semen, then a clot, then He fashioned him into a well-proportioned human being, speaking, hearing, and seeing."*
  * In **[Tafsir al-Tabari 22:5](tabari://22/5)**, al-Ṭabarī records the narration of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd that if the *nuṭfah* is decreed to be unformed (*ghayr mukhallaqah*), *"the wombs expel it as blood"* (*majjat-hā al-arḥām daman*).
  * In **[Tafsir Ibn Kathir 22:5](ibnkathir://22/5)**, Ibn Kathīr notes that after the *nuṭfah* remains in the womb for forty days, *"it turns into a red clot [ʿalaqah ḥamrāʾ] by the permission of Allah, and remains like that for forty days"*, adding that women observe this directly when miscarrying (*kamā tushāhidūnahā*).
  * In **[Tafsir Ibn Kathir 23:14](ibnkathir://23/14)**, Ibn Kathīr writes: *"Then it becomes a red clot, like an elongated clot [ʿalaqah ḥamrāʾ ʿalā shakl al-ʿalaqah mustaṭīlah]. ʿIkrimah said, 'This is blood [wa-hiya dam].'"* Concordist proponents cite the word *mustaṭīlah* ("elongated") to propose an anticipation of a 24-day embryo, whereas ʿIkrimah immediately defines its substance as blood (*wa-hiya dam*), and Ibn Kathīr confirms in [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 22:5](ibnkathir://22/5) that women observe this with the naked eye during miscarriages—describing an elongated decidual or endocervical clot rather than a microscopic 2.5 mm embryo. #### Classical Exegetical Consensus Across Thirteen Centuries

Across thirteen centuries of Quranic commentary—from early authorities like Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, and ʿIkrimah down to al-Qurṭubī (d. AD 1273), Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī (d. AD 1210), al-Bayḍāwī (d. AD 1286), and al-Suyūṭī (d. AD 1505)—commentators consistently interpreted [Quran 96:2](quran://96/2) as referring to coagulated blood rather than an aquatic leech or a microscopic blastocyst.

#### The Chronological Timeline in Canonical Hadith & Evaluation of the "Concurrent 40 Days" Reading

The identity of *ʿalaqah* is further established by canonical Hadith traditions assigning explicit timeframes to each developmental stage. In [Sahih al-Bukhari 3208](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3208) and [Sahih Muslim 2643a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2643a), the Prophet Muhammad states:
> *"Each one of you is collected in the womb of his mother for forty days as a seed [nuṭfah], then he becomes a clinging clot [ʿalaqah] for a like period, then he becomes a chewed lump of flesh [muḍghah] for a like period; then Allah sends an angel who is commanded to breathe the soul into him..."*

Some modern concordist commentators propose compressing all three stages into a single 40-day window by interpreting *thumma yakūnu ʿalaqatan mithla dhālika* as concurrent development. This secondary harmonization is inconsistent with classical Arabic syntax, exegetical consensus, and developmental morphology:
1. **Arabic Grammar:** The coordinating particle `ثُمَّ` (*thumma*) strictly denotes sequence with temporal delay (*al-tartīb maʿa al-tarākhī*), in contrast to immediate sequence (`فَـ`, *fa-*). The phrase `مِثْلَ ذَلِكَ` (*mithla dhālika*) modifies the duration of the verb `يَكُونُ` (*yakūnu*), indicating an equal 40-day duration. Even if divided into three equal periods (~13.3 days each), days 14–27 still fall outside the window of blastocyst implantation (days 6–10).
2. **Theological Consensus:** In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 22:5](ibnkathir://22/5) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 23:14](ibnkathir://23/14) (citing Ibn Masʿūd and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib), as well as Ibn Ḥajar (*Fatḥ al-Bārī* 11/477–481), al-Nawawī (*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 16/190), and Ibn Rajab (*Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam*, Hadith 4), the `40 + 40 + 40 = 120` day timeline is explicitly affirmed across all four Sunni legal schools (*madhāhib*).
3. **Biological Timeline:** By Days 40 to 80 (gestational weeks 6 to 11), a human conceptus is an advanced fetus measuring 15 mm to 60 mm, with distinct fingers, toes, facial features, a functioning four-chambered heart, brain hemispheres, and developing bones. It is neither a microscopic blastocyst, nor a 2 mm organism, nor a congealed clot of blood.

### 4. Verbatim Pre-Islamic Greek, Syriac, and Near Eastern Precedents

The model in which the human embryo originates from a congealed clot of blood constituted the standard medical framework of the ancient Mediterranean and Near East for more than a millennium prior to Islam.

#### Observational Deductions in Ancient Medicine

Ancient populations arrived at this concept through two empirical, naked-eye observations:
1. **Amenorrhea During Gestation:** Ancient observers noted that upon conception, a woman's regular menstrual bleeding ceases. Lacking knowledge of ovulation, hormones, or microscopic gametes, early physicians deduced that retained menstrual blood accumulated inside the womb to serve as the physical substance out of which the fetus was fashioned.
2. **Early Spontaneous Miscarriages:** First-trimester miscarriages are frequently expelled encased within dark red blood clots, organized hematomas, and decidual casts. To naked-eye observers in antiquity, an expelled miscarriage at 4 to 8 weeks appeared entirely as a congealed mass of red blood.

#### Classical Greek Medical Texts

This empirical deduction was formalized into systematic medical theory by Greek physicians whose works circulated throughout the pre-Islamic Near East:
* **Aristotle (384–322 BC), *De Generatione Animalium* (I.19–20, 727b–729a; II.4, 739b):** Aristotle formulated the foundational theory that generation occurs through the interaction of male semen and female menstrual blood (*katamēnia*). He explicitly compared embryonic formation to the curdling of milk by rennet into cheese:
  > *"The action of the semen in the female is like that of rennet upon milk; for rennet is milk containing vital heat, which brings into one mass and curdles the like substance... the semen curdles the catamenia [menstrual blood] and fixes it."* (*De Generatione Animalium* II.4, 739b)
* **Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BC), *On the Nature of the Child* (*De Natura Pueri*, §§ 14–15):** Explains that when conception occurs, maternal blood flows to the womb and wraps around the seed, coagulating into a dense membrane and forming a blood-filled clot that subsequently hardens into flesh.
* **Galen of Pergamon (AD 129–c. 216), *De Semine* (I.7–8, Kühn IV.536–542) and *De Foetuum Formatione* (Kühn XIX.652–705):** Synthesized Mediterranean embryology into four distinct developmental stages: (1) unformed semen (*gonē*), matching *nuṭfah*; (2) a blood-filled mass (*haimatoeides*), where semen coagulates with maternal blood and fills with vessels, matching *ʿalaqah*; (3) unformed flesh (*sarx*), where organs are outlined, matching *muḍghah*; and (4) the differentiation of bones and clothing of bones with flesh, matching [Quran 23:14](quran://23/14). Galen's corpus was translated into Syriac by Sergius of Reshaina (d. AD 536) and was actively taught at Alexandria, Nisibis, and Jundishapur immediately before the rise of Islam.

#### Biblical and Syriac Precedents

The concept of the embryo forming from coagulated blood appears prominently in Late Antique Near Eastern religious literature:
* **The Book of Wisdom ([Wisdom 7:1](bible://ws/7/1)–[7:2](bible://ws/7/2), 1st century BC):**
  > *"In the womb of a mother I was molded into flesh within a ten-month period, compacted in blood [`pagēis en haimati`] from the seed of a man and the pleasure of marriage."*
  The Greek participle `pagēis` (from `pēgnymi`, "to curdle, congeal, or solidify") describes the same process of semen curdling maternal blood into an embryo.
* **Syriac Christian Homilies (4th–6th centuries AD):** Authors such as Ephrem the Syrian (d. AD 373) and Jacob of Serugh (d. AD 521) frequently employed this imagery in their homilies on the Incarnation, describing how the divine Word took flesh through the coagulation of seed and blood according to the natural order of human generation.

Consequently, when [Quran 96:2](quran://96/2) stated that man was created from *ʿalaq* (congealed blood), it reflected the standard physiological model of the 7th-century Near East.

---

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Modern Harmonizations

Modern concordist interpretations of [Quran 96:2](quran://96/2) rely on methodological and linguistic premises that diverge from standard historical-philological practice:

#### Semantic Overextension (*Illegitimate Totality Transfer*)

Concordist writers assert that because the triliteral root `ʿ-l-q` encompasses concepts of clinging, aquatic leeches, and congealed blood, the Quranic occurrence in [Quran 96:2](quran://96/2) signifies all three concepts simultaneously.

In modern lexical semantics, this methodological issue is termed **illegitimate totality transfer**—a phenomenon systematically analyzed by linguist and biblical scholar James Barr (*The Semantics of Biblical Language*, Oxford University Press, AD 1961, pp. 218–222). Polysemy occurs when a root gives rise to multiple distinct lexical meanings over time. In any actual utterance, however, context selects a single specific meaning intended by the speaker. Asserting that a word carries the sum total of all its derived dictionary meanings simultaneously departs from established principles of historical linguistics.

To illustrate: the English word *"staple"* can mean a U-shaped wire fastener, a basic dietary food, or a primary commercial commodity. If a 19th-century historical document states that *"wheat was the staple of the colony"*, an analyst cannot conclude that the text anticipated modern office equipment because staples hold things together. Similarly, interpreting *ʿalaq* in [Quran 96:2](quran://96/2) as simultaneously denoting a blood clot, an implanting blastocyst, and an aquatic leech represents a retrospective construction unsupported by classical Arabic grammar or historical usage.

#### Chronological and Morphological Assessment of the Concordist Reading

Even when evaluated individually against developmental chronology, none of the three proposed meanings aligns with the empirical stages of human embryogenesis:
1. **At Days 6 to 10:** The implanting blastocyst does not resemble a leech, possesses no blood, and contains no somites.
2. **At Days 22 to 24:** The somite embryo does not feed on blood like a leech, does not contain clotted blood, and is not implanting into the uterus (implantation having concluded two weeks prior).
3. **At Days 40 to 80:** During the canonical timeframe assigned to *ʿalaqah* by [Sahih al-Bukhari 3208](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3208), the conceptus is a macroscopic human fetus with distinct limbs, facial structures, internal organs, and an ossifying skeleton—diverging from all three concordist characterizations.

#### Conclusion

The statement in [Quran 96:2](quran://96/2) that man was created from *ʿalaq* reflects the observational deductions and medical theories of antiquity. In alignment with Aristotle, Hippocrates, Galen, and the author of [Wisdom 7:1](bible://ws/7/1)–[7:2](bible://ws/7/2), the 7th-century Quranic text describes human generation in terms of the visible phenomena of menstrual cessation and spontaneous miscarriage, characterizing the early conceptus as a congealed clot of blood.

28:38.refutation:
Historical, archaeological, and materials-science evidence does not support the claim that [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38) records a historical or scientific miracle regarding Egyptian construction. In mainstream Egyptology, Semitic philology, and Near Eastern archaeology, Pharaoh's command to Haman to "kindle a fire upon clay" (*fa-awqid lī yā Hāmānu ʿalā al-ṭīn*) to erect a sky-piercing tower (*ṣarḥ*) is recognized as a literary conflation of the Mesopotamian Tower of Babel narrative ([Genesis 11:3](bible://gn/11/3)–[11:4](bible://gn/11/4)) with the Late Antique wisdom tradition of the *Story of Ahiqar* ([Tobit 14:10](bible://tb/14/10)) and the Persian court minister of the Book of Esther ([Esther 3:1](bible://est/3/1)). Furthermore, attempting to harmonize the verse with Joseph Davidovits's geopolymer limestone hypothesis is incompatible with both the Quranic text and archaeological chronology, as Davidovits posited cold-cast chemical agglomeration without kiln firing, separated from Moses by more than twelve centuries.

---

### 1. Context of Claim & Classical Arabic Philology

In [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38), Pharaoh issues a royal proclamation to his courtiers:
> وَقَالَ فِرْعَوْنُ يَا أَيُّهَا الْمَلَأُ مَا عَلِمْتُ لَكُم مِّنْ إِلَٰهٍ غَيْرِي فَأَوْقِدْ لِي يَا هَامَانُ عَلَى الطِّينِ فَاجْعَل لِّي صَرْحًا لَّعَلِّي أَطَّلِعُ إِلَىٰ إِلَٰهِ مُوسَىٰ وَإِنِّي لَأَظُنُّهُ مِنَ الْكَاذِبِينَ
> *"And Pharaoh said: 'O council, I know of no other god for you than me. So kindle for me, O Haman, [a fire] upon the clay, and make for me a lofty tower so that I may look at the God of Moses. And indeed, I think he is one of the liars.'"* ([Quran 28:38](quran://28/38))

This verse forms a direct companion to [Quran 40:36](quran://40/36)–[40:37](quran://40/37), where Pharaoh similarly commands:
> وَقَالَ فِرْعَوْنُ يَا هَامَانُ ابْنِ لِي صَرْحًا لَّعَلِّي أَبْلُغُ الْأَسْبَابَ ۝ أَسْبَابَ السَّمَاوَاتِ فَأَطَّلِعَ إِلَىٰ إِلَٰهِ مُوسَىٰ
> *"And Pharaoh said: 'O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the pathways—the pathways of the heavens—and look upon the God of Moses...'"* ([Quran 40:36](quran://40/36)–[40:37](quran://40/37))

#### The Two Modern Concordist Claims

Modern concordist writers advance two distinct arguments that interpret [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38) as anticipating modern materials science and Egyptology:
1. **The Fired Clay and Geopolymer Limestone Claim:** Confronted with the fact that monumental Egyptian architecture was constructed of quarried natural stone rather than kiln-baked bricks, popular writers (including Harun Yahya and Zaghloul El-Naggar) argue that [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38) preserves advanced architectural knowledge lost to antiquity. Some claim that the Quran was the first text to reveal that Pharaoh used kiln-fired bricks (*ājurr*). Others cite the geopolymer hypothesis of French materials scientist Joseph Davidovits (AD 1988), asserting that the Quran anticipated modern proposals that Egyptian monuments were cast from synthetic geopolymer limestone slurry.
2. **The Maurice Bucaille Hieroglyphic Claim:** First published in AD 1995 by French physician Maurice Bucaille in *Moïse et Pharaon*, this argument claims that 19th-century AD decipherments of Egyptian hieroglyphs corroborated the Quran by identifying a New Kingdom official named "Haman" who served as "Chief of the workers in the stone-quarries" and an "intimate of Pharaoh." Secondary writers attempt to bolster this by asserting that "Haman" represents an Egyptian priestly title such as *ḥm-nṯr* ("prophet/servant of the god"). However, this is philologically untenable: the priestly title *ḥm-nṯr* ("servant of the god") contracted in Demotic and Coptic into **`ϩⲟⲛⲧ`** (*hont*), the divine name *Jmn* (Amun) is preserved in Greek as `Ἀμοῦν` and in Biblical Hebrew with an initial guttural aleph as **ʾĀmôn** (אָמוֹן, [Jeremiah 46:25](bible://jer/46/25); [Nahum 3:8](bible://na/3/8)), whereas the name Haman derives from Old Persian *Hamāyūna* and entered Northwest Semitic with an initial voiceless glottal fricative *he* as Hebrew **Hāmān** (הָמָן, [Esther 3:1](bible://est/3/1)) and Arabic **Hāmān** (هامان).

#### Classical Arabic Philological Analysis of the Command

A rigorous examination of the Arabic wording in [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38) demonstrates the exact physical process being commanded:
* **`Awqid lī ... ʿalā al-ṭīn` (`فَأَوْقِدْ لِي ... عَلَى الطِّينِ` — "Kindle a fire for me upon the clay"):** In classical Arabic lexicography (*Lisān al-ʿArab*, *Tāj al-ʿArūs*), the verb *awqada* (أَوْقَدَ, root *w-q-d*) denotes igniting and sustaining a high-temperature flame (*ashʿala al-nār wa-adhkāhā*). The preposition *ʿalā* (عَلَى, "upon" or "over") combined with *al-ṭīn* (الطِّين, alluvial river clay, silt, or mud) specifically signifies the thermal kiln-baking of wet clay bricks into ceramic terracotta masonry, known in classical Arabic as *ājurr* (آجُرّ) or *qaramīd* (قَرَامِيد). It does not refer to ambient sun-drying, nor does it describe stone dressing, lime slaking, or cold chemical casting.
* **`Fa-ijʿal lī ṣarḥan` (`فَاجْعَل لِّي صَرْحًا` — "And make for me a lofty tower"):** The noun *ṣarḥ* (صَرْح) designates an elevated, conspicuous tower, citadel, or skyward-reaching palace structure (*kullu bināʾin murtafiʿin ẓāhir*). The purpose of this tower is stated explicitly in the text: to ascend to the cosmic reaches of the heavens (*asbāb al-samāwāt*, [Quran 40:37](quran://40/37)) in order to inspect or challenge the God of Moses.

---

### 2. Archaeological, Architectural & Materials-Science Empirical Analysis (With Markdown Comparison Table)

The claim that [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38) represents accurate Egyptian history or material science is contradicted by the archaeological and geological record of the Nile Valley.

#### Egyptian Sun-Dried Mudbrick (`Libn`) vs. Mesopotamian Kiln-Fired Brick (`Ājurr`)

Ancient Egyptian architecture followed a consistent functional and ecological dichotomy governed by regional geology, climate, and timber availability:
1. **Civil and Domestic Architecture (Sun-Dried Mudbrick):** Royal palaces, villas, residential quarters, administrative storehouses, military fortresses, and town enclosure walls (including the Delta store-cities of Pi-Ramesses and Pithom) were constructed from **sun-dried alluvial mudbrick** (Ancient Egyptian *ḏbt*, Coptic *tōbe*, whence Arabic *ṭūb* and Spanish *adobe*). Silt from the Nile was mixed with sand and chopped straw or chaff to serve as a mechanical binder, poured into standardized wooden rectangular molds, and dried solely under the Egyptian sun ([Exodus 5:7](bible://ex/5/7)–[5:18](bible://ex/5/18); A. J. Spencer, *Brick Architecture in Ancient Egypt*, AD 1979, pp. 3–10). Sun-drying produced sturdy, highly insulating walls suited to the hyper-arid Egyptian climate without consuming scarce wood fuel.
2. **Monumental and Sacred Architecture (Quarried Natural Stone):** Egyptian religious architecture designated temples, pylons, obelisks, and royal tombs as "houses of eternity" (*ḥwt-nṯr*). These were constructed exclusively from **quarried natural stone blocks**—primarily Eocene limestone from the local plateaus, Nubian sandstone from Gebel el-Silsila, and red granite from Aswan.
3. **The Ecological Constraints Against Burnt-Brick Towers in Egypt:** High-temperature kiln-firing of clay requires large quantities of combustible timber fuel. While Mesopotamia possessed abundant bituminous fuel and oil seeps alongside dense river reeds, the Nile Valley experienced acute timber scarcity. Wood in Egypt was a prized, expensive commodity imported from Byblos and Lebanon for elite shipbuilding, temple doors, and sarcophagi. Subjecting millions of clay bricks to kiln fire to erect a monumental sky-tower (*ṣarḥ*) was ecologically and economically impractical in pharaonic Egypt. Consequently, burnt brick (*ājurr*) was virtually absent in New Kingdom Egypt, appearing only in isolated, minor utilitarian contexts (such as damp tomb floorings or water drain conduits at Abydos and Qantir; Spencer AD 1979, pp. 140–141). It was never used for monumental royal towers or palaces until the Roman and Byzantine periods (post-30 BC).

#### The Historical Origin: The Mesopotamian Tower of Babel Formula ([Genesis 11:3](bible://gn/11/3)–[11:4](bible://gn/11/4))

In the Ancient Near East, kiln-fired clay brick was the signature construction technology for building a sky-reaching tower in Mesopotamia—specifically Babylonia.

In southern Mesopotamia (Sumer and Babylonia), natural stone was absent from the alluvial plain. Builders developed the kiln-fired brick, bonded with naturally occurring bitumen, to construct massive ziggurats and fortifications capable of resisting river floods. The Hebrew Bible preserves this technological formula in the narrative of the Tower of Babel:
> *"They said to one another, 'Come, let us make bricks and **burn them thoroughly** (`wə-niśrəpāh liśrēpāh`).' And they had brick for stone, and bitumen for mortar. And they said, 'Come, let us build for ourselves a city, and **a tower whose top will reach into heaven**...'"* ([Genesis 11:3](bible://gn/11/3)–[11:4](bible://gn/11/4))

The command in [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38) (*fa-awqid lī yā Hāmānu ʿalā al-ṭīni fa-ijʿal lī ṣarḥan* to reach *asbāb al-samāwāt*) reproduces the conceptual and mechanical formula of [Genesis 11:3](bible://gn/11/3)–[11:4](bible://gn/11/4), transferring the Mesopotamian kiln-firing of bricks for a sky-tower onto New Kingdom Egypt.

#### Incompatibility with Joseph Davidovits's Geopolymer Hypothesis

Modern concordist writers who cite French materials scientist Joseph Davidovits's AD 1988 hypothesis encounter three major scientific and textual discrepancies:
1. **Chronological Disconnect:** Davidovits's hypothesis concerned the construction of the Great Pyramids at Giza (4th Dynasty, Pharaoh Khufu, c. 2560 BC). Moses and Pharaoh belong to the New Kingdom (18th or 19th Dynasty, c. 13th century BC)—an architectural and historical separation of over 1,200 years.
2. **Direct Textual Contradiction:** Davidovits proposed that the pyramid blocks were created through a **cold-setting, ambient-temperature chemical casting** process, mixing crushed soft limestone slurry with water, kaolin clay, and natron (alkaline sodium carbonate) at normal environmental temperatures without kiln heat. In contrast, [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38) explicitly commands: *"Kindle a fire upon the clay"* (*awqid lī ... ʿalā al-ṭīn*). The Quran describes high-temperature thermal baking in a kiln, directly contradicting Davidovits's unheated alkaline agglomeration.
3. **Petrographic and Geological Evidence:** Mainstream petrologists, geologists, and microscopists have demonstrated that Davidovits's geopolymer hypothesis is inconsistent with empirical findings (Dipayan Jana, *Proceedings of the 29th International Conference on Cement Microscopy*, AD 2007; Dietrich Klemm and Rosemarie Klemm, *The Stones of the Pyramids: Provenance of the Building Stones Associated with the Old Kingdom Pyramid Complexes*, AD 2010; Mark Lehner, *The Complete Pyramids*, AD 1997). Microscopic thin-section petrography and X-ray diffraction confirm that the pyramid blocks are composed of natural Eocene sedimentary limestone (*Nummulites gizehensis* and *Nummulites curvispira*). The limestone contains unbroken, naturally bedded microfossils, undisturbed sedimentary layering, and cross-cutting calcite veins quarried in situ from the Mokattam formation on the Giza plateau—features that do not occur in reconstituted cast geopolymers.

### 3. Classical Islamic Exegesis (Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī & Ibn Kathīr)

The interpretation of [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38) by classical Islamic exegetes establishes two historical points: (1) early Muslims understood *awqid lī ... ʿalā al-ṭīn* as the literal kiln-firing of bricks (*al-ājurr*), and (2) early Islamic tradition attributed the invention of burnt bricks to Pharaoh, an attribution that diverges from the archaeological record by several millennia.

#### Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī (d. 310 AH / AD 923)

In [Tafsir al-Tabari 28:38](tabari://28/38), Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī explains the command:
> القول في تأويل قوله تعالى: {فَأَوْقِدْ لِي يَا هَامَانُ عَلَى الطِّينِ} يقول: فاعمل لي آجرا، وذُكر أنه أوّل من طبخ الآجر وبنى به.
> *"The statement concerning the interpretation of the Almighty's saying: {So kindle for me, O Haman, upon the clay}: He says: Make burnt bricks (ājurran) for me. And it was mentioned that he [Pharaoh] was the first person who ever baked bricks and built with them."* ([Tafsir al-Tabari 28:38](tabari://28/38))

Al-Ṭabarī preserves the transmission chains (*asānīd*) of the earliest authorities:
* **Mujāhid (via Ibn Jurayj):** *"Upon the clay clods, so that it becomes baked bricks (`labinan maṭbūkhan`)."*
* **Ibn Jurayj:** *"The first person who ordered the making of burnt bricks and built with them was Pharaoh (`awwalu man amara bi-ṣanʿati al-ājurri wa-banā bihi Firʿawn`)."*
* **Qatādah (d. 117 AH):** *"He was the first person who baked burnt bricks to build the tower with them (`fa-kāna awwala man ṭabakha al-ājurra yabnī bihi al-ṣarḥ`)."*
* **Ibn Zayd:** *"The baked material upon which a fire is kindled is of clay, with which they construct a building."*

Al-Ṭabarī further records the narrative transmitted from al-Suddī concerning the construction and Pharaoh's ascent:
> فلما بُنِي له الصرح، ارتقى فوقه، فأمر بِنُشابة فرمى بها نحو السماء، فردّت إليه وهي متلطخة دما، فقال: قد قتلت إله موسى، تعالى الله عما يقولون.
> *"So when the tower was built for him, he ascended upon it, and he ordered an arrow, and he shot it towards the heaven, and it was returned to him while it was smeared with blood, so he said: 'I have killed the God of Moses!' Exalted is Allah far above what they say."* ([Tafsir al-Tabari 28:38](tabari://28/38))

#### Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr (d. 774 AH / AD 1373)

In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 28:38](ibnkathir://28/38), Ismāʿīl ibn Kathīr corroborates this classical understanding:
> أي: أمر وزيره هامان ومدبر رعيته ومشير دولته أن يوقد له على الطين، ليتخذ له آجرا لبناء الصرح، وهو القصر المنيف الرفيع... وذلك لأن فرعون بنى هذا الصرح الذي لم ير في الدنيا بناء أعلى منه، إنما أراد بهذا أن يظهر لرعيته تكذيب موسى فيما زعمه من دعوى إله غير فرعون.
> *"Meaning: He commanded his minister Haman, the manager of his subjects and counselor of his realm, to kindle a fire on clay for him, to make baked bricks (ājurran) for building the lofty tower (al-ṣarḥ), which is an exalted towering palace... And that was because Pharaoh built this tower, which was the highest structure ever seen on earth, wanting by this to demonstrate to his subjects the falsification of Moses in what he claimed regarding a deity other than Pharaoh."* ([Tafsir Ibn Kathir 28:38](ibnkathir://28/38); see also [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 40:36](ibnkathir://40/36))

In [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 40:36](ibnkathir://40/36), Ibn Kathīr reiterates that the tower was built of bricks formed from baked clay (`من الآجر المضروب من الطين المشوي`) and cites Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī (via Ibn Abī Ḥātim): *"They used to dislike building with baked bricks (`al-ājurr`), and using them in their graves,"* because Pharaoh was the first to manufacture them. Similarly, in [Tafsir al-Tabari 40:36](tabari://40/36)–[40:37](tabari://40/37), al-Ṭabarī reiterates Qatādah's report that Pharaoh was the first to bake and build with *ājurr*, glosses *asbāb al-samāwāt* as the paths and gates of the heavens, and explains `wa-mā kaydu Firʿawna illā fī tabāb`—citing Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, and Ibn Zayd—as Pharaoh's expenditure and scheme to build the tower ending in complete loss and ruin (`fī khusrān`).

#### The Historical Anachronism Documented in Classical Exegesis

The consensus of early Islamic commentators highlights two critical points:
1. **Unanimous Understanding of Literal Kiln-Baked Brick:** Classical exegetes understood the Arabic text with complete unanimity as literal kiln-baked clay bricks (*al-ājurr*). The modern concordist proposal to reinterpret the verse as limestone geopolymers departs from both the Arabic lexicon and the classical exegetical tradition.
2. **The Chronologically Inaccurate Attribution of Burnt Bricks:** Qatādah's and Ibn Jurayj's statement that Pharaoh was the first person in human history to bake bricks (*awwalu man ṭabakha al-ājurra*) is inconsistent with archaeological evidence by over 2,000 years. Kiln-fired bricks were manufactured in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley (such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro) beginning in the late 4th and 3rd millennia BC. In Egypt, kiln-baked bricks were not used to construct monumental royal towers.

---

### 4. Verbatim Pre-Islamic Literary Sources of the Conflation (Genesis 11:3–4, Esther 3:1, and the Story of Aḥiqar)

Modern comparative literature and Near Eastern historiography—demonstrated in detail by Adam Silverstein (*"Haman's Transition from the Jāhiliyya to Islam"*, *Jerusalem Studies in Arabic and Islam* 34, AD 2008, pp. 285–308; *Veiling Esther, Unveiling Her Story: The Reception of a Biblical Book in Islamic Lands*, Oxford University Press, AD 2018) and Gabriel Said Reynolds (*The Qur'an and the Bible: Text and Commentary*, Yale University Press, AD 2018, pp. 600–602)—identify the textual tributaries that coalesced into [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38). The Quranic narrative represents a synthesis of three documented Late Antique literary traditions:

#### A. Genesis 11:3–4 and the Jewish Aggadah on Nimrod's Tower of Babel

The central structural elements of [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38) correspond to the Mesopotamian Tower of Babel account in [Genesis 11:3](bible://gn/11/3)–[11:4](bible://gn/11/4) and its elaboration in post-biblical Jewish aggadic literature:
* **The Fired Brick Command:** In [Genesis 11:3](bible://gn/11/3), the builders state: *"Come, let us make bricks and burn them thoroughly."* This technical instruction corresponds directly to *awqid lī ... ʿalā al-ṭīn* in [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38).
* **The Sky-Tower Ascendance:** In [Genesis 11:4](bible://gn/11/4), the purpose is to construct a tower *"whose top will reach into heaven,"* matching Pharaoh's directive to build a *ṣarḥ* to reach the heavenly pathways (*asbāb al-samāwāt*, [Quran 40:36](quran://40/36)–[40:37](quran://40/37)).
* **Shooting Arrows at Heaven:** In rabbinic traditions concerning Nimrod and the Tower of Babel (*Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 109a*; *Genesis Rabbah* 38:6; *Sefer ha-Yashar* 9:26–31; *Targum Yerushalmi I* / *Targum Jonathan* on [Genesis 11:4](bible://gn/11/4)), the builders divide into factions, one of which climbs the tower to wage war against the heavens, shooting arrows into the sky that return smeared with blood. This specific narrative motif is preserved verbatim in early Islamic accounts of Pharaoh ascending the tower (via al-Suddī in [Tafsir al-Tabari 28:38](tabari://28/38)).

#### B. The Persian Court Setting of the Book of Esther ([Esther 3:1](bible://est/3/1)–[3:6](bible://est/3/6))

* In the Hebrew Bible, **Haman the Agagite** is the chief minister of the Persian king Ahasuerus (Xerxes I, r. 486–465 BC) in Susa ([Esther 3:1](bible://est/3/1)), living nearly a millennium after the New Kingdom setting of the Exodus.
* In Late Antique Jewish homiletics (such as *Midrash Tanhuma* and *Numbers Rabbah* 18:2), preachers regularly paired **Pharaoh**, **Haman**, and **Korah** (*Qārūn*, [Numbers 16:1](bible://nm/16/1)) together as a typological triad representing quintessential adversaries of Israel.
* The Quran presents this homiletic triad within a single historical setting, placing Pharaoh, Haman, and Qārūn as contemporaries in Egypt confronting Moses ([Quran 28:38](quran://28/38), [Quran 29:39](quran://29/39), [Quran 40:24](quran://40/24); cf. [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 29:39](ibnkathir://29/39)).

#### C. The *Story of Aḥiqar* and Tobit 14:10 (The Sky-Tower in Egypt Built of Bricks and Clay)

The literary bridge explaining how Haman came to be associated with Egypt and the construction of an elevated tower for Pharaoh is the **Story of Aḥiqar**—an Aramaic wisdom narrative originating in the 5th century BC (attested in the Elephantine papyri) that circulated widely across the Near East in Syriac, Arabic, and Armenian recensions:
1. **Pharaoh's Sky-Tower Challenge:** In the narrative, the Pharaoh of Egypt sends a diplomatic challenge to the King of Assyria, demanding: *"Send me a master builder who can build me a castle (or tower, Syriac bīrtā / Arabic qaṣr) suspended between heaven and earth."*
2. **The Identification of Haman with Aḥiqar's Nephew ([Tobit 14:10](bible://tb/14/10)):** In the Aramaic original, Aḥiqar's nephew is named *Nadan*. However, in the Greek and Syriac transmissions of the Book of Tobit—which directly cites this narrative in [Tobit 14:10](bible://tb/14/10)—the nephew's name is rendered as **Aman** or **Haman** (Greek `Ἀμάν` / `Ἁμάν`, the exact spelling of Haman in the Septuagint): *"Remember, my child, what Aman did to Achiacharus [Aḥiqar] who had reared him... but Aman fell into the snare and perished."*
3. **Ascending with Bricks and Clay Mortar in Egypt:** In the *Story of Aḥiqar*, the sage travels to Egypt to answer Pharaoh's challenge. He trains young boys to ascend on eagles carrying building materials—specifically **bricks and clay mortar** (Syriac *ṭīnā*)—calling down to Pharaoh's masons to supply more mortar and bricks for the sky-tower. Pharaoh ultimately acknowledges that the construction of such a tower between earth and heaven cannot be completed.

In pre-Islamic Near Eastern oral transmission, these three narrative streams converged: Pharaoh's challenge to build a tower between heaven and earth with bricks and clay (from *Aḥiqar*), the court minister Haman (from *Esther* and *Tobit*), and the kiln-fired brick construction of a sky-tower to reach the heavens (from *Genesis 11* and Midrashic Babel traditions) combined into the proclamation of [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38).

---

### 5. Scholarly Evaluation of Modern Harmonizations

Modern concordist commentators frequently propose three alternative readings to harmonize [Quran 28:38](quran://28/38) with Egyptian history. Each proposal encounters significant textual and archaeological difficulties:

#### 1. The "Rhetorical Sarcasm / Satire" Reading
* **Proposed Harmonization:** Some modern writers argue that Pharaoh never intended to build a physical tower; rather, his command to Haman was a sarcastic, rhetorical remark meant to mock Moses's belief in an unseen transcendent God.
* **Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:** This reading is not supported by the Quranic text itself. In [Quran 40:37](quran://40/37), the Quran characterizes Pharaoh's tower initiative as an actual undertaking: *"Thus was made fair-seeming to Pharaoh the evil of his deed, and he was averted from the path; and the plot of Pharaoh was only in ruin (`wa-mā kaydu Firʿawna illā fī tabāb`)."* The terms *kayd* (practical plot/scheme) and *sūʾu ʿamalihi* (evil physical undertaking) denote an executed project rather than a figure of speech. Furthermore, the testimony of classical Islamic exegetes in [Tafsir al-Tabari 28:38](tabari://28/38) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 28:38](ibnkathir://28/38) (alongside [Tafsir al-Tabari 40:37](tabari://40/37) and [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 40:36](ibnkathir://40/36)) affirms that the tower was physically constructed of baked bricks and ended in ruin, with al-Ṭabarī further recording Pharaoh's ascent to its summit.

#### 2. The Appeal to Minor Burnt Bricks at Egyptian Sites
* **Proposed Harmonization:** Concordist commentators often point to archaeological discoveries of occasional burnt bricks in New Kingdom Egypt—such as minor paving tiles or drainage conduits found at Qantir (Pi-Ramesses)—to argue that the Quran accurately identified an attested New Kingdom building practice.
* **Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:** This argument conflates localized utilitarian brickwork with monumental royal architecture. As established by architectural surveys (A. J. Spencer, *Brick Architecture in Ancient Egypt*, AD 1979; Barry Kemp, *Ancient Egypt: Anatomy of a Civilization*, AD 2006), the rare presence of burnt bricks in localized wet environments (such as well linings or drainage gullies) does not support the construction of monumental towers or royal palaces from kiln-fired clay. In Egyptian architecture, monumental structures were exclusively built of quarried stone, while monumental brick structures were exclusively unbaked sun-dried mudbrick. Kiln-baking an entire sky-tower (*ṣarḥ*) remains unattested in ancient Egypt and reflects the Mesopotamian architectural tradition.

#### 3. The Maurice Bucaille Epigraphic and Phonetic Incompatibility
* **Proposed Harmonization:** Secondary literature frequently cites Maurice Bucaille's proposal that a 19th-Dynasty inscription in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna (Inv. Nr. ÄS 109) records Pharaoh's master quarryman named "Haman."
* **Primary-Source & Empirical Assessment:** The Vienna doorjamb inscription actually reads **`ḥmn-ḥ (?)`**, an established abbreviation of **`ḥmn-ḥtp`** (*Ḥemen-ḥotep*, meaning "The falcon-god Hemen is gracious"), as documented in Hermann Ranke's *Die Ägyptischen Personennamen* (AD 1935, Vol. I, p. 240, nos. 25–26). Bucaille omitted the final glyphs of the compound theophoric name, isolating only the first element to propose a correspondence with "Haman."
* Furthermore, the phonetic systems of Ancient Egyptian and Semitic languages strictly distinguish between the voiceless pharyngeal fricative **`ḥ`** (Egyptian twisted flax Gardiner V28, Arabic *ḥāʾ* **ح**) and the voiceless glottal fricative **`h`** (Egyptian reed shelter Gardiner O4, Arabic *hāʾ* **ه** / Hebrew *he* **ה**). Quranic *Hāmān* (هامان) and Biblical *Hāmān* (הָמָן) begin with glottal **`h`**, whereas the Egyptian name begins with pharyngeal **`ḥ`** (*Ḥemen*). Similarly, the Egyptian priestly title *ḥm-nṯr* ("servant of the god") contracted in Coptic into **`ϩⲟⲛⲧ`** (*hont*), and the god Amun (*Jmn*) was transcribed into Northwest Semitic with an initial aleph (**ʾĀmôn** in [Jeremiah 46:25](bible://jer/46/25) and [Nahum 3:8](bible://na/3/8)), rendering an identification with Semitic *Hāmān* phonologically untenable.

74:30.refutation:
Proposals that [Quran 74:30](quran://74/30) (*"Over it are nineteen"*, *ʿalayhā tisʿata ʿashara*) encodes a mathematical structure based on the number 19 represent a widely discussed modern concordist hypothesis in Quranic studies. First formulated in the 1970s and 1980s by biochemist Rashad Khalifa and initially circulated by writers such as Ahmed Deedat, the 'Code 19' model posited that the Quran's surahs, verses, words, and individual letters are structured around multiples of 19. Under philological, mathematical, and text-critical examination, however, this hypothesis encounters fundamental empirical discrepancies. Contextually and grammatically, [Quran 74:30](quran://74/30)–[74:31](quran://74/31) refers not to a mathematical formula, but to nineteen angelic wardens (*al-zabāniyah*) presiding over Hellfire (*Saqar*). Mathematically, the proposed counts cannot be replicated against standard concordances of the Arabic text without applying ad-hoc counting criteria and selective exclusions. From a text-critical perspective, maintaining the proposed numerical ratios required Khalifa to excise two canonical verses of the Quran ([Quran 9:128](quran://9/128)–[Quran 9:129](quran://9/129)) to preserve his divisible totals. Historically, classical exegesis ([Tafsir al-Tabari 74:31](tabari://74/31), [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 74:31](ibnkathir://74/31)) confirms that the number nineteen was already known to pre-Islamic Jewish and Christian communities from Late Antique apocalyptic and rabbinic traditions, explaining why [Quran 74:31](quran://74/31) states that mentioning nineteen would confirm the certainty of the People of the Book.
